rules.note: Ich bin zu Hause. Ich gehe nach Hause. Ich spiele im Park.

examples.de: Ich bin am Meer.
examples.en: I am at the sea.

examples.de: Ich fahre nach Japan.
examples.en: I'm going to Japan.

examples.de: Ich komme aus dem Haus.
examples.en: I'm coming out of the house.

examples.de: Ich gehe nach Hause.
examples.en: I'm going home.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich bin auf dem Wald. (treating forest like a surface)
commonMistakes.why: Wald, Park, Garten, Schwimmbad, and Berge (plural) are exceptions that use in rather than auf.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich gehe zu Hause.
commonMistakes.why: zu Hause is for static location (wo?); nach Hause is specifically used for the destination (wohin?) — this pair doesn't follow the normal zu/bei pattern.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Adjective endings before a noun: finding the 'signal'
explanation: When an adjective sits directly before a noun (der nette Mann), it needs an ending, and the key intuition is that a case/gender 'signal' must appear somewhere in the noun phrase — either on the article or, if the article doesn't clearly show it, on the adjective itself. With der/die/das, the article already carries the signal, so the adjective just adds a minimal -e. With ein, which has no ending in masculine nominative and neuter nominative/accusative, the adjective itself has to carry that missing signal, taking on the article-like ending (ein netter Mann — the -er on netter does the job der would normally do). In the masculine accusative specifically, and in the entire dative (see Unit 37), the adjective takes an extra -n regardless of which article is used. When an adjective comes after the noun (as a predicate, following sein), it takes no ending at all.

rules.rule: There's always a gender/case 'signal' somewhere — on the article (der/die/das) or, when the article doesn't show it (mainly with ein), on the adjective itself.
rules.note: der nette Mann (signal on der) vs. ein netter Mann (signal on netter)

rules.rule: In the masculine accusative, the adjective always takes an extra -n.
rules.note: den netten Mann, einen netten Mann, keinen netten Mann

rules.rule: An adjective after the noun (predicate position, after sein) never takes any ending.
rules.note: Der Mann ist nett. Die Leute sind nett.

examples.de: Der nette Mann kommt.
examples.en: The nice man is coming.

examples.de: Ich sehe einen netten Mann.
examples.en: I see a nice man. (masc. accusative)

examples.de: Das ist ein nettes Kind.
examples.en: That's a nice child. (neuter, ein carries no signal, so nettes does)

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich sehe einen nette Mann.
commonMistakes.why: Masculine accusative always adds -n to the adjective, regardless of which article is used.

commonMistakes.wrong: Der Mann ist netter. (adding an ending to a predicate adjective)
commonMistakes.why: An adjective standing alone after sein takes no ending at all — endings only apply directly before a noun.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Adjective endings extend to dative: a shortcut using the article's own ending
explanation: Extending Unit 36's 'signal' idea to the dative case, there's a useful shortcut: whenever the article itself ends in -n or -m (dem, einem, den, keinem...), the adjective automatically also gets an -n ending. This covers the entire dative case (dem netten Mann, der netten Frau — note der in dative feminine still triggers -n on the adjective) and the masculine accusative. In practice this means the dative adjective ending is almost always predictable once you know the dative article. Possessive articles (mein, dein, sein...) behave exactly like kein/ein throughout.

rules.rule: Shortcut: if the article ends in -n or -m, the adjective also gets -n.
rules.note: dem netten Mann, einem netten Kind, der netten Frau, den netten Leuten

rules.rule: This covers the whole dative case and the masculine accusative, since all their articles end in -n or -m.
rules.note: Mit meinem schönen neuen roten Fahrrad. (all three adjectives get -n because meinem ends in -m)

rules.rule: Possessive articles function exactly like kein/ein for these endings.
rules.note: mit ihrem netten Hund

examples.de: Ich fahre mit dem neuen Auto.
examples.en: I'm driving the new car.

examples.de: Wir leben mit einem intelligenten Hund.
examples.en: We live with an intelligent dog.

examples.de: Sie spielt mit den kleinen Kindern.
examples.en: She plays with the small children.

commonMistakes.wrong: mit dem neue Auto
commonMistakes.why: dem ends in -m, so the adjective automatically also needs -n — this shortcut applies throughout the dative case.

commonMistakes.wrong: mit einer faule Katze
commonMistakes.why: einer ends in -r, but dative feminine forms trigger the -n adjective ending across the whole dative case, not only after -n/-m articles specifically in this instance — the dative rule is uniform: all dative adjectives end in -n.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Forming the comparative and comparing two things: wie vs. als
explanation: The comparative form of a German adjective is built by adding -er, and this rule has no major exceptions in terms of the ending itself — though many common short adjectives also add an umlaut (jung → jünger, alt → älter). A handful of very frequent adjectives are irregular beyond just adding -er: gut → besser, viel → mehr, gern → lieber, hoch → höher (dropping the -c-), teuer → teurer (dropping its own -e-). When the comparative adjective stands directly before a noun, it still needs a full adjective ending on top of the -er. For comparing two things, German uses two different words depending on whether they're equal or not: '(genau) so...wie' for equal comparisons ('as...as'), and the comparative + 'als' for unequal comparisons ('...er than').

rules.rule: Regular comparative: adjective + -er, often with umlaut on short adjectives.
rules.note: klein → kleiner; alt → älter; jung → jünger

rules.rule: Irregular comparatives: gut → besser, viel → mehr, gern → lieber, hoch → höher, teuer → teurer.
rules.note: These must be memorized individually.

rules.rule: Equal comparison: (genau) so + adjective + wie. Unequal comparison: comparative + als.
rules.note: Auto 1 ist genauso schnell wie Auto 2. / Auto 2 ist schneller als Auto 1.

rules.rule: A comparative adjective before a noun still needs a full case/gender ending.
rules.note: das schnellere Auto

examples.de: Österreich ist größer als die Schweiz.
examples.en: Austria is bigger than Switzerland.

examples.de: Sie ist genauso alt wie ich.
examples.en: She is exactly as old as me.

examples.de: Das ist das schnellere Auto.
examples.en: That's the faster car.

commonMistakes.wrong: Er ist besser wie ich. (using wie for an unequal comparison)
commonMistakes.why: als is used for unequal comparisons with a comparative adjective; wie is reserved for equal comparisons (so...wie).

commonMistakes.wrong: guter (as the comparative of gut)
commonMistakes.why: gut has a fully irregular comparative form, not a regular -er ending.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: und, aber, oder, denn — connectors that don't count toward word order
explanation: Four common connectors — und, aber, oder, denn — join two main clauses without disturbing the word order of either one. They occupy what's called 'position 0': a slot before the normal position 1, meaning the clause that follows still starts counting its own word order fresh, with its own position 1 and position 2. This is different from words like deshalb (Unit 41), which do count as position 1 and force inversion. Each of the four has a distinct logical role: aber signals contrast, denn signals a reason, und signals addition, oder signals an alternative. When both clauses share the same subject or other repeated element, that repeated part can often be dropped after und, oder, or aber.

rules.rule: und (addition), aber (contrast), oder (alternative), denn (reason) sit in 'position 0' — the clause after them keeps its own normal position 1/position 2 order.
rules.note: Ich habe kein Fahrrad, aber wir haben zwei Autos. (wir stays in position 1, haben in position 2)

rules.rule: Because these don't occupy a counted position, the subject of the second clause is not pushed anywhere — it stays exactly where it would be in a standalone sentence.
rules.note: Contrast this with Unit 41's connectors, which do occupy position 1.

rules.rule: Repeated elements can be dropped after und, oder, aber.
rules.note: Ich möchte mit dir essen gehen und (ich möchte mit dir) einen Film sehen.

examples.de: Ich habe kein Fahrrad, aber wir haben zwei Autos.
examples.en: I don't have a bike, but we have two cars.

examples.de: Wir haben zwei Autos, denn wir mögen Autos.
examples.en: We have two cars because we like cars.

examples.de: Möchtest du meinen Porsche oder willst du seinen Ferrari?
examples.en: Would you like my Porsche or do you want his Ferrari?

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich habe kein Fahrrad, aber haben wir zwei Autos. (inverting word order after aber)
commonMistakes.right: Ich habe kein Fahrrad, aber wir haben zwei Autos.
commonMistakes.why: aber sits in 'position 0' and doesn't count toward word order — the following clause keeps its normal subject-verb order, no inversion.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: deshalb, sonst, dann, danach — connectors that DO count as position 1
explanation: Unlike und/aber/oder/denn (Unit 40), the connectors deshalb, sonst, dann, and danach actually occupy position 1 of the clause they introduce — which means the verb must immediately follow in position 2, and the subject gets pushed to position 3. This is a common source of word-order mistakes precisely because these words look similar in function to the Unit 40 group but behave differently grammatically. Each carries a distinct meaning: deshalb expresses a consequence ('therefore'), sonst expresses a conditional warning ('otherwise, if not...then'), and dann/danach express a time sequence ('then/after that').

rules.rule: deshalb, sonst, dann, danach occupy position 1 — the verb follows immediately in position 2, and the subject moves to position 3.
rules.note: Ich brauche Geld. Deshalb arbeite ich.

rules.rule: deshalb = consequence; sonst = 'otherwise, if not...'; dann/danach = time sequence.
rules.note: Ich brauche Geld, sonst kann ich nichts einkaufen. / Zuerst gehe ich einkaufen, dann koche ich.

examples.de: Mein Fernseher ist kaputt. Deshalb gehe ich ins Kino.
examples.en: My TV is broken. That's why I'm going to the cinema.

examples.de: Geh doch bitte einkaufen, sonst haben wir heute Abend nichts zu essen.
examples.en: Please go shopping, otherwise we'll have nothing to eat tonight.

examples.de: Morgens trinkt er einen Kaffee. Dann fährt er drei Stationen mit der U-Bahn.
examples.en: In the morning he drinks a coffee. Then he takes the subway three stops.

commonMistakes.wrong: Deshalb ich arbeite. (keeping subject before verb)
commonMistakes.why: deshalb takes position 1, so the verb must come immediately after it (position 2), pushing the subject to position 3 — unlike aber/denn/und/oder in Unit 40.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Subordinate clauses: verb goes to the end
explanation: Subordinate clauses (Nebensätze) attach to a main clause with a conjunction and follow a completely different word order rule: the conjugated verb moves all the way to the end of the clause, rather than sitting in position 2. Separable verbs stay joined together as one word at that final position, since there's no reason to split them once the whole verb unit is already at the end. Each conjunction answers a different implicit question: dass answers 'was?' (introducing a that-clause, often after verbs like glauben, sagen, wissen), wenn answers 'wann?' (a temporal or conditional trigger), and weil answers 'warum?' (a reason). If the Nebensatz comes first in the sentence, it occupies the entire position 1 as a single block, and the main clause's verb follows immediately in position 2 — producing a distinctive 'verb, verb' sequence at the comma. In practice, wenn-clauses often lead the sentence this way, while weil- and dass-clauses rarely do.

rules.rule: In a Nebensatz, the conjugated verb goes to the very end of the clause; separable verbs stay joined together there.
rules.note: ..., weil ich meinen Freund abholen will.

rules.rule: dass = answers 'was?'; wenn = answers 'wann?'; weil = answers 'warum?'
rules.note: Ich glaube, dass er kommt. / Er ruft an, wenn er ankommt. / Ich gehe, weil ich ihn abholen will.

rules.rule: If the Nebensatz opens the sentence, it fills position 1 entirely, and the main verb follows immediately — a 'verb, verb' pattern at the comma.
rules.note: Wenn er Zeit hat, geht er ins Theater. (Nebensatz = position 1; geht = position 2)

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass mein Freund heute kommt.
examples.en: I think my friend is coming today.

examples.de: Er geht zum Arzt, weil er Rückenschmerzen hat.
examples.en: He's going to the doctor because he has back pain.

examples.de: Wenn er Zeit hat, geht er ins Theater.
examples.en: If/when he has time, he goes to the theater.

commonMistakes.wrong: ..., weil ich will meinen Freund abholen.
commonMistakes.right: ..., weil ich meinen Freund abholen will.
commonMistakes.why: In a Nebensatz, the conjugated verb (will) must move to the very end, not stay in position 2 as it would in a main clause.

commonMistakes.wrong: Wenn er Zeit hat, er geht ins Theater. (not inverting after the Nebensatz)
commonMistakes.right: Wenn er Zeit hat, geht er ins Theater.
commonMistakes.why: The whole Nebensatz counts as position 1, so the main clause verb must come immediately after the comma, pushing the subject after it.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: vorn/hinten/oben/unten and their nach- direction forms; da/dort vs. dahin/dorthin
explanation: A small set of adverbs describe position without any preposition or noun: vorn(e), hinten, oben, unten, rechts, links — these answer 'wo?' and stand completely on their own. To turn them into direction (answering 'wohin?'), German just adds 'nach' in front: nach vorne, nach hinten, nach oben, nach unten, nach rechts, nach links — importantly, 'nach' here is not functioning as one of the regular prepositions from Unit 31; these combinations are fixed adverb phrases. Separately, da and dort both mean 'there' and replace a previously mentioned location (wo?), while dahin and dorthin mean 'to there' and replace a previously mentioned destination (wohin?) — matching a place that was introduced with 'nach'. da can also be used temporally, meaning 'at that point in time'.

rules.rule: Location-only adverbs (no preposition, no noun): vorn(e), hinten, oben, unten, rechts, links.
rules.note: Ich bin vorne. Wir sind hinten.

rules.rule: Add nach for direction: nach vorne, nach hinten, nach oben, nach unten, nach rechts, nach links.
rules.note: Komm nach vorne! Geh nach hinten!

rules.rule: da/dort = there (replaces a location, wo?); dahin/dorthin = to there (replaces a destination, wohin?)
rules.note: Er ist in Berlin. Dort/Da trifft er seine Familie. / Ich fahre nach Berlin. Fährst du auch dorthin?

examples.de: Die Berge sind oben.
examples.en: The mountains are up there.

examples.de: Bitte geh nach hinten.
examples.en: Please go to the back.

examples.de: Ich fahre nach Berlin. Kommst du auch dahin?
examples.en: I'm going to Berlin. Are you coming there too?

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich gehe oben. (using the static adverb for a direction)
commonMistakes.why: oben alone describes a static location; expressing movement toward it requires adding nach.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich fahre nach Berlin. Kommst du auch da?
commonMistakes.why: da/dort replaces a static location; a destination that was introduced with nach needs dahin/dorthin instead.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: denn, doch, mal — unstressed words that shift tone, not meaning
explanation: German modal particles add tone and attitude to a sentence without changing its factual content, and they're never stressed when spoken. denn in a question makes it sound more personal or genuinely curious ('Was ist denn hier passiert?' feels more engaged than the bare question). doch in a statement implies 'I think you already know this, and I'm a bit annoyed or disappointed about it' — a mild reproach. doch (or doch mal) in a command softens it, making it sound friendlier and less like an order. mal, in both commands and statements, makes the request or claim feel less binding or more casual — 'Ich rufe dich mal an' sounds like a loose maybe, while 'Ich rufe dich an' sounds definite. Two of these words, denn and doch, also have entirely separate grammatical jobs elsewhere: denn can be the coordinating conjunction meaning 'because' (Unit 40), and doch can be the special 'yes' that contradicts a negative question (Unit 10).

rules.rule: denn in questions = makes the question more personal/curious.
rules.note: Was ist denn passiert?

rules.rule: doch in statements = implies mild reproach ('you should already know this'); doch (mal) in commands = softens/friendlier tone.
rules.note: Das geht doch nicht! / Helfen Sie doch bitte.

rules.rule: mal in commands/statements = makes it feel less binding, more casual.
rules.note: Ich rufe dich mal an. (loosely, if I get around to it) vs. Ich rufe dich an. (definitely)

rules.rule: Particles are never stressed in speech, and denn/doch also have separate, unrelated grammatical roles (denn = 'because'; doch = contradicting 'yes').
rules.note: Don't confuse the particle doch with the answer doch.

examples.de: Wann kommst du denn?
examples.en: So when are you actually coming?

examples.de: Du kannst doch nicht mit Flipflops ins Theater gehen!
examples.en: You can't seriously go to the theater in flip-flops!

examples.de: Kannst du mir das mal zeigen?
examples.en: Could you show me that sometime?

commonMistakes.wrong: Stressing denn/doch/mal when speaking, treating them like normal content words
commonMistakes.right: Keep particles unstressed — the emphasis stays on the main content word in the sentence.
commonMistakes.why: Particles carry tone, not new information, so stressing them changes the intended meaning or sounds unnatural.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Building new nouns with -chen/-lein, -er, -in, -ung, and infinitives-as-nouns
explanation: German has several productive suffixes for turning existing words into new nouns, each with predictable gender and plural behavior. Noun + -chen or -lein makes a diminutive (something small), always neuter, with no separate plural form, often adding an umlaut (Haus → Häuschen). Verb stem + -er creates a noun for a male person who does the action, or a device/machine that does it, always masculine, no separate plural, often with umlaut (rechnen → der Taschenrechner). A country name + -er creates a masculine noun for a male person from that country, often with umlaut (die Schweiz → der Schweizer). A masculine person-noun + -in creates the female form, always feminine, with plural -nen (der Physiker → die Physikerin) — with two exceptions worth noting: der Deutsche/die Deutsche uses adjective-style endings instead of -in, and der Gast has no separate feminine form at all. Verb stem + -ung creates an abstract noun, always feminine, plural -en (einladen → die Einladung). Using a bare infinitive as a noun always makes it neuter with no plural, and it's frequently used without an article or with a preposition (das Tanzen; beim Tanzen; zum Tanzen).

rules.rule: -chen/-lein: always das, no plural, often umlaut (diminutive).
rules.note: das Haus → das Häuschen

rules.rule: Verb stem + -er: male person or device/machine, always der, no plural, often umlaut.
rules.note: rechnen → der Taschenrechner; Fußball spielen → der Fußballspieler

rules.rule: Country + -er: male person from that country, always der, often umlaut.
rules.note: die Schweiz → der Schweizer

rules.rule: Male person + -in: female version, always die, plural -nen. Exceptions: der Deutsche/die Deutsche (adjective pattern), der Gast (no female form).
rules.note: der Ausländer → die Ausländerin

rules.rule: Verb stem + -ung: abstract noun, always die, plural -en.
rules.note: sich verspäten → die Verspätung

rules.rule: Infinitive as noun: always das, no plural, often used without an article or with a preposition.
rules.note: Beim Tanzen bin ich glücklich.

examples.de: das Städtchen
examples.en: the small town

examples.de: der Taschenrechner
examples.en: the calculator

examples.de: die Physikerin
examples.en: the (female) physicist

examples.de: die Einladung
examples.en: the invitation

commonMistakes.wrong: der Häuschen
commonMistakes.why: The -chen ending always makes a noun neuter, regardless of the base word's original gender.

commonMistakes.wrong: die Deutschin (forming the female form of Deutscher with -in)
commonMistakes.why: der Deutsche is an exception: it's grammatically an adjective used as a noun, so its female form follows adjective endings (die Deutsche), not the regular -in pattern.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: The superlative: der/die/das ...ste(n) before a noun, am ...sten with a verb
explanation: The superlative has two forms depending on where it sits in the sentence. Before a noun, it always uses a definite article plus the adjective with -ste(n) and a normal adjective ending: der schnellste Mann. With a verb (no noun involved, describing how an action is performed), it uses am + adjective + -sten, and this am-form never changes regardless of gender or number: Er läuft am schnellsten; Sie sind am schnellsten. The same irregular comparatives from Unit 38 carry through here with matching irregularities (gut → am besten, viel → am meisten, gern → am liebsten, hoch → am höchsten, teuer → am teuersten), and the same adjectives that take an umlaut in the comparative also take it in the superlative (kurz → kürzer → am kürzesten). One spelling rule: adjectives ending in t, d, s, sch, x, or z add an extra -e before -ste(n) for pronounceability (härtesten, kürzeste).

rules.rule: Before a noun: der/die/das + adjective + -ste(n) + normal adjective ending. With a verb: am + adjective + -sten (invariable).
rules.note: Das ist der schnellste Mann. / Er läuft am schnellsten.

rules.rule: Same irregulars as the comparative: gut → am besten, viel → am meisten, gern → am liebsten, hoch → am höchsten, teuer → am teuersten.
rules.note: Memorize alongside Unit 38's comparative irregulars.

rules.rule: Adjectives ending in t/d/s/sch/x/z add -este(n) instead of just -ste(n).
rules.note: hart → am härtesten; kurz → der kürzeste Weg

examples.de: Die schnellsten Sportler kommen aus Jamaika.
examples.en: The fastest athletes come from Jamaica.

examples.de: Sie sind am schnellsten.
examples.en: They are the fastest.

examples.de: Das Kleid ist zwar am teuersten, aber ich finde es nicht am schönsten.
examples.en: The dress is the most expensive, but I don't find it the prettiest.

commonMistakes.wrong: die am schnellsten Leute
commonMistakes.why: am + -sten is only used with a verb, never combined with an article before a noun — before a noun it's just der/die/das + -ste(n).

commonMistakes.wrong: am kurzsten
commonMistakes.why: kurz both takes an umlaut and needs the extra -e- (t-ending) for pronounceability, matching its irregular comparative kürzer.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Building the simple past for regular and irregular verbs; when to use it
explanation: Regular (weak) verbs form the Präteritum by adding -te, -test, -te, -ten, -tet, -ten to the stem — the same endings across every regular verb, with an extra -e- inserted for stems ending in -d or -t for pronounceability (arbeiten → arbeitete, baden → badete). Irregular (strong) verbs change their stem vowel and use a different, unpredictable set of forms that must be memorized individually (kommen → kam, the appendix lists them from page 214) — note the ich- and er/sie/es-forms are identical with no ending at all. A handful of mixed verbs combine a vowel change with the weak -te ending: denken → dachte, bringen → brachte, nennen → nannte, wissen → wusste. In terms of usage: Präteritum is the standard tense for narrating the past in writing (stories, news, formal writing), while Perfekt is preferred in speech and everyday writing like emails — except that modal verbs, sein, and haben are spoken in Präteritum even in casual conversation (see Unit 28), and wusste, fand, es ging, es gab are also commonly used in speech.

rules.rule: Regular verbs: stem + -te, -test, -te, -ten, -tet, -ten (extra -e- after d/t stems).
rules.note: sagen → sagte; arbeiten → arbeitete

rules.rule: Irregular verbs: unpredictable stem change, memorized individually; ich and er/sie/es share the same form with no ending.
rules.note: kommen → kam, kamst, kam, kamen, kamt, kamen

rules.rule: Mixed verbs: vowel change + weak -te ending: denken → dachte, bringen → brachte, nennen → nannte, wissen → wusste.
rules.note: These don't fit either the pure weak or pure strong pattern.

rules.rule: Präteritum is used for narrating the past in writing; Perfekt is preferred in speech, except for modal verbs, sein, haben, and a few common verbs (wusste, fand, es gab, es ging).
rules.note: See also Unit 28.

examples.de: Es waren einmal zwei Geschwister. Sie hießen Hänsel und Gretel.
examples.en: Once upon a time there were two siblings. They were called Hänsel and Gretel.

examples.de: Die Frau verkaufte ihren Mercedes.
examples.en: The woman sold her Mercedes.

examples.de: Ich wusste es nicht.
examples.en: I didn't know.

commonMistakes.wrong: badte
commonMistakes.why: Stems ending in -d need an inserted -e- before -te, matching the same rule as present tense endings.

commonMistakes.wrong: denkte
commonMistakes.why: denken is a mixed verb — it keeps a -te-style ending but changes its vowel irregularly, unlike a purely regular verb.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: The past-before-the-past: sein/haben in Präteritum + participle
explanation: The Plusquamperfekt describes something that happened even earlier than another past event already being discussed — 'the train had already left' when you arrived, for instance. It's built from sein or haben in the simple past (Präteritum) plus the past participle, using the exact same sein/haben choice as the regular perfect tense (Unit 25: motion/state-change verbs use sein, most others use haben). It's especially common in sentences with nachdem (Unit 73), where the nachdem-clause needs to describe an event one step further back in time than the main clause. Critically, the Plusquamperfekt is never used on its own — it only appears alongside another sentence that's already set in the past, to show that this particular event came before that one.

rules.rule: Plusquamperfekt = sein/haben in Präteritum (war/hatte) + past participle.
rules.note: Der Zug war schon abgefahren. / Ich hatte zu lange geschlafen.

rules.rule: Uses the same sein/haben choice as the ordinary Perfekt (Unit 25).
rules.note: war gegangen (motion) vs. hatte gemacht (most other verbs)

rules.rule: Only used alongside another past-tense sentence, to show one event happened before the other — never standalone.
rules.note: Ich hatte die Treppe geputzt, da kamen die Kinder mit schmutzigen Schuhen.

examples.de: Ich bin zu spät gekommen, denn ich hatte zu lange geschlafen.
examples.en: I arrived too late because I had slept too long.

examples.de: Der Zug war schon abgefahren.
examples.en: The train had already left.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich hatte zu lange geschlafen. (used as a standalone statement about the past, with no other past event referenced)
commonMistakes.right: Reserve Plusquamperfekt for when a second past-tense event is also mentioned; otherwise use Perfekt or Präteritum.
commonMistakes.why: Plusquamperfekt only makes sense in relation to another past event — it shows relative sequencing, not just 'something happened in the past'.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: When the reflexive pronoun switches to dative: if there's already an accusative object
explanation: From Unit 29 you know the reflexive pronoun normally matches the accusative pronoun (mich, dich, sich...). But when the sentence already has a separate accusative object — like a body part in 'Ich wasche mir die Hände' (I wash my hands, literally 'I wash to-myself the hands') — the reflexive pronoun switches to dative instead, since the accusative slot is already taken by the other object. Only the 1st and 2nd person singular/plural actually change form (mich→mir, dich→dir, uns/euch stay the same); the 3rd person and Sie-form already use 'sich' for both cases, so nothing changes there. A handful of verbs always use the dative reflexive pronoun because they inherently pair with an accusative object or a following clause: sich etwas kaufen, sich etwas wünschen, sich etwas aussuchen, sich etwas vorstellen, sich etwas vornehmen.

rules.rule: If the sentence already has an accusative object, the reflexive pronoun becomes dative.
rules.note: Ich wasche mich. (no other object → accusative) vs. Ich wasche mir die Hände. (die Hände is accusative, so mir is dative)

rules.rule: Only mich/dich change to mir/dir; wir/ihr-forms (uns/euch) and 3rd person/Sie (sich) stay the same in both cases.
rules.note: Zieh dir eine Jacke an. (dir, because eine Jacke is accusative)

rules.rule: Some verbs always take a dative reflexive pronoun because they inherently combine with an accusative object or clause: sich etwas kaufen, sich etwas wünschen, sich etwas aussuchen, sich etwas vorstellen, sich etwas vornehmen.
rules.note: Ich kann mir nicht vorstellen, dass...

examples.de: Ich kämme mir die Haare.
examples.en: I'm combing my hair.

examples.de: Wasch dir die Hände!
examples.en: Wash your hands!

examples.de: Beim Sport habe ich mir die Hand verletzt.
examples.en: I hurt my hand playing sports.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich wasche mich die Hände.
commonMistakes.why: die Hände is already the accusative object, so the reflexive pronoun must switch to dative — it can't also be accusative.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: A full comparison table: how separable and inseparable verbs behave across every tense and structure
explanation: This unit pulls together everything about separable vs. inseparable verbs into one side-by-side comparison across every context you'll need them in. In the present tense, separable verbs split their prefix to the end while inseparable ones stay whole. In the perfect tense, separable verbs insert ge- between prefix and stem, while inseparable ones (be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, ver-, zer- — always inseparable) skip ge- entirely. In the Präteritum, separable verbs still split the prefix to the end. With a modal verb, both types stay as one word in the infinitive at the end of the clause. In a subordinate clause, both types stay together as one word at the very end, since the whole verb belongs there anyway. The one genuinely new piece here is the zu + infinitive construction (Unit 68 covers this in general): separable verbs insert zu between the prefix and the base verb (einzukaufen), while inseparable verbs simply put zu in front as normal (zu bestellen).

rules.rule: Present/Präteritum, main clause: separable verbs split (prefix at the end); inseparable verbs stay whole.
rules.note: Ich kaufe heute ein. / Ich bestelle heute Pizza.

rules.rule: Perfect tense: separable verbs insert ge- between prefix and stem; inseparable verbs (be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, ver-, zer-) never take ge- at all.
rules.note: eingekauft / bestellt (no ge-)

rules.rule: zu + infinitive: separable verbs insert zu between prefix and stem; inseparable verbs put zu directly in front.
rules.note: einzukaufen / zu bestellen

rules.rule: Modal verb or subordinate clause: both types stay together as one word.
rules.note: Ich möchte einkaufen. / ..., weil ich einkaufe.

examples.de: Ich habe gestern eingekauft.
examples.en: I went shopping yesterday.

examples.de: Ich habe Lust, heute einzukaufen.
examples.en: I feel like going shopping today.

examples.de: Ich habe viel Zeit, weil ich heute einkaufe.
examples.en: I have a lot of time because I'm shopping today.

commonMistakes.wrong: zu einkaufen
commonMistakes.why: For separable verbs, zu is inserted inside the word, between the prefix and the stem — it doesn't go in front of the whole verb.

commonMistakes.wrong: bestellen zu
commonMistakes.why: Inseparable verbs place zu normally in front, exactly like any single-word verb.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Fixed verb+preposition combinations, and the wo(r)-/preposition+wen/wem question words
explanation: Many German verbs pair with a specific preposition whose meaning can't be guessed and must be learned together with the verb, like a single vocabulary unit — sich freuen über, sich interessieren für, warten auf, denken an. The object of that preposition follows normal case rules, but knowing which preposition goes with which verb has no shortcut besides memorization (the book's appendix, p.213, lists common ones). To ask about the object of one of these fixed prepositions, the question word depends on whether you're asking about a thing or a person: for things, use wo(r) + preposition, inserting an extra -r- when the preposition starts with a vowel (worauf, woran); for people, use preposition + wen (accusative) or wem (dative) — für wen, von wem. In casual spoken German, many speakers also just use preposition + was for things instead of the wo(r)-form.

rules.rule: Verb + fixed preposition combinations must be learned together as a unit; the following object still takes the case that preposition normally requires.
rules.note: sich freuen über + Akkusativ; warten auf + Akkusativ; träumen von + Dativ

rules.rule: Question word for a thing: wo(r) + preposition (add -r- before a vowel).
rules.note: Worauf wartest du? Wofür interessierst du dich?

rules.rule: Question word for a person: preposition + wen (accusative) or wem (dative).
rules.note: Auf wen wartest du? Von wem träumst du?

examples.de: Sie freut sich über die Blumen.
examples.en: She's happy about the flowers.

examples.de: Ich interessiere mich für Politik.
examples.en: I'm interested in politics.

examples.de: Worauf wartest du?
examples.en: What are you waiting for?

examples.de: Auf wen wartest du?
examples.en: Who are you waiting for?

commonMistakes.wrong: Wofür wartest du? (asking about a person)
commonMistakes.why: wo(r)-question words are only for things; for people, the preposition combines with wen/wem instead.

commonMistakes.wrong: Sie freut sich für die Blumen.
commonMistakes.right: Sie freut sich über die Blumen.
commonMistakes.why: sich freuen pairs specifically with über, not für — the preposition has to be memorized with the verb.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: da(r) + preposition replaces things (and can introduce a clause); preposition + pronoun replaces people
explanation: When you want to refer back to a thing (not a person) that's the object of a fixed preposition, German uses da(r) + preposition — inserting the extra -r- before a vowel, just like with the wo(r)-question words. This works for place references (daneben = next to that/it), time references (danach = after that), and as a stand-in pronoun for a thing tied to a verb+preposition combination (dafür = for it/that, replacing 'für + thing'). For people, you don't use da(r)-forms at all; you use the preposition plus a normal personal pronoun instead. da(r)-forms can also introduce an entire following clause, functioning like a placeholder that gets explained afterward (Ich interessiere mich dafür, dass...).

rules.rule: da(r) + preposition replaces a thing (add -r- before a vowel-initial preposition).
rules.note: daneben, danach, dafür, darauf

rules.rule: For people, use preposition + personal pronoun instead of a da(r)-form.
rules.note: Interessierst du dich für Woody Allen? Ja, ich interessiere mich für ihn. (not: dafür)

rules.rule: da(r)-forms can introduce a following subordinate clause.
rules.note: Interessierst du dich dafür, welche Filmstars kommen?

examples.de: Links daneben ist das Kino.
examples.en: Right next to it is the cinema.

examples.de: Ich muss erst essen. Danach können wir gehen.
examples.en: I need to eat first. After that we can go.

examples.de: Interessierst du dich für Filme? Ja, ich interessiere mich sehr dafür.
examples.en: Are you interested in films? Yes, I'm very interested in that.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich interessiere mich dafür. (referring to a person, Woody Allen)
commonMistakes.why: da(r)-forms are only used for things; people always use preposition + personal pronoun.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: würde + infinitive for most verbs; special short forms for sein, haben, and modals
explanation: Konjunktiv 2 is built for most verbs with würde (itself the Konjunktiv 2 of werden, conjugated: würde, würdest, würde, würden, würdet, würden) plus the infinitive at the end of the clause — a structure that works for essentially any verb. But sein, haben, and the modal verbs have their own shorter, more idiomatic forms that are strongly preferred over their würde-equivalents: sein → wäre, haben → hätte, können → könnte, wollen → wollte, müssen → müsste, dürfen → dürfte, sollen → sollte. These forms are built from the Präteritum stem (Unit 49/27) with the umlaut restored (unlike the indicative Präteritum, which drops the umlaut — compare können's Präteritum konnte with its Konjunktiv 2 könnte) plus the endings -e, -(e)st, -e, -en, -(e)t, -en.

rules.rule: Most verbs: würde (conjugated) + infinitive at the end.
rules.note: Ich würde gerne tanzen.

rules.rule: sein → wäre, haben → hätte — always preferred over würde sein/würde haben.
rules.note: Ich wäre gerne glücklich. (not: Ich würde gerne glücklich sein)

rules.rule: Modal verbs use their own short forms: könnte, wollte, müsste, dürfte, sollte — built from the Präteritum stem with the umlaut restored.
rules.note: Wenn ich tanzen könnte, würde ich sie fragen.

examples.de: Wenn ich den Mut hätte, würde ich sie fragen.
examples.en: If I had the courage, I would ask her.

examples.de: Ich wäre gerne glücklich.
examples.en: I would love to be happy.

examples.de: Könntest du mir helfen?
examples.en: Could you help me?

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich würde haben mehr Zeit.
commonMistakes.why: haben has its own short Konjunktiv 2 form (hätte), which German strongly prefers over the würde-construction.

commonMistakes.wrong: ich könte (missing umlaut)
commonMistakes.why: Konjunktiv 2 restores the umlaut that the ordinary Präteritum (konnte) drops.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Five everyday uses: wishes, unreal conditions, politeness, advice, suggestions
explanation: Konjunktiv 2 shows up in five common, everyday situations, all connected by the idea of something not being real or certain. As a wish, it often pairs with gerne/lieber/am liebsten (Er hätte gerne einen Porsche). As an unreal (hypothetical) condition, it appears in both the wenn-clause and the main clause of a conditional sentence (Wenn ich viel Geld hätte, wäre ich glücklich). As a politeness marker, it softens a request, making könnten/würden feel noticeably more polite than the plain present tense (Könnten Sie mir helfen?). With the modal verb sollen specifically, Konjunktiv 2 is used to give advice (Du solltest früher schlafen gehen). With können, it's used to make a casual suggestion (Wir könnten ins Kino gehen).

rules.rule: Wish: Konjunktiv 2, often with gerne/lieber/am liebsten.
rules.note: Er hätte gerne einen Porsche.

rules.rule: Unreal condition: Konjunktiv 2 in both the wenn-clause and the main clause.
rules.note: Wenn ich viel Geld hätte, wäre ich glücklich.

rules.rule: Politeness: könnten/würden soften a request.
rules.note: Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?

rules.rule: Advice: sollen in Konjunktiv 2 (sollte). Suggestion: können in Konjunktiv 2 (könnte).
rules.note: Du solltest früher schlafen gehen. / Wir könnten ins Kino gehen.

examples.de: Wenn Blumen sprechen könnten, wäre es im Garten laut.
examples.en: If flowers could talk, it would be loud in the garden.

examples.de: Du solltest mehr schlafen.
examples.en: You should sleep more.

examples.de: Wir könnten heute Abend ins Kino gehen.
examples.en: We could go to the cinema tonight.

commonMistakes.wrong: Du musst mehr schlafen. (intending gentle advice)
commonMistakes.why: sollen in Konjunktiv 2 (solltest) is the natural way to give friendly advice; müssen states a hard obligation, which sounds much more forceful.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Building the passive: werden + participle; the accusative object becomes the subject
explanation: The passive voice shifts focus from who does an action to what happens to something — appropriate when the doer is unknown, obvious, or simply unimportant. It's built with werden (conjugated, position 2) plus the past participle at the end of the clause. Structurally, the accusative object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive sentence: 'Der Mechaniker montiert den Motor' (active) becomes 'Der Motor wird montiert' (passive) — den Motor, the accusative object, becomes der Motor, the new subject. The original subject (the doer) is usually dropped entirely; if you do want to mention it, add von + dative. With a modal verb, the modal takes position 2, and the sentence ends with participle + werden (as an infinitive) — this already forms a three-part verb bracket.

rules.rule: Passive = werden (position 2) + past participle (end of clause).
rules.note: Der Motor wird montiert.

rules.rule: The active sentence's accusative object becomes the passive sentence's subject; the original subject is dropped or added with von + dative.
rules.note: Der Mechaniker montiert den Motor. → Der Motor wird (von dem Mechaniker) montiert.

rules.rule: Passive with a modal verb: modal (position 2) + ... + participle + werden (infinitive, at the very end).
rules.note: Hier muss Lärmschutz getragen werden.

examples.de: Das Paket wird gesendet.
examples.en: The package is being sent.

examples.de: Die Getränke werden verkauft.
examples.en: The drinks are being sold.

examples.de: Die Pizza muss bestellt werden.
examples.en: The pizza has to be ordered.

commonMistakes.wrong: Der Motor wird den Mechaniker montiert. (keeping the original object case)
commonMistakes.right: Der Motor wird von dem Mechaniker montiert.
commonMistakes.why: The original subject, if mentioned at all, needs von + dative — it can't simply be dropped into the sentence in its old case.

commonMistakes.wrong: Hier muss werden Lärmschutz getragen.
commonMistakes.why: With a modal verb, werden moves to the very end alongside the participle, forming getragen werden as a unit — it doesn't stay near the modal.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Passive in Präteritum and Perfekt: 'worden' instead of 'geworden'
explanation: The passive extends into other tenses the same way active sentences do. In Präteritum, wurde (the simple past of werden) replaces wird: Der Kölner Dom wurde gebaut. In the perfect tense, the passive uses sein (not haben) plus the past participle plus a special form of werden's own participle: worden — not geworden, and critically without the usual ge- prefix, since 'worden' is reserved specifically for passive perfect constructions (geworden is used when werden means 'to become', as in Unit 60). Combined with a modal verb in the past, the modal itself goes into Präteritum, and the sentence still ends with participle + werden.

rules.rule: Passive Präteritum: wurde (conjugated) + participle.
rules.note: Der Kölner Dom wurde von 1248 bis 1880 gebaut.

rules.rule: Passive Perfekt: sein (conjugated) + participle + worden (not geworden, no ge-).
rules.note: Er ist lange gebaut worden.

rules.rule: Passive Präteritum with modal: modal in Präteritum + ... + participle + werden (infinitive).
rules.note: Er musste im 20. Jahrhundert renoviert werden.

examples.de: Die Zeitung wurde gelesen.
examples.en: The newspaper was read.

examples.de: Die Zeitung ist gelesen worden.
examples.en: The newspaper has been read.

examples.de: Der Verletzte musste operiert werden.
examples.en: The injured person had to be operated on.

commonMistakes.wrong: Die Zeitung ist gelesen geworden.
commonMistakes.why: The passive perfect uses worden, a special reduced form reserved for this construction — geworden is only used when werden means 'to become'.

commonMistakes.wrong: Die Zeitung hat gelesen worden.
commonMistakes.why: Passive perfect always uses sein as the helper verb, never haben, regardless of what helper the underlying active verb would normally use.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: werden + infinitive: for formal future statements, or for assumptions
explanation: Futur 1 is built with werden (conjugated) plus the infinitive at the end, and it carries two distinct meanings depending on context: a future event, or a present-tense assumption/guess. Words like wohl, vielleicht, and wahrscheinlich make the assumption reading explicit. In everyday informal speech, though, German usually just uses the present tense with a time expression to talk about the future (Ich fahre morgen nach Berlin) — Futur 1 sounds more formal and shows up more in news broadcasts, official announcements, and written predictions than in casual conversation.

rules.rule: Futur 1 = werden (position 2) + infinitive (end of clause).
rules.note: Die Schulen werden mehr Geld bekommen.

rules.rule: Meaning: future event, or a present assumption — words like wohl, vielleicht, wahrscheinlich signal the assumption reading.
rules.note: Er wird wahrscheinlich zu spät kommen. (assumption, not necessarily about the future)

rules.rule: Informal speech usually prefers present tense + time word for the future; Futur 1 is more common in formal/written contexts.
rules.note: Formal: Der Präsident wird morgen Berlin besuchen. Informal: Der Präsident kommt morgen nach Berlin.

examples.de: Die Schulen werden nächstes Jahr mehr Geld bekommen.
examples.en: The schools will get more money next year.

examples.de: Er wird wohl in ein Restaurant gehen.
examples.en: He's probably going to a restaurant.

commonMistakes.wrong: Treating every werden + infinitive sentence as strictly about the future
commonMistakes.right: Check for wohl/vielleicht/wahrscheinlich or context — it might be an assumption about the present, not a future statement.
commonMistakes.why: Futur 1 covers both future events and present-tense guesses; the two meanings are distinguished by context and by these adverbs, not by the grammar itself.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: werden's three jobs: normal verb ('become'), passive helper, future/assumption helper
explanation: werden does three completely different grammatical jobs, and telling them apart is mostly about what follows it. As an ordinary verb meaning 'to become', it's followed by a noun or adjective, and its perfect tense uses geworden (Ich bin Arzt geworden). As the passive helper (Unit 57–58), it's followed by a past participle, and its own perfect-tense form becomes the special reduced worden (Der Motor ist montiert worden). As the future/assumption helper (Unit 59), it's followed by an infinitive (Die Schulen werden mehr Geld bekommen). Recognizing which of the three is in play just requires looking at what comes right after werden: noun/adjective → 'become'; participle → passive; infinitive → future/assumption.

rules.rule: werden + noun/adjective = 'to become' (normal verb); Perfekt uses geworden.
rules.note: Ich werde Arzt. Ich bin Arzt geworden.

rules.rule: werden + past participle = passive; Perfekt uses worden (no ge-).
rules.note: Der Motor wird montiert. Der Motor ist montiert worden.

rules.rule: werden + infinitive = future or assumption (Futur 1).
rules.note: Die Schulen werden mehr Geld bekommen.

examples.de: Mein Sohn möchte Pilot werden.
examples.en: My son wants to become a pilot. (normal verb)

examples.de: Der Salat wird gewaschen.
examples.en: The salad is being washed. (passive)

examples.de: Das Baby muss gefüttert werden.
examples.en: The baby has to be fed. (passive with modal)

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich bin Arzt worden.
commonMistakes.why: worden is reserved for the passive perfect specifically; when werden means 'to become', its own perfect participle is geworden.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: lassen's three meanings: leave behind, allow, or have someone else do it
explanation: lassen covers three related but distinct ideas. First, leaving something behind or not taking it with you — used as a normal verb with an object, and a normal weak-verb participle in the perfect: Ich habe meinen Koffer hier gelassen. Second, allowing or permitting something — lassen + infinitive (no zu, matching Unit 69's rule): Ich lasse mein Kind nicht fernsehen. Third, having someone else do something instead of doing it yourself — same structure, lassen + infinitive: Ich lasse meine Haare schneiden. For the second and third meanings, the perfect tense uses a 'double infinitive' construction instead of the normal participle: habe + [the other verb, infinitive] + lassen (with lassen itself staying in the infinitive, not becoming gelassen) — this is a notable exception worth remembering.

rules.rule: Meaning 1 (leave behind, no other infinitive involved): normal verb, Perfekt = habe/hat + gelassen.
rules.note: Ich habe meinen Koffer hier gelassen.

rules.rule: Meaning 2 (allow) and meaning 3 (have done by someone else): lassen + infinitive (no zu).
rules.note: Ich lasse mein Kind nicht fernsehen. / Ich lasse meine Haare schneiden.

rules.rule: For meanings 2 and 3, Perfekt uses a double infinitive: habe + [verb infinitive] + lassen (lassen stays as an infinitive, not gelassen).
rules.note: Ich habe mein Kind nicht fernsehen lassen. / Ich habe meine Haare schneiden lassen.

examples.de: Kann ich meine Koffer hier lassen?
examples.en: Can I leave my bags here?

examples.de: Ich lasse mein Kind nicht fernsehen.
examples.en: I don't let my child watch TV.

examples.de: Ich habe meine Haare schneiden lassen.
examples.en: I had my hair cut.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich habe meine Haare geschnitten lassen.
commonMistakes.right: Ich habe meine Haare schneiden lassen.
commonMistakes.why: When lassen means 'have something done', the perfect tense uses the double-infinitive pattern — lassen stays an infinitive at the end, and the other verb also stays as an infinitive rather than becoming a participle.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: stellen/stehen, setzen/sitzen, legen/liegen, hängen/hängen — action vs. resulting position
explanation: German has matched pairs of verbs for describing where something is placed versus where it already sits, and this distinction doesn't exist as clearly in English. stellen (regular, weak) describes the action of placing something upright, taking an accusative object and a wohin-preposition; its resulting-position counterpart is stehen (irregular, strong: stand, gestanden), describing something already standing, with no object and a wo-preposition. The same pattern repeats for setzen/sitzen (seated position) and legen/liegen (flat/lying position). hängen is unusual: the same word covers both meanings, but it conjugates differently depending on which sense is meant — as an action verb (to hang something up) it's regular (hängte, gehängt) and takes an accusative object; as a position verb (to be hanging) it's irregular (hing, gehangen) and takes no object.

rules.rule: Action verbs (regular/weak, take accusative object, use wohin-prepositions): stellen, setzen, legen, hängen (as action).
rules.note: Er stellt die Vase auf den Tisch.

rules.rule: Position verbs (irregular/strong, no object, use wo-prepositions): stehen (stand, gestanden), sitzen (saß, gesessen), liegen (lag, gelegen), hängen (as position: hing, gehangen).
rules.note: Die Vase steht auf dem Tisch.

rules.rule: hängen uses the same infinitive for both meanings but conjugates differently depending on whether it's the action or the resulting position.
rules.note: Er hängt das Bild auf. (action, regular) / Das Bild hängt an der Wand. (position, irregular)

examples.de: Sie stellt die Vase auf den Tisch. Die Vase steht auf dem Tisch.
examples.en: She places the vase on the table. The vase is standing on the table.

examples.de: Er setzt das Kind auf den Stuhl. Das Kind sitzt auf dem Stuhl.
examples.en: He sits the child on the chair. The child is sitting on the chair.

examples.de: Die Jeans liegt auf dem Bett.
examples.en: The jeans are lying on the bed.

commonMistakes.wrong: Die Vase stellt auf dem Tisch. (using the action verb for a resulting state)
commonMistakes.right: Die Vase steht auf dem Tisch.
commonMistakes.why: Once the vase is simply positioned there with no ongoing action, the position verb (stehen) is correct, not the action verb (stellen), which needs someone actively placing it.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Showing possession: des/eines + noun+s; names take a genitive -s of their own
explanation: The genitive case shows possession or a close relationship between two nouns, roughly matching English 's or 'of'. For masculine and neuter nouns, the article becomes des/eines and the noun itself adds -s (or -es if the noun is a short/one-syllable word, or ends in s, ß, sch, x, or z, for pronounceability): des Vaters, des Mannes. Feminine and plural nouns just use der/einer with no ending added to the noun itself — and notably, plural nouns have no genitive indefinite article at all (there's no 'einer' equivalent for plural; you either use von + dative, or an adjective alone, like guter Eltern). For names, German attaches -s directly to the name with no article at all: Davids Auto — but names ending in -s or -x get an apostrophe instead of an added -s: Hans' Auto. In every case, the genitive can always be replaced with von + dative, which is common in spoken German.

rules.rule: Masculine/neuter: des/eines + noun + -s (or -es for short/s-ß-sch-x-z-ending nouns). Feminine/plural: der/einer, no ending on the noun.
rules.note: des Vaters, des Mannes, der Mutter, der Eltern

rules.rule: Plural has no genitive indefinite article; use von + dative or an adjective alone.
rules.note: von Eltern / guter Eltern (not: einer Eltern)

rules.rule: Names: attach -s directly, no article (Davids Auto); names ending in -s/-x get an apostrophe instead (Hans' Auto).
rules.note: Davids Auto = das Auto von David = das Auto seines Vaters

examples.de: Das Auto meiner Chefin
examples.en: My boss's car (fem.)

examples.de: Der Name der Straße
examples.en: The name of the street

examples.de: Judiths Bilderbuch
examples.en: Judith's picture book

commonMistakes.wrong: des Mann
commonMistakes.why: Masculine and neuter nouns in the genitive also add -s or -es to the noun itself, not just change the article.

commonMistakes.wrong: Hans's Auto
commonMistakes.why: Names already ending in -s or -x take an apostrophe instead of an additional -s.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: A group of masculine nouns that add -(e)n in every case except nominative singular
explanation: A specific group of masculine nouns — called 'n-Deklination' nouns — add -(e)n not just in the plural but also in the accusative, dative, and genitive singular, unlike ordinary masculine nouns which only change the article. This group includes: male people and animals ending in -e (der Junge, der Kollege, der Löwe); nouns ending in -and, -ant, -ent, -at, or -ist (der Student, der Doktorand, der Praktikant); a handful of abstract nouns (der Friede, der Name, der Buchstabe) which additionally add -s in the genitive specifically (des Namens); and an irregular list that must simply be memorized (der Bär, Bauer, Fürst, Graf, Held, Herr, Architekt, Mensch, Nachbar, Fotograf, Prinz, Ungar), plus one neuter exception, das Herz. In casual spoken German, the final -n is often dropped in speech even though it's grammatically expected.

rules.rule: N-Deklination nouns add -(e)n in accusative, dative, AND genitive singular (not just plural).
rules.note: der Herr → den Herrn, dem Herrn, des Herrn

rules.rule: Groups: male people/animals ending in -e; nouns with -and/-ant/-ent/-at/-ist; abstract nouns like Name/Friede/Buchstabe (which also add -s in genitive: des Namens); a memorized irregular list (Bär, Bauer, Fürst, Graf, Held, Herr, Architekt, Mensch, Nachbar, Fotograf, Prinz, Ungar) plus das Herz.
rules.note: der Student → den Studenten; der Name → des Namens

rules.rule: In spoken German the final -n is often dropped even though it's grammatically required.
rules.note: This is a spoken-register simplification, not the written standard.

examples.de: Kennen Sie den Herrn da?
examples.en: Do you know that gentleman over there?

examples.de: Ich spreche mit dem Studenten.
examples.en: I'm talking with the student.

examples.de: Das ist das Auto des Nachbarn.
examples.en: That's the neighbor's car.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich sehe den Student.
commonMistakes.why: Student is an n-Deklination noun and needs -en in the accusative singular, not just the plural.

commonMistakes.wrong: des Namen
commonMistakes.why: Name is one of the abstract n-Deklination nouns that additionally add -s in the genitive, on top of the usual -n.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Adjectives used as nouns for people: capitalized, but still declined like adjectives
explanation: Many adjectives that describe a type of person can be used directly as nouns instead — der Kranke (the sick man), instead of always saying der kranke Mann. These are capitalized like any noun, but they're declined exactly like an ordinary adjective (following the same signal-based endings from Units 36, 37, and 79), not like a regular noun. This means the same word changes its ending based on gender, case, and whether an article is present — der Kranke (with article, weak ending) versus ein Kranker (no strong signal from ein, so the adjective carries it), and this pattern extends across all four cases and both singular and plural.

rules.rule: Adjectives-as-nouns for people are capitalized but declined exactly like adjectives, not like regular nouns.
rules.note: der Jugendliche, ein Jugendlicher, die Jugendlichen (plural)

rules.rule: The same signal-based rule from adjective declension applies: with a strong article (der/die/das), the ending is minimal; with a weak/no article, the adjective carries the full signal.
rules.note: der Kranke (article carries signal) vs. ein Kranker (adjective carries it)

examples.de: Ich bin ja auch noch ein Jugendlicher!
examples.en: I'm still young too, you know!

examples.de: Mit 30 ist man schon lange ein Erwachsener.
examples.en: By 30 you've long been an adult.

examples.de: Ich spreche mit der Angestellten.
examples.en: I'm speaking with the (female) employee.

commonMistakes.wrong: der Krankee / des Krankes (treating it like a regular noun with a fixed ending)
commonMistakes.why: These words are still grammatically adjectives, so their ending changes with case and article type — they don't have one fixed noun-like form.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: alles/das Gute vs. etwas/nichts Gutes — different endings after different quantity words
explanation: Adjectives can also be turned into neuter abstract nouns, capitalized just like the person-nouns in Unit 65, but following a different, simpler ending rule based on which word comes before them. After alles or das, the adjective-noun takes just -e: alles Gute, das Beste. After etwas, nichts, viel, wenig, or ein bisschen, the adjective-noun takes -es instead: etwas Gutes, nichts Schlechtes, ein bisschen Interessantes. This pattern is used constantly in everyday fixed phrases and general statements about abstract qualities.

rules.rule: After alles/das: adjective + -e.
rules.note: Alles Gute! Das Beste kommt noch.

rules.rule: After etwas/nichts/viel/wenig/ein bisschen: adjective + -es.
rules.note: Ich wünsche dir etwas Schönes. Nichts Neues.

examples.de: Ich wünsche euch alles Gute!
examples.en: I wish you all the best!

examples.de: Die Braut trägt etwas Altes, etwas Neues.
examples.en: The bride wears something old, something new.

examples.de: Wir wünschen euch nur das Beste!
examples.en: We wish you only the best!

commonMistakes.wrong: alles Gutes
commonMistakes.why: alles takes the -e ending on the following adjective-noun, not -es, which belongs to the etwas/nichts/viel/wenig group.

commonMistakes.wrong: etwas Neue
commonMistakes.why: etwas requires the -es ending, unlike alles/das which take -e.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Embedding a question inside a polite phrase: W-word or ob, verb to the end
explanation: An indirect question embeds a question inside a more polite introductory phrase like 'Können Sie mir sagen...' or 'Ich möchte wissen...', and it behaves grammatically as a subordinate clause: the verb moves to the end. If the original question had a question word (wo, warum, wann, auf welchem Gleis...), that same word introduces the indirect question. If the original was a yes/no question with no question word, the indirect version uses ob ('whether') as the connector instead. Indirect questions are generally considered more polite than asking the direct question outright, which is why they're common with strangers or in formal requests.

rules.rule: Indirect W-question: [polite phrase], + W-word + ... + verb (end).
rules.note: Können Sie mir sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist?

rules.rule: Indirect yes/no question: [polite phrase], + ob + ... + verb (end).
rules.note: Wissen Sie, ob es noch weit ist?

rules.rule: Indirect questions are a politer way to ask than the direct form.
rules.note: Compare: Wo ist der Bahnhof? (direct, plainer) vs. Wissen Sie, wo der Bahnhof ist? (indirect, more polite)

examples.de: Können Sie mir sagen, wie viel ein Doppelzimmer kostet?
examples.en: Can you tell me how much a double room costs?

examples.de: Ich habe keine Ahnung, ob wir den Zug noch erreichen.
examples.en: I have no idea whether we'll still catch the train.

examples.de: Weißt du, ob Peter auch eingeladen ist?
examples.en: Do you know if Peter is invited too?

commonMistakes.wrong: Wissen Sie, wo ist der Bahnhof?
commonMistakes.right: Wissen Sie, wo der Bahnhof ist?
commonMistakes.why: Because the question is now embedded as a subordinate clause, the verb must move to the end, not stay in its direct-question position.

commonMistakes.wrong: Wissen Sie, es ist noch weit zum Bahnhof? (dropping ob)
commonMistakes.right: Wissen Sie, ob es noch weit zum Bahnhof ist?
commonMistakes.why: A yes/no question with no question word needs ob to introduce it as an indirect question.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: When a second verb needs zu + infinitive, and where zu goes
explanation: A second verb attached to the main clause often needs zu before its infinitive, and this happens in three main situations: after 'es ist/ich finde es' + an adjective (Es ist wunderbar, ... zu feiern); after certain abstract nouns (Ich habe die Chance, ... zu reisen; Es ist mein Traum, ...); and after specific verbs that can take a following verb (hoffen, versuchen, anfangen, aufhören, raten/empfehlen/vorschlagen). Placement of zu depends on the verb type: for a single verb, zu goes right before it; for a separable verb, zu is inserted between the prefix and the stem (anzurufen); when there are two verbs together (like spazieren gehen), zu goes before the final one; and with a modal verb involved, zu goes before the modal, since the modal itself is now the infinitive at the end. The zu-infinitive clause has no subject of its own — it shares the main clause's subject; if the two actions have different subjects, you need a dass-clause instead (Unit 42).

rules.rule: zu + infinitive appears after es ist/ich finde es + adjective; after abstract nouns (Chance, Traum, Zeit, Angst); after verbs like hoffen, versuchen, anfangen, aufhören, empfehlen.
rules.note: Es ist gefährlich, hier zu schwimmen. Ich habe die Chance, zu reisen.

rules.rule: Placement of zu: before a single verb; inside a separable verb (between prefix and stem); before the last of two verbs; before a modal verb.
rules.note: zu kochen / anzurufen / spazieren zu gehen / machen zu können

rules.rule: No subject appears in the zu-clause — it shares the main clause's subject. Different subjects require a dass-clause instead.
rules.note: Ich hoffe, pünktlich zu kommen. vs. Ich hoffe, dass er pünktlich kommt.

examples.de: Ich habe versucht, dich anzurufen.
examples.en: I tried to call you.

examples.de: Es ist gut, oft spazieren zu gehen.
examples.en: It's good to go for walks often.

examples.de: Es ist schön, viel Urlaub machen zu können.
examples.en: It's nice to be able to take a lot of vacation.

commonMistakes.wrong: zu anrufen
commonMistakes.why: With separable verbs, zu goes inside the word, between the prefix and the stem, not in front of the whole verb.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich hoffe, dass zu kommen pünktlich.
commonMistakes.why: When the subject is the same in both clauses, a plain zu-infinitive is used, not a dass-clause; dass is reserved for when the subjects differ.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Six verb groups that take a bare infinitive: modals, lassen, gehen, sehen, hören, bleiben
explanation: While most verbs that take a following infinitive need zu (Unit 68), a specific set does not. The modal verbs (müssen, können, dürfen, möchten, sollen, wollen) always take a bare infinitive, as covered back in Unit 5. Alongside them, five more verbs also take a bare infinitive: lassen (Ich lasse das Auto stehen), gehen (Ich gehe schwimmen), sehen (Ich sehe die Kinder spielen), hören (Ich höre die Nachbarin singen), and bleiben (Er bleibt sitzen). One verb, lernen, is flexible and can go either way (Das Kind lernt laufen / Das Kind lernt zu laufen). Every other verb that takes a following infinitive uses zu.

rules.rule: Bare infinitive (no zu) after: müssen, können, dürfen, möchten, sollen, wollen (modals); lassen, gehen, sehen, hören, bleiben.
rules.note: Ich sehe die Kinder spielen. Er bleibt vor dem Fernseher sitzen.

rules.rule: lernen can go either way.
rules.note: Das Kind lernt laufen. / Das Kind lernt zu laufen.

rules.rule: Every other verb taking a following infinitive uses zu (Unit 68) — these six/seven are the exceptions.
rules.note: Contrast: Ich versuche, zu kommen. (needs zu) vs. Ich sehe ihn kommen. (no zu)

examples.de: Ich gehe schwimmen.
examples.en: I'm going swimming.

examples.de: Ich höre die Nachbarin singen.
examples.en: I hear the neighbor singing.

examples.de: Er lässt seine Tochter den Film sehen.
examples.en: He lets his daughter watch the film.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich sehe die Kinder zu spielen.
commonMistakes.why: sehen is one of the verbs that takes a bare infinitive without zu, unlike most other verbs that introduce a following action.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich gehe zu schwimmen.
commonMistakes.why: gehen + activity uses a bare infinitive, not zu + infinitive.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Relative clauses: verb-final, and the relative pronoun matches the reference word's gender
explanation: A relative clause adds extra information about a noun just mentioned (the Bezugswort), using a relative pronoun that mostly looks identical to the definite article and matches that noun's gender and number. Like any subordinate clause, the conjugated verb goes to the end. The relative clause almost always follows directly after the noun it describes, which often means it sits in the middle of the main clause, splitting it in two around a pair of commas: 'Der Mann, der immer meine Nachbarin besucht, kommt heute mit Blumen.' The relative pronoun's case (nominative, accusative, or dative) depends on its role inside the relative clause itself, not on the noun it refers back to.

rules.rule: The relative pronoun matches the gender/number of the noun it refers to (the Bezugswort), and mostly looks like the definite article.
rules.note: der Mann, der ... / die Frau, die ... / das Kind, das ...

rules.rule: The relative clause is a subordinate clause: the verb goes to the end.
rules.note: ..., der immer meine Nachbarin besucht.

rules.rule: The relative clause usually sits directly after its noun, which often places it in the middle of the main clause.
rules.note: Der Mann, der immer meine Nachbarin besucht, kommt heute mit Blumen.

examples.de: Das ist der Mann, der immer meine Nachbarin besucht.
examples.en: That's the man who always visits my neighbor.

examples.de: Ist das das Kind, das so toll Geige spielen kann?
examples.en: Is that the child who can play violin so well?

examples.de: Wer ist die Frau, die das große Motorrad fährt?
examples.en: Who is the woman who rides the big motorcycle?

commonMistakes.wrong: Das ist der Mann, der besucht immer meine Nachbarin.
commonMistakes.right: Das ist der Mann, der immer meine Nachbarin besucht.
commonMistakes.why: The relative clause is a subordinate clause, so the verb must move to the very end, not stay in its main-clause position.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Relative pronouns get their gender from the noun, but their case from the verb — plus the dative plural exception
explanation: The relative pronoun's gender/number always comes from the noun it refers back to (the Bezugswort), but its case comes from what role it plays inside the relative clause — determined by the verb there, or by a preposition if one is present. When a preposition governs the relative pronoun, that preposition moves to the front of the relative clause, directly before the pronoun, and determines its case: 'Wie heißt das Ding, mit dem man Flaschen öffnen kann?' (mit requires dative, so dem, matching neuter Ding). The relative pronouns are otherwise identical to the definite article across all cases, with exactly one exception: the dative plural is denen, not den.

rules.rule: Gender/number of the relative pronoun comes from the noun it refers to; its case comes from its role in the relative clause (verb or preposition).
rules.note: Ist das der Schlüssel, den du suchst? (den = accusative, because suchst needs an accusative object)

rules.rule: A preposition governing the relative pronoun moves to the front of the relative clause and determines its case.
rules.note: Wie heißt das Ding, mit dem man Flaschen öffnen kann?

rules.rule: Relative pronouns match the definite article in every case except dative plural: denen (not den).
rules.note: Die Nachbarn, mit denen du gesprochen hast, ...

examples.de: Ist das der Schlüssel, den du seit gestern suchst?
examples.en: Is that the key you've been looking for since yesterday?

examples.de: Wie heißt das Ding, mit dem man Flaschen öffnen kann?
examples.en: What's that thing called that you can open bottles with?

examples.de: Die Nachbarn, mit denen du gerade gesprochen hast, sind erst zwei Wochen hier.
examples.en: The neighbors you were just talking with have only been here two weeks.

commonMistakes.wrong: Die Nachbarn, mit den du gesprochen hast
commonMistakes.right: Die Nachbarn, mit denen du gesprochen hast
commonMistakes.why: The dative plural relative pronoun is denen, the one case where it differs from the plain definite article den.

commonMistakes.wrong: Wie heißt das Ding, das man mit öffnen kann? (leaving the preposition stranded)
commonMistakes.right: Wie heißt das Ding, mit dem man öffnen kann?
commonMistakes.why: The preposition governing the relative pronoun must move to the front of the clause, directly before the pronoun — it can't be left at the end as in some other languages.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

topic: Temporale Nebensätze mit wenn und als
summary: wenn for present/future or repeated past events; als for a single past event
explanation: Both wenn and als introduce a time-related subordinate clause, but they're not interchangeable — the choice depends on when the event happened and whether it repeated. wenn is used for anything in the present or future, and also for repeated or habitual events in the past (often signaled by immer, jedes Mal). als is reserved specifically for a single, one-time event that's already finished in the past. This distinction trips up many learners because English 'when' covers both meanings without distinguishing them.

rules.rule: wenn: present, future, or repeated/habitual past events.
rules.note: Wenn ich mit dem Zug fahre, lese ich immer. (habitual) / Wenn du kommst, gehen wir ins Kino. (future)

rules.rule: als: a single, one-time event in the past.
rules.note: Als ich letzte Woche nach Hause gefahren bin, hielt der Zug plötzlich an.

rules.rule: A signal for the habitual-past use of wenn: words like immer, jedes Mal.
rules.note: Immer wenn ich im letzten Jahr mit dem Zug gefahren bin, habe ich gelesen.

examples.de: Wenn sie morgen Zeit hat, will sie shoppen gehen.
examples.en: If she has time tomorrow, she wants to go shopping.

examples.de: Als er letztes Jahr in unsere Stadt kam, kannte er keinen Menschen.
examples.en: When he came to our city last year, he didn't know anyone.

examples.de: Immer wenn ich nach Hause kam, hatte Marlen schon gekocht.
examples.en: Whenever I came home, Marlen had already cooked.

commonMistakes.wrong: Wenn ich letztes Jahr in die Stadt kam, kannte ich keinen Menschen. (single past event)
commonMistakes.right: Als ich letztes Jahr in die Stadt kam, kannte ich keinen Menschen.
commonMistakes.why: This describes one specific, unrepeated event in the past, which requires als, not wenn.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

topic: Temporale Nebensätze mit bevor, nachdem, während, seit(dem)
summary: Four more time conjunctions, and nachdem's strict tense-shifting rule
explanation: Four more conjunctions describe temporal relationships between two events. bevor ('before') and nachdem ('after') both connect two actions where one happens before the other; während ('while') connects two actions happening at the same time; seit(dem) ('since') marks something that began in the past and continues into the present. Like all subordinate clauses, the verb goes to the end. The one rule that needs special attention is nachdem: because it describes something that already finished before the main clause's action, the nachdem-clause must be one tense-step earlier than the main clause — if the main clause is in Präsens, the nachdem-clause uses Perfekt; if the main clause is in Perfekt or Präteritum, the nachdem-clause uses Plusquamperfekt (Unit 50).

rules.rule: bevor = before; nachdem = after; während = while (parallel actions); seit(dem) = since (began in past, continues now).
rules.note: Bevor ich frühstücke, putze ich meine Zähne. / Während ich frühstücke, höre ich Radio.

rules.rule: nachdem requires the nachdem-clause to be one tense-step earlier than the main clause.
rules.note: Nachdem ich gefrühstückt habe, mache ich Gymnastik. (Perfekt → Präsens) / Nachdem ich gefrühstückt hatte, habe ich Gymnastik gemacht. (Plusquamperfekt → Perfekt)

rules.rule: All four are subordinate clauses: verb goes to the end.
rules.note: ..., seitdem ich immer meine Zähne putze, ...

examples.de: Bevor ich ins Bett gehe, putze ich mir die Zähne.
examples.en: Before I go to bed, I brush my teeth.

examples.de: Nachdem ich gefrühstückt habe, mache ich Gymnastik.
examples.en: After I've had breakfast, I do exercises.

examples.de: Seitdem ich immer meine Zähne putze, muss ich nicht mehr zum Zahnarzt.
examples.en: Since I've started always brushing my teeth, I no longer have to go to the dentist.

commonMistakes.wrong: Nachdem ich frühstücke, mache ich Gymnastik. (same tense in both clauses)
commonMistakes.right: Nachdem ich gefrühstückt habe, mache ich Gymnastik.
commonMistakes.why: nachdem specifically requires its clause to be one tense-step earlier than the main clause, showing the breakfast is already finished before the exercise starts.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Expressing purpose/goal: um...zu when the subject is the same, damit when it's different
explanation: Both um...zu and damit express a goal or purpose (answering the question wozu?), but the choice between them depends on whether the sentence has one subject or two. When both the main clause and the purpose clause share the same subject, um...zu can be used — this construction has no subject of its own (it's an infinitive clause, just like Unit 68's zu-infinitives), with zu placed directly before the final infinitive. When the two clauses have different subjects, only damit works, since it introduces a full clause with its own conjugated verb and subject at the end. If there's only one subject, damit can still be used as an alternative to um...zu, just with a full clause instead of an infinitive. Note that möchten/wollen are already 'built into' the meaning of um...zu, and sollen/wollen/möchten are similarly built into damit — so you don't add them explicitly.

rules.rule: Same subject in both clauses: um...zu (infinitive clause, no subject of its own) OR damit (full clause).
rules.note: Ich koche ohne Fett, um abzunehmen. / Ich koche ohne Fett, damit ich abnehme.

rules.rule: Different subjects: only damit works (full clause with its own subject and conjugated verb at the end).
rules.note: Ich koche ohne Fett, damit mein Mann abnimmt.
