rules.rule: Question word: wozu? The modal meaning (wanting/should) is already implied in um...zu and damit — don't add möchten/wollen/sollen explicitly.
rules.note: Wozu kochst du ohne Fett? — Um abzunehmen. (not: um zu wollen abnehmen)

examples.de: Ich lese Zeitung, um mich zu informieren.
examples.en: I read the newspaper to stay informed.

examples.de: Ich koche ohne Fett, damit mein Mann abnimmt.
examples.en: I cook without fat so that my husband loses weight.

examples.de: Ich ziehe aufs Land, damit mein Kind in der Natur aufwächst.
examples.en: I'm moving to the countryside so my child grows up in nature.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich koche ohne Fett, um mein Mann abnimmt.
commonMistakes.right: Ich koche ohne Fett, damit mein Mann abnimmt.
commonMistakes.why: Because the purpose clause has a different subject (mein Mann) than the main clause (ich), only damit works here — um...zu requires the same subject in both clauses.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Four two-part connectors: sowohl...als auch, nicht nur...sondern auch, weder...noch, entweder...oder
explanation: German has four common two-part ('double') connectors, each with a distinct logical meaning. sowohl...als auch means 'both...and', treating two things as equally true without emphasizing either. nicht nur...sondern auch also means 'both', but puts extra emphasis on the second element, as if it's the more surprising or noteworthy of the two. weder...noch means 'neither...nor', negating both options entirely. entweder...oder means 'either...or', presenting exactly two alternatives where one applies. These are all coordinating connectors, so — unlike deshalb/sonst (Unit 41) — the clause they introduce keeps its normal word order rather than inverting.

rules.rule: sowohl...als auch = both, neutral emphasis.
rules.note: Ich trinke Kaffee sowohl mit Milch als auch mit Zucker.

rules.rule: nicht nur...sondern auch = both, emphasizing the second part.
rules.note: Er trinkt Kaffee nicht nur mit viel Zucker sondern auch mit Sahne.

rules.rule: weder...noch = neither...nor (both negated).
rules.note: Sie trinkt Kaffee weder mit Milch noch mit Zucker.

rules.rule: entweder...oder = either...or (exactly one applies).
rules.note: Ich trinke Tee entweder mit Zitrone oder mit Milch.

examples.de: Im Fernsehen kann man sowohl Filme als auch Nachrichten sehen.
examples.en: On TV you can watch both movies and the news.

examples.de: Es gibt nicht nur gute Serien, sondern auch interessante Dokumentationen.
examples.en: There aren't just good shows, but also interesting documentaries.

examples.de: Ich mag weder Krimis noch Science-Fiction-Filme.
examples.en: I like neither crime shows nor sci-fi movies.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich mag weder Krimis oder Science-Fiction-Filme.
commonMistakes.right: Ich mag weder Krimis noch Science-Fiction-Filme.
commonMistakes.why: weder must pair with noch, not oder — the two halves of a double connector are fixed and can't be mixed with parts of a different one.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: je + comparative (verb-final) paired with desto/umso + comparative (verb-second)
explanation: je...desto (or je...umso — the two are interchangeable) expresses a proportional relationship: as one thing increases or decreases, another changes correspondingly ('the more..., the more...'). Structurally, the je-clause is a subordinate clause and always comes first, with je + comparative adjective and the verb at the end. The desto/umso-clause is the main clause, and it inverts: desto/umso + comparative adjective comes first, immediately followed by the conjugated verb (position 2), then the subject. This is a case where a subordinate clause opening the sentence (je...) is followed by a main clause with a distinctive comparative-first, verb-second order.

rules.rule: je + comparative (+ noun) + ... + verb (end) — a subordinate clause, always first.
rules.note: Je schneller man arbeitet, ...

rules.rule: desto/umso + comparative (+ noun) + verb (position 2) + subject — the main clause, inverted.
rules.note: ..., desto müder wird man.

rules.rule: desto and umso are interchangeable.
rules.note: Je mehr man arbeitet, umso müder wird man. = ..., desto müder wird man.

examples.de: Je mehr man arbeitet, desto müder wird man.
examples.en: The more you work, the more tired you get.

examples.de: Je besser sie ihn kennt, umso sympathischer findet sie ihn.
examples.en: The better she knows him, the more likeable she finds him.

examples.de: Je größer die Wohnung ist, desto mehr muss man putzen.
examples.en: The bigger the apartment, the more you have to clean.

commonMistakes.wrong: Je mehr man arbeitet, desto man wird müder. (not inverting the desto-clause)
commonMistakes.right: Je mehr man arbeitet, desto müder wird man.
commonMistakes.why: The desto-clause requires the comparative adjective and the verb to come right after desto, with the subject pushed after the verb — a distinctive inverted order.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: während, wegen, trotz, innerhalb, außerhalb — five genitive prepositions
explanation: Five prepositions govern the genitive case, each carrying a distinct meaning close to a conjunction you may already know. während expresses two parallel/simultaneous actions, similar in meaning to a temporal 'while'. wegen expresses a reason, functioning much like weil but as a preposition rather than a conjunction. trotz expresses a counter-argument, similar to obwohl ('although'). innerhalb and außerhalb express either a location (inside/outside a place) or a time frame (within/beyond a period), depending on context. In everyday spoken German, während, wegen, and trotz are often used with dative instead of genitive, even though genitive remains the standard/written form.

rules.rule: während (genitive) = parallel actions, like a prepositional 'while'.
rules.note: Während des Essens raucht er.

rules.rule: wegen (genitive) = reason, like a prepositional 'weil'.
rules.note: Wegen des Rauchs kann sie nicht essen.

rules.rule: trotz (genitive) = counter-argument, like a prepositional 'obwohl'.
rules.note: Trotz des Rauchs isst er.

rules.rule: innerhalb/außerhalb (genitive) = inside/outside a place, OR within/beyond a time frame.
rules.note: Innerhalb des Restaurants ist das Rauchen verboten. / Innerhalb eines Tages raucht er 40 Zigaretten.

rules.rule: In spoken German, während/wegen/trotz are often used with dative instead.
rules.note: This is common in casual speech even though genitive is the standard form.

examples.de: Wegen des Lärms kann er nicht schlafen.
examples.en: He can't sleep because of the noise.

examples.de: Trotz der Krankheit ist sie nicht fit.
examples.en: Despite the illness, she's not fit.

examples.de: Außerhalb der Öffnungszeiten kann man die Berater nur telefonisch erreichen.
examples.en: Outside of opening hours, you can only reach the advisors by phone.

commonMistakes.wrong: wegen der Rauch
commonMistakes.why: wegen governs genitive, so a masculine noun like Rauch needs des and an added -s: des Rauchs.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: vor/nach, vor/in, vor/seit, bei, während, außerhalb/innerhalb — a full time-preposition toolkit
explanation: This unit rounds out the time prepositions by contrasting pairs that are easy to confuse. vor and nach (dative) work with clock times to mean 'to' and 'past' (fünf vor zwölf, fünf nach zwölf). vor and in (dative) both relate to a reference point, but vor points to the past ('X time ago') while in points to the future ('in X time') — from the perspective of now, one arrow points backward, the other forward. vor and seit (dative) both involve the past, but vor marks a single point in time, while seit marks a duration that continues up to the present. bei (dative) expresses simultaneity between two activities, similar to 'wenn/während', typically combined with a nominalized verb (Beim Lernen höre ich Musik = 'while I study'). während (genitive) expresses two ongoing parallel activities, similar to bei but usually with more emphasis on 'the whole time'. außerhalb/innerhalb (genitive) frame a defined time range, like opening hours or a calendar period.

rules.rule: vor/nach (dative) + clock time = 'to'/'past'.
rules.note: Es ist fünf vor zwölf. / Es ist fünf nach zwölf.

rules.rule: vor (dative) = X time ago (past); in (dative) = in X time (future).
rules.note: Vor einer Woche war ich im Theater. / In einer Woche gehe ich ins Konzert.

rules.rule: vor (dative) = a point in the past; seit (dative) = a duration up to now.
rules.note: Vor einer Woche war der erste Schultag. / Seit einer Woche geht sie zur Schule.

rules.rule: bei (dative) = simultaneity, often with a nominalized verb. während (genitive) = two parallel ongoing activities.
rules.note: Beim Lernen höre ich Musik. / Während des Lernens höre ich Musik.

examples.de: Vor dem Gespräch war ich sehr nervös.
examples.en: Before the conversation I was very nervous.

examples.de: In einer Woche fahre ich in die Türkei.
examples.en: In a week I'm going to Turkey.

examples.de: Seit einer Woche geht sie zur Schule.
examples.en: She's been going to school for a week.

commonMistakes.wrong: Seit einer Woche fahre ich in die Türkei. (referring to a future trip)
commonMistakes.right: In einer Woche fahre ich in die Türkei.
commonMistakes.why: seit marks a duration continuing to now; a future event needs in, not seit.

commonMistakes.wrong: Vor einer Woche geht sie zur Schule. (meaning an ongoing duration)
commonMistakes.right: Seit einer Woche geht sie zur Schule.
commonMistakes.why: vor marks a single past point; an ongoing duration up to the present needs seit.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: The complete adjective ending system, including when there's no article at all
explanation: This unit completes the adjective declension picture from Units 36–37 by adding the case where there's no article whatsoever — no der/die/das, no ein, no kein, no possessive. Without any article, the adjective alone must carry the full case/gender signal, taking on endings that closely match the definite article itself (netter Mann, nettes Kind, nette Frau, nette Leute) — consistent with the 'there's always a signal somewhere' principle from Unit 36, just pushed to its logical extreme when the signal has nowhere else to go. One exception is worth flagging: in the masculine and neuter genitive without an article, the adjective takes -en rather than the expected -es, because the noun itself already carries the genitive -s ending, and doubling that signal on the adjective too would be redundant (netten Mannes, not nettes Mannes).

rules.rule: With no article at all, the adjective takes on endings close to the definite article, carrying the full signal alone.
rules.note: netter Mann (nominative, no article) — compare der nette Mann, ein netter Mann

rules.rule: Exception: masculine/neuter genitive without an article uses -en on the adjective, not -es, since the noun's own -s ending already signals genitive.
rules.note: netten Mannes (not nettes Mannes)

rules.rule: Possessive articles (mein, dein...) follow exactly the same pattern as kein throughout.
rules.note: See Units 36–37 for the full system.

examples.de: Gutes Wetter macht mich glücklich.
examples.en: Good weather makes me happy.

examples.de: Ich trinke gerne guten Kaffee.
examples.en: I like drinking good coffee.

examples.de: Das ist die Farbe netter Leute.
examples.en: That's the color of nice people.

commonMistakes.wrong: nettes Mannes
commonMistakes.why: In the masculine/neuter genitive without an article, the adjective takes -en, not the -es you might expect by pattern, because the noun's own -s already marks the genitive.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: Verb + d + adjective ending: describing something happening right now, actively
explanation: Partizip 1 turns a verb into an adjective describing an action happening at the same time and actively performed by the noun it describes — built simply as the infinitive + d + a normal adjective ending. A 'bellender Hund' is a dog that is barking right now; it's grammatically equivalent to a relative clause: ein Hund, der jetzt bellt. This is different from the past participle (Partizip 2, used for the perfect tense and passive), which describes something passive or already completed. Partizip 1 can only be used directly before a noun, not standalone as a predicate — you can't say 'Die Frau ist joggend' the way you can with a genuine adjective. A handful of Partizip 1 forms have become fully independent adjectives over time and can stand alone: spannend, anstrengend, dringend.

rules.rule: Partizip 1 = infinitive + d + adjective ending. Meaning: active and simultaneous, equivalent to a relative clause with the verb happening now.
rules.note: ein bellender Hund = ein Hund, der jetzt bellt

rules.rule: Can only be used directly before a noun, not as a standalone predicate.
rules.note: Not: Die Frau ist joggend. (but: eine joggende Frau is fine)

rules.rule: A few Partizip 1 forms have become independent adjectives that CAN stand alone: spannend, anstrengend, dringend.
rules.note: Der Film ist spannend. (fine, because spannend has become a normal adjective)

examples.de: Ein spielendes Kind
examples.en: A child who is playing

examples.de: Singende Vögel
examples.en: Singing birds

examples.de: Eine joggende Frau
examples.en: A jogging woman

commonMistakes.wrong: Die Frau ist joggend.
commonMistakes.right: Die Frau joggt. (or: Das ist eine joggende Frau.)
commonMistakes.why: Partizip 1 can only be used directly before a noun; it can't be used as a standalone predicate the way ordinary adjectives can.

commonMistakes.wrong: fliegend Fische (dropping the adjective ending)
commonMistakes.why: Partizip 1 still needs a normal adjective ending matching the noun's gender, case, and number — the -d alone isn't enough.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv A1-B1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only

summary: A full review of the verb bracket across every tense and structure, plus the rules for Position 1
explanation: This is a consolidating overview: the same 'bracket' pattern — a conjugated element in position 2, and a second part pushed to the end — runs through every German verb structure. It applies to the perfect tense, separable verbs, modal verbs, the passive, the Plusquamperfekt, the future, the conditional, and verb+verb / noun+verb / adjective+verb combinations. Regardless of which of these is in play, the underlying skeleton is always: Subject/other element (position 1) — conjugated verb (position 2) — everything else — second verb part (end). Beyond the bracket itself, several practical rules govern position 1: the subject sits directly to the left or right of the verb; almost any sentence part can occupy position 1, including multiple words together; if a subordinate clause fills position 1, the main clause simply starts with its verb right after; no comma follows position 1 (unless that position is itself a subordinate clause); and after a leading 'ja' or 'nein' plus a comma, position 1 starts fresh for what follows. One more detail: the reflexive pronoun 'sich' can move to sit before the subject when that subject is a full noun (not a pronoun) — 'Heute hat sich meine Mutter angekündigt.'

rules.rule: Every German sentence structure with two verb parts follows the same bracket: position 2 (conjugated) — ... — end (second part).
rules.note: This applies uniformly to Perfekt, separable verbs, modals, Passiv, Plusquamperfekt, Futur, Konjunktiv, and verb/noun/adjective+verb combinations.

rules.rule: The subject sits directly next to the verb, left or right depending on what else took position 1.
rules.note: Ich gehe heute ins Kino. / Heute gehe ich ins Kino.

rules.rule: No comma follows position 1 unless position 1 is itself a subordinate clause; a reflexive pronoun can precede a noun subject.
rules.note: Wie jeden Dienstag möchte ich auch heute ins Kino gehen. / Heute hat sich meine Mutter angekündigt.

examples.de: Obwohl ich wenig Zeit habe, gehe ich auch heute ins Kino.
examples.en: Although I have little time, I'm going to the cinema today too.

examples.de: Ja, ich möchte unbedingt ins Kino gehen.
examples.en: Yes, I really want to go to the cinema.

examples.de: Heute hat sich meine Mutter angekündigt.
examples.en: My mother announced she's coming today.

commonMistakes.wrong: Wie jeden Dienstag, ich möchte ins Kino gehen. (adding a comma after position 1)
commonMistakes.right: Wie jeden Dienstag möchte ich ins Kino gehen.
commonMistakes.why: No comma follows position 1 — it flows directly into the verb — unless position 1 is itself a full subordinate clause.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Extending the connector system: Nebensatzkonnektoren, Position-1 adverbial connectors, and Position-0 connectors
explanation: Building on the basic distinction between subordinating and coordinating connectors, this unit adds structural detail and a wider vocabulary. In a subordinate clause (introduced by während, dass, and similar connectors), the subject comes directly after the connector, and the conjugated verb goes to the end — with any second verb part sitting directly before the conjugated verb, not after it. A wider set of adverbial connectors (trotzdem, deshalb, zuerst, dann...) can occupy position 1, forcing the verb into position 2 and the subject after it — but these connectors are still just adverbs, so they can also move to position 3 or further into the sentence, matching whatever role they play (temporal, causal...); wherever they land, they must always come after any pronoun objects. Finally, the coordinating connectors that sit in 'position 0' (outside the counted positions) now include a fifth word: aber, denn, und, sondern, oder — remembered with the mnemonic 'aduso' — plus doch when it's used adversatively.

rules.rule: In a subordinate clause: connector — subject — ... — second verb part — conjugated verb (at the very end, second verb part comes just before it).
rules.note: Wir haben uns geärgert, dass er nicht mithilft.

rules.rule: Position-1 adverbial connectors (trotzdem, deshalb, zuerst, dann...) can also move later in the sentence to match their semantic role, but must always follow any pronouns.
rules.note: Es regnet, ich gehe trotzdem ins Schwimmbad. / Es regnet, ich kaufe mir trotzdem ein Eis.

rules.rule: Position-0 connectors ('aduso'): aber, denn, und, sondern, oder — plus doch when adversative.
rules.note: Ich gehe heute spazieren, denn das Wetter ist schön.

examples.de: Er hat sich ausgeruht, während wir den ganzen Tag gearbeitet haben.
examples.en: He rested while we worked all day.

examples.de: Ich müsste arbeiten, trotzdem werde ich ins Schwimmbad gehen.
examples.en: I should be working, but I'll go swimming anyway.

examples.de: Heute habe ich keine Lust, aber morgen komme ich gerne mit.
examples.en: I don't feel like it today, but I'll gladly come along tomorrow.

commonMistakes.wrong: Es regnet, ich trotzdem gehe ins Schwimmbad. (placing trotzdem before the pronoun without inverting)
commonMistakes.right: Es regnet, ich gehe trotzdem ins Schwimmbad.
commonMistakes.why: When trotzdem moves later in the sentence, it must still come after any pronoun objects/subjects already placed — it can't interrupt that sequence.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Full object-ordering rules: nouns go Nominativ-Dativ-Akkusativ; pronouns always come first and go Nominativ-Akkusativ-Dativ
explanation: When a sentence has both a dative and an accusative object as full nouns, the order is nominative–dative–accusative. But pronouns behave differently on two counts: first, any pronoun object always comes before a noun object, regardless of case; second, when both objects are pronouns, their relative order flips to nominative–accusative–dative — the reverse of the noun-only order. This reordering applies consistently even when other sentence elements (time, place) are added, and reflexive pronouns follow the exact same placement rules as object pronouns.

rules.rule: Two full-noun objects: Nominativ – Dativ – Akkusativ.
rules.note: Der Kellner serviert der Dame den Kaffee.

rules.rule: A pronoun object always precedes a noun object, regardless of case.
rules.note: Der Kellner serviert ihr den Kaffee. / Der Kellner serviert ihn der Dame.

rules.rule: Two pronoun objects: Nominativ – Akkusativ – Dativ (reversed from the noun-only order).
rules.note: Er serviert ihn ihr.

rules.rule: This fixed order doesn't change even when other elements (time, place) are added to the sentence.
rules.note: Im Garten serviert der Kellner heute der Dame den Kaffee.

examples.de: Ich habe es ihm gestern gegeben.
examples.en: I gave it to him yesterday.

examples.de: Ich habe mir die Haare gewaschen.
examples.en: I washed my hair.

examples.de: Der Hund leckt unserer Tochter die Hand.
examples.en: The dog licks our daughter's hand.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich habe ihm es gestern gegeben.
commonMistakes.right: Ich habe es ihm gestern gegeben.
commonMistakes.why: When both objects are pronouns, accusative comes before dative — the opposite of the noun-only order, where dative leads.

commonMistakes.wrong: Der Kellner serviert der Dame ihn. (mixing a pronoun into noun-order position)
commonMistakes.right: Der Kellner serviert ihn der Dame.
commonMistakes.why: A pronoun object must move before any noun object, regardless of which case it is.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: The full temporal-kausal-modal-lokal order, and how to stack multiple items of the same type
explanation: When a sentence contains several adverbial phrases — answering wann?, warum?, wie?, and wo?/wohin?/woher? — they normally appear in a fixed sequence: temporal, kausal, modal, lokal, remembered with the mnemonic 'tekamolo'. Any one of these can still move to position 1 for emphasis (a temporal phrase does this especially often), but lokal information should never be placed before temporal information in the middle of a sentence. When multiple phrases of the same type stack together, they follow their own internal ordering: temporal phrases go from the largest unit of time to the smallest (year, month, specific day, time of day, clock time), while lokal phrases go the opposite way, from the smallest/most specific place to the largest (a specific point, then a country or region).

rules.rule: Standard order: temporal – kausal – modal – lokal (tekamolo).
rules.note: Ich bin gestern wegen des Streiks mit dem Taxi zur Arbeit gefahren.

rules.rule: Any single element can move to position 1; temporal phrases do this especially often. Lokal should never precede temporal mid-sentence.
rules.note: Gestern bin ich wegen des Streiks mit dem Taxi zur Arbeit gefahren.

rules.rule: Stacked temporal phrases: largest unit to smallest. Stacked lokal phrases: smallest/most specific to largest.
rules.note: vor einem Jahr, im Mai, an einem Dienstag, morgens, um 4 Uhr / zu unseren Freunden, in ein kleines Dorf, im Süden, von Kroatien

examples.de: Wir sind vor einem Jahr im Mai an einem Dienstag hier angekommen.
examples.en: We arrived here a year ago in May, on a Tuesday.

examples.de: Sie fahren zu ihren Freunden in ein kleines Dorf im Süden von Kroatien.
examples.en: They're driving to their friends in a small village in southern Croatia.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich bin mit dem Taxi gestern zur Arbeit gefahren. (modal before temporal)
commonMistakes.right: Ich bin gestern mit dem Taxi zur Arbeit gefahren.
commonMistakes.why: The default order is temporal before modal — placing the manner phrase first disrupts the tekamolo sequence.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: A unifying concept: fixed prepositional objects, adjective+sein, noun+verb combos, and Funktionsverbgefüge all behave like one verb unit
explanation: Several different-looking German structures share one underlying behavior: a piece of information sits so close to the verb's meaning that it effectively becomes part of it, called a 'Verbgefährte' (verb companion). This category covers fixed prepositional objects (sich freuen auf) and their da(r)-pronoun replacements (sich darauf freuen); adjective+sein combinations describing a state (müde sein), which behave the same way as their equivalents machen/werden/sich fühlen + adjective (müde machen, müde werden, sich müde fühlen); noun+verb combinations where the noun takes no article (Tennis spielen, Klavier spielen — importantly different in meaning from buying an instrument, ein Klavier kaufen); and Funktionsverbgefüge, fixed noun+verb pairings like ein Referat halten. In every case, this 'verb companion' sits at the very end of the clause, or directly before the second verb part if there is one.

rules.rule: A 'Verbgefährte' (fixed prepositional object, adjective+sein, article-less noun+verb combo, or Funktionsverbgefüge) sits at the end of the clause or directly before the second verb part.
rules.note: Er hat sich schon lange auf die Party gefreut. / Wir halten oft Referate.

rules.rule: adjective+sein has equivalent forms with machen/werden/sich fühlen.
rules.note: müde sein / müde machen / müde werden / sich müde fühlen

rules.rule: Noun+verb combinations use no article, and differ in meaning from a normal accusative object.
rules.note: Klavier spielen (to play piano) ≠ ein Klavier kaufen (to buy a piano)

examples.de: Ich bin zurzeit immer schon mittags im Büro müde.
examples.en: These days I'm already tired by midday at the office.

examples.de: Sie spielt täglich drei Stunden mit ihrem Freund Tennis.
examples.en: She plays tennis with her boyfriend for three hours every day.

examples.de: Wir halten oft im Unterricht Referate.
examples.en: We often give presentations in class.

commonMistakes.wrong: Sie will Tennis im Urlaub täglich spielen. (placing the Verbgefährte too early)
commonMistakes.right: Sie will im Urlaub täglich mit ihrem Freund Tennis spielen.
commonMistakes.why: The verb companion (Tennis) belongs directly before the final verb part (spielen), not scattered earlier in the sentence.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Whole-sentence negation places nicht fairly far right; partial negation places it directly before the negated element
explanation: For whole-sentence negation (Satznegation), nicht tends to sit fairly far toward the right of the sentence — but not at the very end. It comes after the subject, after pronoun objects, after definite dative/accusative objects, and after temporal and kausal phrases, but almost always before a modal (manner) phrase, a lokal phrase, and any Verbgefährte (Unit 5). For partial negation (Teilnegation), nicht instead goes directly in front of the one specific word or phrase being denied, and that element receives extra stress; this construction very often continues with 'sondern' to state what's actually true instead.

rules.rule: Satznegation: nicht comes after the subject, pronouns, definite objects, temporal and kausal phrases — but before modal phrases, lokal phrases, and any Verbgefährte.
rules.note: Ich konnte meinen Vater gestern wegen eines Termins nicht pünktlich am Bahnhof abholen.

rules.rule: Teilnegation: nicht goes directly before the specific element being denied, which is stressed; often followed by sondern.
rules.note: Nicht ich schenke ihr den Ring (sondern er). / Ich schenke ihr nicht heute den Ring (sondern morgen).

examples.de: Ich kann mich heute wegen einer Konferenz nicht um meinen Kollegen kümmern.
examples.en: I can't take care of my colleague today because of a conference.

examples.de: Ich schenke ihr heute nicht den Ring, sondern die Blumen.
examples.en: I'm not giving her the ring today, but the flowers.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich konnte meinen Vater nicht gestern abholen. (placing nicht before a temporal phrase in whole-sentence negation)
commonMistakes.right: Ich konnte meinen Vater gestern nicht abholen.
commonMistakes.why: In whole-sentence negation, nicht comes after temporal and kausal phrases, not before them.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: würde + infinitive for most verbs, special short forms for sein/haben/modals, and a set of other verbs that also commonly use their own old Konjunktiv 2 form
explanation: Most verbs form the present Konjunktiv 2 with würde plus the infinitive at the end of the clause. sein, haben, and the modal verbs use their own dedicated short forms instead (wäre, hätte, könnte, müsste, dürfte, wollte, sollte), which are always preferred over their würde-equivalents. Beyond this core group, several other frequent verbs also commonly appear in their own old Konjunktiv 2 form rather than the würde-construction: es ginge, es gäbe, ich fände, ich bräuchte, ich wüsste, das ließe sich machen, das käme darauf an, er bliebe, das sähe gut aus, er käme zurecht. All of these old forms are built the same way: Präteritum stem + Konjunktiv ending (+ umlaut where the Präteritum itself doesn't already have one). Many other old Konjunktiv 2 forms exist and appear in literature, but are not used productively in speech or writing today — you only need to recognize them. The passive can also go into Konjunktiv 2, formed as würde + past participle.

rules.rule: Most verbs: würde (conjugated) + infinitive.
rules.note: Ich würde nie mehr arbeiten.

rules.rule: sein, haben, modals: dedicated short forms, always preferred over würde-forms.
rules.note: wäre, hätte, könnte, müsste, dürfte, wollte, sollte

rules.rule: A further set of common verbs regularly use their own old form instead of würde + infinitive.
rules.note: es gäbe, ich fände, ich wüsste, ich bräuchte, das käme darauf an

rules.rule: Passive in Konjunktiv 2: würde + past participle (replacing the whole werden-conjugation).
rules.note: Das Buch würde bestellt, wenn die Software funktionieren würde.

examples.de: Ich fände es gut, wenn du mitkommen würdest.
examples.en: I'd think it was good if you came along.

examples.de: Das ließe sich sicher machen.
examples.en: That could surely be arranged.

examples.de: Wenn die Maschine funktionieren würde, würde die Bestellung sofort bearbeitet.
examples.en: If the machine worked, the order would be processed immediately.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich würde es gut finden. (defaulting to würde+infinitive for a verb that commonly uses its own old form)
commonMistakes.why: finden is one of the verbs where the old Konjunktiv 2 form is the natural, commonly used choice rather than the würde-construction.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Konjunktiv 2 has only one past-tense form: sein/haben in Konjunktiv 2 + past participle
explanation: Unlike the indicative, which distinguishes Präteritum, Perfekt, and Plusquamperfekt, Konjunktiv 2 collapses all past meaning into a single form: the Konjunktiv 2 of sein or haben (wäre/hätte) plus the past participle — following exactly the same sein/haben choice as the ordinary perfect tense. With a modal verb, this extends to a double infinitive: hätte + the other verb's infinitive + the modal's infinitive. Because there's only one past form in Konjunktiv 2, it can express what would correspond to any of the three indicative past tenses, depending on context.

rules.rule: Konjunktiv 2 Vergangenheit = hätte/wäre (matching the ordinary Perfekt's sein/haben choice) + past participle.
rules.note: Ich hätte gearbeitet. / Ich wäre gegangen.

rules.rule: With a modal verb: hätte + verb infinitive + modal infinitive (double infinitive).
rules.note: Ich hätte arbeiten müssen.

rules.rule: There is only one Konjunktiv 2 past form — it covers what Präteritum, Perfekt, and Plusquamperfekt each express separately in the indicative.
rules.note: No separate Konjunktiv 2 Plusquamperfekt exists.

examples.de: Hätte ich doch den Hammer mitgenommen!
examples.en: If only I had brought the hammer!

examples.de: Wäre ich doch zu Hause geblieben!
examples.en: If only I had stayed home!

examples.de: Ich hätte früher kommen sollen.
examples.en: I should have come earlier.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich hätte kommen gesollt.
commonMistakes.why: With a modal in the Konjunktiv 2 past, both verbs stay as infinitives at the end (double infinitive) — the modal doesn't take a normal participle form here.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Konjunktiv 2 for polite requests, suggestions, advice — and, in the past tense, for reproach or regret
explanation: Konjunktiv 2 covers a family of related everyday functions. For politeness, könnten/würden/dürfte/wären Sie so freundlich soften a request — often paired with fixed phrases like 'Könnten/Würden Sie mir einen Gefallen tun...' or 'Hätten Sie einen Moment Zeit für mich?'. For suggestions, können in Konjunktiv 2 proposes an option (Wir könnten ins Kino gehen). For advice, sollen in Konjunktiv 2 gives a recommendation (Du solltest mehr Sport machen), and the fixed phrase 'an deiner/Ihrer Stelle' + Konjunktiv 2 works the same way (An deiner Stelle würde ich das nicht machen). When any of these — suggestions or advice — are put into the Konjunktiv 2 past tense, the meaning shifts to a reproach or expression of regret about something that didn't happen: 'Wir hätten ins Kino gehen können, aber du bist zu spät gekommen' implies blame; 'Du hättest Rückengymnastik machen sollen, dann hättest du jetzt keine Probleme' implies both advice and regret.

rules.rule: Politeness: könnten/würden/dürfte + infinitive, or fixed phrases like 'Wären Sie so freundlich...?'
rules.note: Würden Sie mir bitte erklären...?

rules.rule: Suggestion: können in Konjunktiv 2. Advice: sollen in Konjunktiv 2, or 'an deiner Stelle' + Konjunktiv 2.
rules.note: Wir könnten ins Kino gehen. / An deiner Stelle würde ich ins Kino gehen.

rules.rule: Konjunktiv 2 past tense of a suggestion/advice implies reproach or regret about something that didn't happen.
rules.note: Wir hätten ins Kino gehen können, aber du bist zu spät gekommen.

examples.de: Dürfte ich Sie etwas fragen?
examples.en: Might I ask you something?

examples.de: Du solltest mehr Sport machen.
examples.en: You should exercise more.

examples.de: Du hättest Rückengymnastik machen sollen, dann hättest du jetzt keine Probleme.
examples.en: You should have done back exercises, then you wouldn't have any problems now.

commonMistakes.wrong: Wir konnten ins Kino gehen, aber du bist zu spät gekommen. (using the indicative Präteritum instead of Konjunktiv 2)
commonMistakes.right: Wir hätten ins Kino gehen können, aber du bist zu spät gekommen.
commonMistakes.why: The reproach meaning ('we could have, but...') requires Konjunktiv 2 past, not the plain indicative past, which would just state a past ability without implying blame.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

topic: Wünsche, irreale Wünsche und irreale Bedingungen
summary: Wishes use Konjunktiv 2 with gerne; irreal wishes stand alone with a particle; irreal conditions use Konjunktiv 2 in both clauses
explanation: A simple wish combines Konjunktiv 2 with gerne, lieber, or am liebsten (Ich würde gerne gewinnen). An irreal (unrealistic) wish is more dramatic: it's introduced with wenn or has the verb moved to position 1 with no wenn at all, and it always carries an intensifying particle — doch, bloß, or nur — giving it an imploring tone. Crucially, an irreal wish stands alone as just the subordinate-clause-shaped sentence, with no accompanying main clause (Wenn er doch gewinnen würde! / Würde er bloß gewinnen!). In the past tense, these often carry a sense of regret. An irreal (unreal/hypothetical) condition is a full sentence: Konjunktiv 2 appears in both the wenn-clause and the main clause. The same idea can also be phrased without wenn by expressing the missing condition negatively with sonst ('otherwise') or by using ohne + noun + hätte ('without X, would have').

rules.rule: Simple wish: Konjunktiv 2 + gerne/lieber/am liebsten.
rules.note: Ich würde gerne gewinnen. Ich hätte gerne gewonnen.

rules.rule: Irreal wish: wenn-clause OR verb-first with no wenn, always with a particle (doch, bloß, nur); stands alone, no main clause.
rules.note: Wenn ich doch bloß den Lottoschein abgegeben hätte!

rules.rule: Irreal condition: Konjunktiv 2 in both the wenn-clause and the main clause; can be rephrased with sonst or ohne...hätte.
rules.note: Wenn ich Geld hätte, würde ich eine Weltreise machen. / Ich hatte kein Geld. Sonst hätte ich eine Weltreise gemacht.

examples.de: Ich würde gerne im Lotto gewinnen!
examples.en: I'd love to win the lottery!

examples.de: Wenn ich doch nur mehr Zeit hätte!
examples.en: If only I had more time!

examples.de: Wenn ich viel Geld hätte, könnte ich mir alle Träume erfüllen.
examples.en: If I had a lot of money, I could fulfill all my dreams.

commonMistakes.wrong: Wenn ich mehr Zeit hätte! (irreal wish without a particle)
commonMistakes.right: Wenn ich doch nur mehr Zeit hätte!
commonMistakes.why: An irreal wish needs an intensifying particle like doch, bloß, or nur — without one it just sounds like an unfinished conditional sentence.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: als ob/als wenn (subordinate clause) vs. als (main-clause-style, verb-second) for hypothetical comparisons
explanation: An irreal comparison describes something 'as if' it were true, using Konjunktiv 2. There are two grammatical shapes for this, both meaning the same thing. With als ob or als wenn, the sentence is a genuine subordinate clause: the connector comes first, and the conjugated verb goes to the end, exactly like any other Nebensatz. With just als on its own, the structure is different: als itself takes position 1, and the conjugated verb follows immediately in position 2 — matching ordinary main-clause word order rather than subordinate-clause order. Both the present and past tense of the comparison are possible, following the usual Konjunktiv 2 formation rules.

rules.rule: als ob / als wenn: subordinate clause, verb at the end.
rules.note: Du siehst aus, als ob du müde wärst.

rules.rule: als alone: acts like a main clause — als in position 1, conjugated verb in position 2.
rules.note: Du machst den Eindruck, als würdest du einen Kaffee brauchen.

rules.rule: Past-tense irreal comparisons use the Konjunktiv 2 past (hätte/wäre + participle).
rules.note: Es scheint, als ob du gestern schlecht geschlafen hättest.

examples.de: Du siehst aus, als ob du sehr müde wärst.
examples.en: You look as if you were very tired.

examples.de: Du tust so, als hättest du gestern schlecht geschlafen.
examples.en: You're acting as if you slept badly last night.

commonMistakes.wrong: Du tust so, als du hättest schlecht geschlafen. (using subordinate order after bare als)
commonMistakes.right: Du tust so, als hättest du schlecht geschlafen.
commonMistakes.why: als on its own behaves like a main clause — the verb comes immediately after it, before the subject, not at the end as with als ob/als wenn.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

topic: Passiv in allen Zeiten (Präsens, Präteritum, Perfekt)
summary: The passive extends across tenses with werden/wurde/ist...worden, plus von/durch/mit for the agent
explanation: The passive shifts focus onto the action rather than who performs it, used whenever that focus matters more than naming the doer. In the subject/'Täter' relationship, the active sentence's subject and the passive sentence's subject are different things, and the original doer can simply be dropped. Across tenses: Präsens uses wird + participle; Präteritum uses wurde + participle; Perfekt uses ist + participle + worden (not geworden — worden is the special reduced form used only in the passive perfect). When the doer is mentioned, three different prepositions are used depending on what it represents: von + dative for a person or institution; durch + accusative for a process or intermediary; mit + dative for a tool or instrument. More than one of these can appear together in the same sentence.

rules.rule: Präsens: wird + participle. Präteritum: wurde + participle. Perfekt: ist + participle + worden.
rules.note: Die Gruppe wird informiert. / wurde informiert. / ist informiert worden.

rules.rule: von + Dativ = the doer (person/institution). durch + Akkusativ = a process or mediator. mit + Dativ = a tool/instrument.
rules.note: vom Reiseleiter (von); durch den Anschlag (durch); mit einer Schere (mit)

rules.rule: Multiple agent-prepositions can combine in one sentence.
rules.note: Wir wurden vom Reiseleiter durch eine E-Mail informiert.

examples.de: Die Reisegruppe wird heute informiert.
examples.en: The tour group is being informed today.

examples.de: Die Gruppe wurde gestern informiert.
examples.en: The group was informed yesterday.

examples.de: Die Gruppe ist bereits informiert worden.
examples.en: The group has already been informed.

commonMistakes.wrong: Die Gruppe ist informiert geworden.
commonMistakes.why: The passive perfect uses the reduced form worden, not geworden — geworden is reserved for werden meaning 'to become'.

commonMistakes.wrong: Wir wurden durch den Reiseleiter informiert. (using durch for a person)
commonMistakes.why: A person or institution acting as the doer takes von, not durch — durch is for a process or mediating factor, like an announcement or a document.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

topic: Passiv mit Modalverben in allen Zeiten
summary: Passive + modal across tenses, with a preference for Präteritum over Perfekt/Plusquamperfekt
explanation: Combining the passive with a modal verb builds a three-part verb bracket: the modal (conjugated, position 2), then eventually participle + werden (as an infinitive) at the very end. Across tenses, this looks like: Präsens — muss + ... + participle + werden; Präteritum — musste + ... + participle + werden; Perfekt — hat + ... + participle + werden müssen (a chain of three verb forms). In practice, German usually avoids the Perfekt and Plusquamperfekt forms of passive-with-modal because they get unwieldy, preferring the simpler Präteritum instead even when describing something further in the past.

rules.rule: Präsens: muss + ... + participle + werden. Präteritum: musste + ... + participle + werden. Perfekt: hat + ... + participle + werden müssen.
rules.note: Die Gruppe muss informiert werden. / musste informiert werden. / hat informiert werden müssen.

rules.rule: Präteritum is generally preferred over Perfekt/Plusquamperfekt for passive-with-modal, because those forms become unwieldy.
rules.note: Die Gruppe musste informiert werden. (preferred over the Perfekt form in most contexts)

examples.de: Das muss heute noch erledigt werden.
examples.en: That still has to be taken care of today.

examples.de: Die E-Mails müssen beantwortet werden.
examples.en: The emails need to be answered.

examples.de: Das Gerät sollte überprüft werden.
examples.en: The device should be checked.

commonMistakes.wrong: Die Gruppe hat informiert werden müssen. (favoring Perfekt when Präteritum would be more natural)
commonMistakes.why: German strongly prefers the simpler Präteritum form for passive-with-modal over the heavier Perfekt/Plusquamperfekt constructions.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: lassen+sich+Infinitiv, sein+zu+Infinitiv, and the -bar/-abel/-lich adjective suffixes all express a passive-like 'can be done'
explanation: Several structures let you express passive-like meaning without literally using werden. lassen + sich + infinitive expresses possibility ('das Problem lässt sich lösen' = the problem can be solved). sein + zu + infinitive is ambiguous on its own — depending on context it can mean 'can be...', 'must be...', or 'may not be...' — so the intended strength has to come from context. Three adjective-forming suffixes convert a verb directly into a 'can be done' adjective: -bar is by far the most common and productive (lösen → lösbar; for -igen verbs, use -igbar, as in entschuldigbar); -abel is used specifically for verbs ending in -ieren (diskutieren → diskutabel); and various forms ending in -lich, almost always with an umlaut, cover a smaller set of verbs (verstehen → verständlich). Occasionally a verb has two different suffixed adjectives with genuinely different meanings (löslich = dissolvable, lösbar = solvable). All of these alternatives extend across other tenses and the Konjunktiv the same way the passive itself does.

rules.rule: lassen + sich + infinitive = 'can be done' (possibility).
rules.note: Das Problem lässt sich lösen. (= kann gelöst werden)

rules.rule: sein + zu + infinitive is ambiguous between kann/muss/darf nicht — the meaning depends on context.
rules.note: Die Diskussion ist nicht zu vermeiden. (= kann/muss/darf nicht — context decides)

rules.rule: -bar (most common; -igen verbs use -igbar), -abel (only for -ieren verbs), -lich (mostly with umlaut) all turn a verb into a 'can be done' adjective.
rules.note: lösbar, entschuldigbar, diskutabel, verständlich

examples.de: Das Problem lässt sich lösen.
examples.en: The problem can be solved.

examples.de: Mein Vorschlag ist sofort zu diskutieren!
examples.en: My suggestion needs to be discussed right away!

examples.de: Der Vorschlag ist diskutabel.
examples.en: The suggestion is open to discussion.

commonMistakes.wrong: kontrollabel (forming -abel from a non -ieren verb)
commonMistakes.why: -abel is reserved specifically for verbs ending in -ieren; other verbs use -bar instead.

commonMistakes.wrong: Confusing löslich and lösbar as interchangeable
commonMistakes.right: Check which one the context needs — löslich means physically dissolvable, lösbar means solvable/resolvable.
commonMistakes.why: A few verbs have two different suffixed adjectives with genuinely different meanings, not stylistic variants of each other.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Reviewing wo/wohin with a subtler nuance: some activity verbs take dative even though they involve movement
explanation: The nine Wechselpräpositionen (in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen) still follow the basic rule: dative for a static location (wo?), accusative for a destination (wohin?). A subtler point worth knowing at this level: some verbs that clearly involve motion — like joggen or laufen — can still take dative if the focus is on where the activity happens generally, rather than on reaching a destination. 'Joggen Sie im Park' (jogging as an ongoing activity within an area) contrasts with 'Joggen Sie in den Park' (heading toward the park to start jogging there) — the same verb, but the case depends on whether you're describing an activity-in-a-place or a movement-toward-a-goal.

rules.rule: wo? (static, or an activity generally located somewhere) = dative. wohin? (a destination being moved toward) = accusative.
rules.note: Sie joggen im Park. (activity within the area) vs. Sie joggen in den Park. (heading there to jog)

rules.rule: Contractions: in+dem=im, an+dem=am, an+das=ans, in+das=ins.
rules.note: Sie springen ins Wasser.

examples.de: Er geht auf der Straße.
examples.en: He's walking along the street.

examples.de: Das Auto fährt an die Kreuzung.
examples.en: The car is driving up to the intersection.

examples.de: Sie joggt im Park.
examples.en: She's jogging in the park.

commonMistakes.wrong: Sie joggt in den Park. (meaning she jogs around inside the park as an ongoing activity)
commonMistakes.why: When the sentence describes where an activity happens generally, rather than movement toward a destination, dative is correct even though jogging involves motion.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: The complete wo/wohin/woher system across in, an, auf, bei, nach, zu, aus, von — plus the compass-direction exception
explanation: This unit assembles the full location-preposition system into one grid. For rooms, countries with an article, and cities: wo=in+dative, wohin=in+accusative, woher=aus+dative (with the exception of cities/countries without an article, which use nach for wohin instead of in). For a vertical or watery surface (a screen, a shore): wo=an+dative, wohin=an+accusative, woher=von+dative. For a horizontal surface (a place, a mountain, a street): wo=auf+dative, wohin=auf+accusative, woher=von+dative. For people, firms, activities, and situations: wo=bei+dative, wohin=zu+dative, woher=von+dative. One extra nuance: compass directions (Norden, Süden...) behave differently depending on whether you mean the direction itself or the region — 'nach Süden' (toward the direction) vs. 'in den Süden' (into the region as a place) vs. 'im Süden' (in the region).

rules.rule: Rooms/countries-with-article/cities: wo=in+Dativ, wohin=in+Akkusativ, woher=aus+Dativ. Countries/cities without article: wohin=nach (not in).
rules.note: im Supermarkt / in den Supermarkt / aus dem Supermarkt; but nach Italien (not in Italien)

rules.rule: Vertical/watery contact: wo=an+Dativ, wohin=an+Akkusativ, woher=von+Dativ. Horizontal surface: wo=auf+Dativ, wohin=auf+Akkusativ, woher=von+Dativ.
rules.note: am Strand / an den Strand / vom Strand

rules.rule: People/firms/activities: wo=bei+Dativ, wohin=zu+Dativ, woher=von+Dativ.
rules.note: bei Thomas / zu Thomas / von Thomas

rules.rule: Compass directions: nach Süden (toward the direction) vs. in den Süden (into the region) vs. im Süden (in the region).
rules.note: Distinguishes direction from region.

examples.de: Wir fahren morgen in die Berge.
examples.en: We're driving into the mountains tomorrow.

examples.de: Sie kommt gerade vom Markt.
examples.en: She's just coming from the market.

examples.de: Der Wind kommt aus Westen.
examples.en: The wind is coming from the west.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich fahre in Italien. (for a country without an article)
commonMistakes.why: Countries and cities without an article use nach for the destination, not in — in is reserved for places that do take an article, like die Schweiz.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: A larger set of spatial prepositions: entlang, gegenüber, inmitten, unweit, oberhalb/unterhalb, jenseits/diesseits/beiderseits, ab, von...aus, bis (zu)
explanation: Beyond the core spatial prepositions, several more precise ones are common at this level, mostly governing genitive. entlang can appear before its noun (genitive, describing a static parallel position) or after it (accusative, describing movement alongside something). gegenüber (dative) can also appear before or after its noun and describes being face-to-face with something. inmitten (genitive) means 'in the middle of'; unweit (genitive) means 'not far from'; oberhalb/unterhalb (genitive) mean 'above/below'; jenseits/diesseits/beiderseits (genitive) mean 'on the far side/this side/both sides of'. Separately, ab (dative) marks a starting point ('from this point onward'); von...aus (dative) marks the vantage point something is seen or measured from; and bis (with no article) or bis zu (dative, with an article or adjective) marks an endpoint or goal.

rules.rule: entlang: genitive before the noun (static, parallel position) or accusative after the noun (movement alongside).
rules.note: Entlang des Flusses stehen Bäume. / Er geht den Fluss entlang.

rules.rule: gegenüber (dative), inmitten/unweit/oberhalb/unterhalb/jenseits/diesseits/beiderseits (all genitive) each add a precise spatial relationship.
rules.note: gegenüber dem Haus; inmitten des Dorfes; unweit des Sees

rules.rule: ab + dative = starting point. von...aus + dative = vantage point. bis (no article) / bis zu + dative (with article) = endpoint.
rules.note: Ab einer Höhe von 2000m gibt es keine Bäume. / Von dem Berg aus hat man einen Blick. / Ich wandere bis zum Gipfel.

examples.de: Die Bushaltestelle ist gegenüber dem gelben Haus.
examples.en: The bus stop is across from the yellow house.

examples.de: Die Kühe befinden sich unweit des Dorfes.
examples.en: The cows are not far from the village.

examples.de: Von dem Turm aus hat man einen herrlichen Blick.
examples.en: From the tower you have a wonderful view.

commonMistakes.wrong: Der Fluss entlang stehen Bäume. (using accusative-after-noun order for the static meaning)
commonMistakes.why: entlang before the noun with genitive describes a static parallel position; the accusative-after-noun form is specifically for describing movement alongside something.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

topic: Die wichtigsten temporalen Präpositionen (Review und Erweiterung)
summary: Extending the A1 time-preposition set with gegen (approximate), auf (events), bei (activities/weather), and the no-preposition rule for relative time words
explanation: This unit reviews and extends the core temporal prepositions. um can mean an approximate time as well as a precise one ('gegen' does the same, meaning roughly/around a time). auf + dative covers ways, routes, and events/festivals (auf dem Heimweg, auf der Party). bei + dative covers activities and weather conditions (beim Tennisspielen, bei Sonnenschein). A separate, important rule concerns relative time expressions built with (vor)letzte, nächste, vorige, or vergangene: these never take a preposition at all, and always appear in the accusative — 'letzten Mittwoch' rather than 'am letzten Mittwoch'. Bare years also take no preposition, as at A1.

rules.rule: gegen + accusative = approximately (a clock time).
rules.note: Ich komme gegen 8 Uhr.

rules.rule: auf + dative = ways, events, festivals. bei + dative = activities, weather.
rules.note: auf der Reise, auf dem Festival; beim Tennisspielen, bei Sonnenschein

rules.rule: (vor)letzte/nächste/vorige/vergangene + time word: never a preposition, always accusative.
rules.note: letzten Mittwoch (not: am letzten Mittwoch); vorige Woche (not: in der vorigen Woche)

examples.de: Ich komme gegen 8 Uhr zurück.
examples.en: I'll be back around 8.

examples.de: Wir haben uns auf der Party kennengelernt.
examples.en: We met at the party.

examples.de: Letzten Mittwoch hatte ich keine Zeit.
examples.en: Last Wednesday I had no time.

commonMistakes.wrong: am letzten Mittwoch
commonMistakes.why: Relative time expressions with letzte/nächste/vorige/vergangene never take a preposition — they stand alone in the accusative.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: A fuller toolkit for time ranges: ab/von...an, bis(zu), von...bis(zu), zwischen, innerhalb/binnen, über, als, mit+Zahl, zeit, lang
explanation: Beyond the core set, several more prepositions express time ranges precisely. ab or von...an mark a starting point. zu appears fixed before Anfang, Schluss, and Mal. bis (no article) marks an endpoint alone, while bis zu (dative) is used when an article or adjective is present. von...bis (no article) and von...bis zu (with article) express a full range. zwischen + dative gives an approximate window. innerhalb or binnen + genitive marks a limited deadline or timeframe. über + accusative, placed after the noun, follows words like Woche, Wochenende, and Feiertage to mean 'the whole ... through'. als + nominative describes a role or status held during a period ('as a student, I...'). mit + a number marks an age ('at 17 you can...'). zeit + genitive is used only for long stretches of time ('in the time of his whole life'). Duration itself is expressed with lang placed after the noun, or with no preposition at all.

rules.rule: ab / von...an = starting point. bis (no article) / bis zu (dative, with article) = endpoint. von...bis / von...bis zu = full range.
rules.note: Ab morgen. / Von morgen an. / bis Freitag / bis zum 29.6. / von Mai bis Juli

rules.rule: zwischen + dative = approximate window. innerhalb/binnen + genitive = deadline. über + accusative (after the noun) = 'the whole ... through'.
rules.note: zwischen 9 und 11 Uhr; innerhalb von zwei Tagen; die ganze Woche über

rules.rule: als + nominative = role/status during a time. mit + number = age marker. zeit + genitive = only for long periods. lang (after the noun) or no preposition = duration.
rules.note: Als Studentin war ich...; mit 17; drei Monate lang / drei Monate

examples.de: Die Arbeit muss binnen zwei Tagen fertig sein.
examples.en: The work has to be done within two days.

examples.de: Man kann mit 17 den Führerschein machen.
examples.en: You can get your driver's license at 17.

examples.de: Wir fahren drei Monate lang in Urlaub.
examples.en: We're going on vacation for three months.

commonMistakes.wrong: bis der 29.6.
commonMistakes.why: bis alone is only used without an article; once a date takes an article, bis zu (dative) is required instead.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: aus vs. vor for emotional causes (controlled vs. uncontrolled), plus wegen, aufgrund, infolge, angesichts, dank, anlässlich, kraft, mangels
explanation: Several prepositions express a cause or reason, each carrying a distinct shade of meaning. aus + dative (almost always used without an article) expresses an emotion that leads to a controlled, deliberate action, and is often combined with the word Grund. vor + dative (also almost always without an article) expresses an emotion that leads to an uncontrolled reaction. wegen + genitive is the neutral, general-purpose reason word with no emotional coloring (colloquially also used with dative). aufgrund + genitive names the motivation behind a deliberate action, not an event or emotion. infolge + genitive names a prior event that has led to a consequence. angesichts + genitive is used when seeing something directly causes a reaction. dank + genitive (or dative, when the following noun has no article/adjective) is reserved for positive outcomes. anlässlich + genitive marks a specific occasion. kraft + genitive means 'by virtue of' someone's authority. mangels + genitive (or dative under the same no-article/adjective condition) means 'for lack of'.

rules.rule: aus + Dativ (no article) = emotion → controlled action. vor + Dativ (no article) = emotion → uncontrolled reaction.
rules.note: aus Leichtsinn zu schnell fahren; vor Angst zittern

rules.rule: wegen + Genitiv = neutral reason. aufgrund + Genitiv = motivation behind an action. infolge + Genitiv = a preceding event with a consequence. angesichts + Genitiv = reacting to seeing something.
rules.note: wegen der nassen Straße; aufgrund einer Wette; infolge des Unfalls; angesichts eines Unfalls

rules.rule: dank + Genitiv/Dativ (positive outcomes only). anlässlich + Genitiv (a specific occasion). kraft + Genitiv (by authority). mangels + Genitiv/Dativ (for lack of something).
rules.note: Dank seines Airbags ist ihm nichts passiert. / kraft seines Amtes / mangels eines Zeugen

examples.de: Er ist aus Leichtsinn zu schnell gefahren.
examples.en: He drove too fast out of carelessness.

examples.de: Der Fahrer hat vor Angst gezittert.
examples.en: The driver trembled with fear.

examples.de: Dank seines Airbags ist ihm nichts passiert.
examples.en: Thanks to his airbag, nothing happened to him.

commonMistakes.wrong: Er hat vor Wut den Brief zerrissen, um sich zu beruhigen. (treating vor as a controlled/deliberate cause)
commonMistakes.right: Keep vor for uncontrolled reactions and aus for controlled, deliberate ones — tearing something up in anger is uncontrolled, so vor is correct as written; the mistake would be reaching for aus here.
commonMistakes.why: vor marks an emotion driving an uncontrolled reaction; aus marks an emotion behind a deliberate, controlled action — mixing them up reverses the intended nuance.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Some prepositions always follow their noun (Postposition); some can go either side, occasionally with a meaning shift
explanation: Most prepositions sit before their noun, but a few — zuliebe, zufolge, lang, halber — always come after it (Postposition). A more interesting group can appear on either side, sometimes with a subtle difference. nach in its temporal/local sense always precedes the noun, but the fixed idiom 'seiner Meinung nach' places nach after. entlang is genitive before the noun (a static description) but accusative after it (paired with a motion verb) — already covered in Unit 22. gegenüber can go either side of a dative noun, and tends to follow when the noun is a person. ungeachtet + genitive rarely appears after its noun, and only in formal writing. gemäß + dative can appear on either side. wegen + genitive occasionally follows its noun too, but this is rare and mostly limited to formal writing or fixed phrases like 'der Liebe wegen'.

rules.rule: Always Postposition (after the noun): zuliebe (+dative), zufolge (+dative), lang (+accusative), halber (+genitive).
rules.note: meiner Mutter zuliebe

rules.rule: Can go either side, sometimes with a meaning difference: nach (temporal/local always before; 'seiner Meinung nach' fixed after), entlang, gegenüber (often after for people), gemäß, wegen (rare after, mostly formal/fixed phrases).
rules.note: Gegenüber dem Bahnhof gibt es ein Café. / Dem Bahnhof gegenüber liegt ein Café.

examples.de: Seiner Meinung nach ist das keine gute Idee.
examples.en: In his opinion, that's not a good idea.

examples.de: Mir gegenüber verhält sie sich immer korrekt.
examples.en: She always behaves properly toward me.

examples.de: Gemäß Artikel 1 ist die Würde des Menschen unantastbar.
examples.en: According to Article 1, human dignity is inviolable.

commonMistakes.wrong: nach seiner Meinung (using the default before-noun position for this fixed idiom)
commonMistakes.why: This is a fixed expression where nach always follows the noun, unlike its normal temporal/local use, which always precedes the noun.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

topic: Verben mit Nominativ, Akkusativ und Dativ
summary: A full map of verb valency: which objects a verb requires, from nominative-only to nominative+dative+accusative
explanation: German verbs can be grouped by which case combinations they require, and seeing all the patterns side by side clarifies structures that otherwise look scattered. Some verbs take only a subject (nominative), with no object at all — lachen. The largest group takes nominative plus accusative — lieben. A smaller but important group takes nominative, dative, and accusative together, where dative marks the second person involved — schenken (Er schenkt seinem Sohn ein Fahrrad). A separate, small group of verbs takes only nominative and dative, without any logical pattern to predict which verbs belong here — gefallen, helfen — and these have to be memorized as a list, with the rule of thumb that the dative object is almost always a person or something animate. Finally, many verbs pair with a fixed preposition instead of a bare case — warten auf, bitten um. As a side note, sein and werden can take a second nominative to express identity (Er ist Deutscher), and some adjectives behave like dative verbs too (Er ist mir treu).

rules.rule: Nominativ only (no object): lachen. Nominativ + Akkusativ (largest group): lieben. Nominativ + Akkusativ + Dativ (Dativ = second person): schenken, geben, zeigen.
rules.note: Er liebt seine Frau. / Er schenkt seinem Sohn ein Fahrrad.

rules.rule: Nominativ + Dativ only, a small memorized list, Dativ almost always a person/animate: gefallen, helfen, danken, gehören.
rules.note: Deutsch gefällt ihm.

rules.rule: Fixed-preposition verbs take an object governed by a specific preposition rather than a bare case.
rules.note: Er wartet auf seine Frau. Er bittet seine Frau um Hilfe.

examples.de: Er lacht.
examples.en: He laughs. (no object)

examples.de: Er liebt seine Frau.
examples.en: He loves his wife.

examples.de: Deutsch gefällt ihm.
examples.en: He likes German.

commonMistakes.wrong: Deutsch gefällt ihn.
commonMistakes.why: gefallen is a dative-only verb, so the person experiencing the liking takes dative, not accusative.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

topic: Verben, Nomen und Adjektive mit Präpositionen
summary: Question words, da(r)-pronouns, and how the same rules extend to nouns and adjectives, not just verbs
explanation: For any verb with a fixed preposition, asking about a thing uses wo(r) + preposition (adding -r- before a vowel), while asking about a person uses preposition + question word (auf wen, von wem). To refer back to a thing without repeating it, German uses da(r) + preposition, which can also refer back to an entire preceding statement, not just a single noun. When the preposition's object is itself a following clause (a dass-clause or a zu-infinitive), the da(r)-pronoun is still required as a placeholder — it carries no meaning of its own but is grammatically necessary, sitting as a Verbgefährte at the end of the clause, just before any second verb part. Crucially, this whole system — question words, da(r)-pronouns, and clause constructions — works identically when the fixed preposition belongs to an adjective or a noun instead of a verb.

rules.rule: Question word for a thing: wo(r) + preposition. For a person: preposition + question word.
rules.note: Worauf wartest du? / Auf wen wartest du?

rules.rule: da(r) + preposition refers back to a thing or an entire preceding statement.
rules.note: Sie hat den Termin vergessen. Ihr Chef hat sich darüber geärgert.

rules.rule: When the preposition governs a following clause, the da(r)-pronoun is still grammatically required, even though it has no meaning of its own.
rules.note: Sie warten darauf, dass der Bus kommt.

rules.rule: The same system applies to adjectives and nouns with fixed prepositions, not just verbs.
rules.note: Worauf ist er neidisch? Er ist neidisch auf den Mercedes seines Nachbarn.

examples.de: Worauf warten Sie?
examples.en: What are you waiting for?

examples.de: Auf wen wartest du?
examples.en: Who are you waiting for?

examples.de: Sie hatte die berechtigte Hoffnung darauf, die Prüfung zu bestehen.
examples.en: She had the justified hope of passing the exam.

commonMistakes.wrong: Sie ärgert sich, dass alle zu spät kommen. (dropping the required da(r)-pronoun before a following clause)
commonMistakes.right: Sie ärgert sich darüber, dass alle zu spät kommen.
commonMistakes.why: The da(r)-pronoun is grammatically required before a following clause, even though it adds no meaning of its own — omitting it is a common source of error, even though it's occasionally dropped in casual speech.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: A memory aid: auf=focus/future, für=goal, gegen=rejection, über=emotional/topical, um=intense engagement, an=contact
explanation: Memorizing dozens of fixed verb-preposition pairs is easier with a loose meaning pattern to anchor them. auf tends to appear where the meaning involves focus on something (achten auf, stolz auf) or anticipation of the future (warten auf, sich freuen auf). für tends to mark a goal or target one works toward (sich entscheiden für, kämpfen für). gegen marks rejection or opposition (protestieren gegen, sich verteidigen gegen). über covers both emotional reactions to a topic (sich ärgern über, sich freuen über) and simply discussing a topic (sprechen über, sich informieren über). um marks an object being pursued with intensity or effort (sich bewerben um, kämpfen um). an marks contact, in the broad sense of a mental or physical connection to something, and can take either accusative or dative depending on the specific verb (denken an with accusative; teilnehmen an with dative). As a general principle, a verb, its related noun, and its related adjective usually all share the same preposition.

rules.rule: auf = focus or anticipated future. für = goal/target. gegen = rejection.
rules.note: achten auf; sich entscheiden für; protestieren gegen

rules.rule: über = emotional reaction to a topic, or just discussing a topic. um = intense pursuit of an object.
rules.note: sich ärgern über; sich bewerben um

rules.rule: an = contact (mental or physical); can be accusative or dative depending on the specific verb.
rules.note: denken an (Akkusativ); teilnehmen an (Dativ)

rules.rule: A verb and its related noun/adjective usually share the same preposition.
rules.note: sich interessieren für / das Interesse an (an exception worth noting) / interessiert an

examples.de: Ich freue mich auf die Ferien.
examples.en: I'm looking forward to the vacation.

examples.de: Sie kämpfen für die Freiheit.
examples.en: They're fighting for freedom.

examples.de: Zwei Männer kämpfen um eine Frau.
examples.en: Two men are fighting over a woman.

commonMistakes.wrong: sich interessieren an
commonMistakes.why: Despite the related noun das Interesse and adjective interessiert both pairing with an, the verb itself is one of the exceptions and takes für instead.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: A memory aid for dative-preposition verbs: mit=partner, bei=person/institution, nach=search/sense, von=topic/origin, vor=danger, zu=occasion
explanation: The same kind of meaning-based memory aid works for verbs pairing with dative prepositions. mit marks a partner doing something together with the subject (diskutieren mit, sich streiten mit) or a beginning/end point (anfangen mit, aufhören mit). bei marks a person or institution one turns to (sich bewerben bei, sich beschweren bei). nach marks either a search (fragen nach, sich sehnen nach) or a sense-perception (riechen nach, schmecken nach). von marks either a topic (träumen von, handeln von) or an origin/starting point (abhängen von, sich befreien von). vor marks a danger being fled or feared (sich fürchten vor, flüchten vor). zu marks either an occasion (gratulieren zu) or a fit/combination (gehören zu, passen zu). As with the accusative-preposition patterns, a verb's related noun and adjective typically share its preposition.

rules.rule: mit = partner, or beginning/end. bei = person/institution.
rules.note: diskutieren mit; sich bewerben bei

rules.rule: nach = search, or sense-perception. von = topic, or origin/starting point.
rules.note: fragen nach; riechen nach; träumen von; abhängen von

rules.rule: vor = danger/fear. zu = occasion, or fit/combination.
rules.note: sich fürchten vor; gratulieren zu; gehören zu

examples.de: Er hat mit dem Rauchen aufgehört.
examples.en: He's quit smoking.

examples.de: Sie sehnt sich nach Ruhe.
examples.en: She longs for peace and quiet.

examples.de: Das gehört nicht zu meinen Aufgaben.
examples.en: That's not part of my responsibilities.

commonMistakes.wrong: Sie träumt über eine Reise. (borrowing über from erzählen/berichten, which can take either über or von)
commonMistakes.why: träumen von is fixed and only takes von, even though a few related verbs like erzählen/berichten can flexibly take either über or von.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: A precise rule for sein vs. haben: it depends on whether the verb has an accusative object, even for the same verb
explanation: This unit sharpens the sein/haben distinction from earlier levels with a more precise test. Perfekt with sein is used only for verbs that have no accusative object — this covers verbs describing a change of position (kommen, gehen, fahren, springen, fallen...), a change of situation (aufwachen, wachsen, erschrecken, sterben, werden, zerbrechen...), pure event-verbs (passieren, vorkommen, geschehen, gelingen, scheitern...), and the exceptions sein and bleiben. Perfekt with haben covers most other verbs, and always covers reflexive verbs. The genuinely useful insight is that the exact same verb can switch helpers depending on whether an accusative object is present: 'Das Glas ist zerbrochen' (no object, sein) vs. 'Ich habe das Glas zerbrochen' (das Glas is the accusative object, haben); 'Ich bin nach Hause gefahren' (no object, sein) vs. 'Ich habe das Auto in die Garage gefahren' (das Auto is the accusative object, haben) — even though 'Ich bin Auto gefahren' also uses sein, because Auto there is a Verbgefährte, not a true accusative object.

rules.rule: Perfekt with sein: only verbs with no accusative object — position change, situation change, pure event verbs, plus sein/bleiben.
rules.note: kommen, gehen, aufwachen, sterben, passieren, gelingen, sein, bleiben

rules.rule: The same verb can take sein or haben depending on whether an accusative object is present.
rules.note: Das Glas ist zerbrochen. (no object) vs. Ich habe das Glas zerbrochen. (accusative object)

rules.rule: Reflexive verbs always take haben in the Perfekt.
rules.note: Sie hat sich gefreut.

examples.de: Ich bin nach Hause gefahren.
examples.en: I drove home. (no accusative object)

examples.de: Ich habe das Auto in die Garage gefahren.
examples.en: I drove the car into the garage. (das Auto = accusative object)

examples.de: Ich bin heute Auto gefahren.
examples.en: I drove (a car) today. (Auto is a Verbgefährte, not a true object)

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich habe nach Hause gefahren.
commonMistakes.why: fahren without an accusative object describes a change of position and takes sein, not haben.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich bin das Auto in die Garage gefahren.
commonMistakes.right: Ich habe das Auto in die Garage gefahren.
commonMistakes.why: Once fahren has a genuine accusative object (das Auto), the Perfekt switches to haben, even though the same verb takes sein without one.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

topic: Besondere Perfektformen: Modalverben und sehen, hören, lassen
summary: Double infinitive only applies when a second verb is present; alone, these verbs use a normal participle
explanation: Modal verbs, along with sehen, hören, and lassen, form their Perfekt with haben plus a double infinitive — the main verb's infinitive followed by the modal/sehen/hören/lassen's own infinitive — but only when a second full verb is actually present in the sentence: 'Ich habe gehen müssen', 'Ich habe sie winken sehen'. If one of these verbs stands completely alone, with no second verb, it takes a perfectly ordinary participle instead: 'Ich habe Englisch gekonnt', 'Ich habe den Film gesehen', 'Ich habe das Buch hier gelassen'. Also worth remembering: möchten has no Präteritum, and for its Perfekt too, wollen substitutes ('Ich habe gehen wollen' covers a reported möchte as well). In a subordinate clause with three verb forms (a modal, a second verb, and the conjugated auxiliary), the conjugated verb moves to sit before both infinitives rather than after them.

rules.rule: Double infinitive (habe + verb infinitive + modal/sehen/hören/lassen infinitive) only when a second full verb is present.
rules.note: Ich habe gehen müssen. Ich habe die Freunde winken sehen.

rules.rule: Alone, with no second verb, these take a normal ge-...-t participle.
rules.note: Ich habe Englisch gekonnt. Ich habe den Film gesehen. Ich habe das Buch hier gelassen.

rules.rule: In a subordinate clause with a double infinitive, the conjugated verb moves before both infinitives.
rules.note: Ich bin nicht gekommen, weil ich habe arbeiten müssen.

examples.de: Ich habe gehen müssen.
examples.en: I had to go. (with a second verb: double infinitive)

examples.de: Ich habe Englisch gekonnt.
examples.en: I knew English. (alone: normal participle)

examples.de: Ich habe das Buch hier gelassen.
examples.en: I left the book here.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich habe gemusst gehen.
commonMistakes.why: With a second verb present, müssen takes the double-infinitive pattern (gehen müssen), not a normal participle (gemusst).

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich habe Englisch können. (treating the modal alone as needing a bare infinitive)
commonMistakes.why: With no second verb, können takes the ordinary participle gekonnt, not an infinitive.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Plusquamperfekt is often optional outside of nachdem, where it's the only strictly mandatory case
explanation: Building on the core Perfekt/Präteritum usage rule (Perfekt in speech and everyday writing; Präteritum in narrative texts; sein/haben/modals and a few frequent verbs in Präteritum even in speech), this unit adds a practical nuance about the Plusquamperfekt: German isn't always strict about using it. The Plusquamperfekt describes an event that had already finished before another past event, but this relative sequencing is frequently expressed just as clearly with ordinary Perfekt or Präteritum when context makes the order obvious — 'Er hatte/hat schon viele Praktika gemacht, bevor er sich bei der Firma beworben hat' works either way. The one place the Plusquamperfekt is genuinely required, not just possible, is after the conjunction nachdem, where the sequencing rule from Unit 73 (Book 1) is strict.

rules.rule: Plusquamperfekt can often be replaced by Perfekt/Präteritum when the sequence of events is already clear from context.
rules.note: Er hatte/hat schon viele Praktika gemacht, bevor er sich beworben hat.

rules.rule: Only after nachdem is the Plusquamperfekt strictly required (matching the mandatory tense-shift rule).
rules.note: Nachdem er den Anruf beendet hatte, ist er in die Kantine gegangen.

examples.de: Ich habe schon viele Praktika gemacht, bevor ich mich beworben habe.
examples.en: I'd already done a lot of internships before I applied.

examples.de: Nachdem er den Anruf beendet hatte, ging er in die Kantine.
examples.en: After he'd finished the call, he went to the cafeteria.

commonMistakes.wrong: Nachdem er den Anruf beendet hat, ging er in die Kantine. (using Perfekt after nachdem instead of Plusquamperfekt)
commonMistakes.right: Nachdem er den Anruf beendet hatte, ging er in die Kantine.
commonMistakes.why: nachdem is the one context where the earlier-tense requirement is mandatory, not optional — everywhere else, Perfekt/Präteritum can often substitute for Plusquamperfekt.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)
