topic: Vermutung und Zukunft mit dem Futur (Erweiterung)
summary: Informal speech uses Futur 1 mainly for assumptions, promises, and prophecies — not routine future statements
explanation: This unit refines when Futur 1 (werden + infinitive) is actually chosen over the present tense. In informal speech, Futur 1 is mostly reserved for expressing an assumption — strengthened by words like wohl, vielleicht, or bestimmt (Er wird wohl krank sein). For genuine future events, informal speech normally just uses the present tense with a time word (Ich fahre morgen nach Berlin), the same rule established earlier. Two exceptions where informal speech does reach for Futur 1 even for a future event: making a personal promise (Ich werde morgen kommen) and stating a prophecy or firm prediction (Du wirst wahrscheinlich nicht im Lotto gewinnen). Formal speech — news broadcasts, official announcements — uses Futur 1 more broadly, for ordinary future events too (Die Präsidentin wird die Veranstaltung um 20 Uhr eröffnen).

rules.rule: Informal speech: Futur 1 mainly signals an assumption (often with wohl/vielleicht/bestimmt), not a routine future event.
rules.note: Er wird (wohl) krank sein.

rules.rule: Exceptions where informal speech still uses Futur 1 for a future event: promises and prophecies/predictions.
rules.note: Ich werde morgen kommen. (promise) / Du wirst wahrscheinlich nicht gewinnen. (prediction)

rules.rule: Formal speech (news, official announcements) uses Futur 1 for ordinary future events too.
rules.note: Die Präsidentin wird die Rede um 20 Uhr halten.

examples.de: Er wird wohl krank sein.
examples.en: He's probably sick.

examples.de: Ich werde morgen kommen, versprochen.
examples.en: I'll come tomorrow, I promise.

examples.de: Die Präsidentin wird die Veranstaltung eröffnen.
examples.en: The president will open the event. (formal/news register)

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich werde morgen ins Kino gehen. (as a routine plan, in casual conversation)
commonMistakes.why: For an ordinary future plan in informal speech, the present tense is standard; Futur 1 there would sound oddly formal or would be read as a solemn promise rather than a casual plan.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: The core meaning of each modal, plus haben+zu+infinitiv as an authoritative alternative to müssen/dürfen
explanation: Each modal verb's core meaning is worth restating precisely. müssen expresses necessity or obligation. können covers ability, and also permission or possibility. sollen covers an outside request or expectation, asking about someone's wish (only in questions), or reporting an instruction someone gave. wollen expresses a personal plan or aspiration one actively strives for; möchten is its softer, more polite cousin used for everyday wishes (historically the Konjunktiv 2 of mögen, but now treated as its own independent verb). dürfen expresses permission, and its negation nicht dürfen expresses prohibition. mögen mostly expresses a preference and is usually followed directly by a noun rather than an infinitive (Sie mag Jazzmusik). Two modals have an authoritative alternative construction: haben + zu + infinitive can replace müssen when the obligation is imposed by someone on someone else (Du hast das sofort zu tun); the same pattern with a negated infinitive can replace nicht dürfen (Du hast mir gar nichts zu sagen!). müssen's negation can also be softened with nicht brauchen...zu, which is equivalent to nicht müssen.

rules.rule: müssen = necessity. können = ability/permission/possibility. dürfen = permission; nicht dürfen = prohibition.
rules.note: Sie müssen zu Fuß gehen. / Er kann jonglieren. / Bei Grün darf man fahren.

rules.rule: sollen = outside request/expectation, question about a wish, or reported instruction. wollen = personal plan/aspiration; möchten = softer/politer wish.
rules.note: Er soll früh nach Hause kommen. (his mother said so) / Er will studieren. (his own plan)

rules.rule: haben + zu + infinitive (authoritative alternative to müssen or, negated, to nicht dürfen). nicht brauchen...zu = equivalent of nicht müssen.
rules.note: Du hast das sofort zu tun. / Du hast mir nichts zu sagen. / Sie brauchen nicht zu kommen.

examples.de: Was habe ich zu tun?
examples.en: What do I have to do?

examples.de: Sie brauchen nicht zu Fuß zu gehen. Das Auto ist wieder repariert.
examples.en: You don't have to walk. The car is fixed again.

examples.de: Sie mag lieber Walzer als Hiphop.
examples.en: She prefers waltz to hip-hop.

commonMistakes.wrong: Du hast gar nichts zu sagen mir.
commonMistakes.right: Du hast mir gar nichts zu sagen.
commonMistakes.why: The dative pronoun mir belongs before the accusative object in this authoritative construction, following normal object order.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

topic: Andere Bedeutung von Modalverben: Vermutungen über die Gegenwart
summary: können, müssen, dürfen express a precise scale of certainty about a present situation
explanation: können, müssen, and dürfen (in their Konjunktiv 2 or plain present forms) can express how certain the speaker is about something happening right now, forming a specific scale. muss (present indicative) signals near-total certainty, around 99%. müsste (Konjunktiv 2) signals very high confidence, around 85%. dürfte (Konjunktiv 2) signals a likely but less certain guess, around 75%. kann, könnte, or mag signal genuine uncertainty, somewhere between 30 and 50%. The choice of modal verb here directly communicates how sure the speaker is, separate from werden's own assumption use (Unit 39) — these are alternative ways of expressing the same underlying idea, chosen partly for register and partly for exactly how confident the speaker wants to sound.

rules.rule: muss = ~99% certain. müsste (Konjunktiv 2) = ~85%, very likely. dürfte (Konjunktiv 2) = ~75%, likely/probably.
rules.note: Er muss gleich da sein. / Er müsste gleich da sein. / Er dürfte gleich da sein.

rules.rule: kann / könnte / mag = ~30-50%, genuinely uncertain.
rules.note: Er könnte im Stau stecken.

examples.de: Der Bus müsste gleich kommen.
examples.en: The bus should be coming any moment.

examples.de: Sie dürfte keine Lust mehr haben, zur Party zu kommen.
examples.en: She's probably lost interest in coming to the party.

examples.de: Er kann eine Panne haben.
examples.en: He might have had a breakdown.

commonMistakes.wrong: Treating müsste and dürfte as interchangeable levels of certainty
commonMistakes.right: müsste signals higher confidence (~85%) than dürfte (~75%) — they're adjacent but distinct points on the scale.
commonMistakes.why: Both are common ways to express a guess, but choosing between them communicates a real difference in how sure the speaker is.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Beyond leave/allow/have-done, lassen also expresses joint invitations, doing something for someone, passive alternatives, stopping an action, and causation
explanation: Building on the three meanings already familiar (leave something behind, allow, have something done by someone else), lassen has five more common everyday uses. 'Lass(t) uns...' invites joint action ('let's...'), always in the imperative, with no Perfekt form. lassen can express doing something for someone else's benefit ('Lass mich das tragen' = let me carry that for you), also always imperative with no Perfekt form. 'sich lassen + Infinitiv' works as a passive alternative meaning 'can be done' (Unit 16) — 'Viele Krankheiten lassen sich heilen'. lassen can mean stopping or refraining from an action, especially with negation ('kann das Rauchen nicht lassen' = can't stop smoking) — this meaning's Perfekt uses the plain participle gelassen, unlike the double-infinitive forms elsewhere. Finally, lassen can mean being the cause of something happening ('Das schlechte Wetter ließ sie depressiv werden' = the weather made her depressed), using the double-infinitive pattern in the Perfekt.

rules.rule: 'Lass(t) uns...' = joint invitation ('let's...'); always imperative, no Perfekt.
rules.note: Lasst uns gehen!

rules.rule: lassen = doing something for someone's benefit; always imperative, no Perfekt.
rules.note: Lass mich das tragen.

rules.rule: sich lassen + Infinitiv = passive alternative ('can be done'). lassen = stop/refrain from (Perfekt: gelassen). lassen = cause something to happen (Perfekt: double infinitive).
rules.note: Er hat das Rauchen nicht lassen können. / Das Wetter hat sie depressiv werden lassen.

examples.de: Lass uns endlich aufhören zu arbeiten!
examples.en: Let's finally stop working!

examples.de: Der Koffer ist zu schwer für dich. Lass mich ihn tragen.
examples.en: The suitcase is too heavy for you. Let me carry it.

examples.de: Viele Leute können das Rauchen nicht lassen.
examples.en: A lot of people can't quit smoking.

commonMistakes.wrong: Wir haben uns gelassen gehen. (trying to form a Perfekt for the 'let's' meaning)
commonMistakes.right: There is no Perfekt form for this meaning — it's always used in the imperative.
commonMistakes.why: The 'Lass(t) uns' invitation and the 'do something for someone' meaning of lassen only exist in the imperative; they don't have a corresponding past tense form.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Structural rules confirmed (stress, ge- placement, zu placement), the 8 always-inseparable prefixes, and meanings of ab-/an-/aus-/ein-
explanation: Separable prefixes can stand alone as independent words (prepositions or adverbs) and always carry the word stress; they split off in main-clause conjugation but stay joined in the infinitive and in subordinate clauses. Inseparable prefixes are not independent words and are never stressed; exactly eight of them are always inseparable: be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, miss- (though its stress actually falls on the prefix itself, an exception), ver-, and zer-. Inseparable verbs never take ge- in the participle, and their zu-infinitive puts zu in front of the whole verb rather than splitting it. Among the separable prefixes, four are especially productive with distinct core meanings: ab- often signals an ending or moving away (den Fernseher abschalten, um 9 Uhr abfahren); an- signals a beginning or contact (den Fernseher anschalten, die Jacke anziehen); aus- signals movement outward (aus der Wohnung ausziehen); ein- signals movement inward or adjustment (in die Wohnung einziehen, die Lautstärke einstellen).

rules.rule: Separable prefixes: can stand alone, always stressed, split in main-clause conjugation, stay joined in infinitive/subordinate clause.
rules.note: Ich komme mit. / Ich möchte mitkommen. / Er will, dass ich mitkomme.

rules.rule: Eight always-inseparable prefixes: be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, miss- (stressed on the prefix, an exception), ver-, zer-. No ge- in the participle; zu goes in front of the whole verb.
rules.note: habe bekommen (not: bekommen habe ge-); zu bekommen

rules.rule: Core meanings: ab- = ending/away. an- = beginning/contact. aus- = outward. ein- = inward/adjustment.
rules.note: abschalten (end); anschalten (begin); ausziehen (move out); einstellen (adjust)

examples.de: Ich schalte den Fernseher ab.
examples.en: I'm turning off the TV.

examples.de: Ich habe bekommen, was ich wollte.
examples.en: I got what I wanted.

examples.de: Wir ziehen aus der Wohnung aus.
examples.en: We're moving out of the apartment.

commonMistakes.wrong: gebekommen
commonMistakes.why: be- is one of the eight always-inseparable prefixes, which never take ge- in the participle.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: A much larger set of gender-predicting categories, including academic/formal suffixes beyond A1's everyday list
explanation: Beyond the everyday categories from A1 (alcohol, car brands, time periods, weather for der; motorcycle brands, female people for die; diminutives for das), a wider set of academic and formal patterns predicts gender reliably at this level. der: nouns derived from a verb without adding -en (der Flug, from fliegen); -ling; -er (about 90% of the time); -ismus; -ist; -ant/-and/-ent. die: nouns derived from a verb without -en but with an added -t (die Fahrt, from fahren — note: if the verb stem already ends in -t, some of these nouns are actually masculine or feminine unpredictably, like der Rat or die Antwort); zahlen (numbers); -ei; -eit; -in; -schaft; -ung; -e (about 90%); -enz; -ie; -ik; -ion; -itis; -tät; -ur. das: infinitives used as nouns; substantivized adverbs, colors, and adjectives with -e; letters; metals; chemical elements; languages; -chen; -lein; Ge- (about 90%); -nis (about 90%); -ment; -um. Two further rules apply regardless of these categories: in a compound noun, the last word decides the gender (der Englischlehrer); an abbreviation takes the same gender as its spelled-out original (der Lkw, from der Lastkraftwagen).

rules.rule: der: verb-derived nouns without -en; -ling; -er (~90%); -ismus; -ist; -ant/-and/-ent.
rules.note: der Flug (fliegen); der Anarchist; der Praktikant

rules.rule: die: verb-derived nouns without -en but with added -t; numbers; -ei, -eit, -in, -schaft, -ung, -e (~90%), -enz, -ie, -ik, -ion, -itis, -tät, -ur.
rules.note: die Fahrt (fahren); die Freiheit; die Universität

rules.rule: das: infinitives-as-nouns, substantivized adverbs/colors/adjectives, letters, metals, chemical elements, languages, -chen, -lein, Ge- (~90%), -nis (~90%), -ment, -um.
rules.note: das Schlafen; das Silber; das Ergebnis; das Museum

rules.rule: Compounds take the gender of the last word; abbreviations take the gender of the spelled-out term.
rules.note: der Englischlehrer; der Lkw (= der Lastkraftwagen)

examples.de: die Freundschaft
examples.en: the friendship

examples.de: das Museum
examples.en: the museum

examples.de: der Doktorand
examples.en: the doctoral candidate

commonMistakes.wrong: der Freiheit
commonMistakes.why: Nouns ending in -eit are reliably feminine, one of the most consistent B2-level gender patterns.

commonMistakes.wrong: der Sozialismus
commonMistakes.right: ... actually correct — this one is a good check: -ismus nouns are masculine.
commonMistakes.why: Since -ismus nouns are consistently masculine, der Sozialismus is right; the mistake would be doubting this pattern and guessing another gender.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: A complete framework for choosing definite, indefinite, or no article at all
explanation: Article choice follows a fuller logic at this level. The indefinite article marks a first mention or a generalizing statement (Ein Hund ist ein Haustier). The definite article marks something the listener/reader already knows — from earlier in the text, from the immediate situation, because it's unique (der Bundeskanzler), or because a superlative or specific date is involved (der schnellste Läufer, der dritte Mai) — and it can also mark a generalizing statement, so both articles are sometimes possible for generalizations depending on framing; a name with an adjective attached also takes a definite article (das alte Rom), even though bare names normally take none. No article at all appears with uncountable nouns lacking a plural (Hunger, Zeit, Leder), with bare names, with professions/roles stated simply (Ich bin Lehrer), often after ohne/mit/zu, with Verbgefährte noun-verb combinations (Gitarre spielen), and in some Funktionsverbgefüge. One subtlety: some uncountable nouns shift meaning when used in the plural, as with 'Zeit' — 'in Kriegszeiten' means 'during the years of the war', a different sense than the ordinary singular 'Zeit'.

rules.rule: Indefinite: first mention, or generalizing. Definite: already known (text, situation, uniqueness, superlative/date), or generalizing; also required for a name with an adjective.
rules.note: Ein Hund ist ein Haustier. / der Bundeskanzler / das alte Rom

rules.rule: No article: uncountables with no plural, bare names, plain professions/roles, often after ohne/mit/zu, Verbgefährte combos, some Funktionsverbgefüge.
rules.note: Ich habe Hunger. / Sie heißt Lisa. / Er ist Arzt. / Gitarre spielen

rules.rule: Some uncountable nouns shift meaning in the plural.
rules.note: die Zeit (time, singular) vs. in Kriegszeiten (during the war years, plural idiom)

examples.de: Sie ist Krankenschwester von Beruf.
examples.en: She's a nurse by profession.

examples.de: Das schöne Paris hat mich verzaubert.
examples.en: Beautiful Paris enchanted me.

examples.de: In Kriegszeiten war das Leben hart.
examples.en: Life was hard during the war years.

commonMistakes.wrong: Schöne Paris hat mich verzaubert. (dropping the article once an adjective is added to a name)
commonMistakes.right: Das schöne Paris hat mich verzaubert.
commonMistakes.why: A bare name normally takes no article, but as soon as an adjective is attached to it, a definite article becomes necessary.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: The -e insertion exception for foreign words, the no-article-no-genitive rule, and genitive with names/geography
explanation: This unit deepens the genitive rules from B1. The -e- normally inserted before genitive -s (des Mannes) is skipped for foreign/loanwords (des Chefs, des Jobs, not des Chefes). A noun with no article and no adjective simply has no genitive form at all — von + dative is used instead (der Einsatz von Robotern, not der Einsatz Robotern). trotz and wegen use dative rather than genitive when the following noun has no article (trotz Problemen, wegen Gewitters becomes wegen Gewitter informally, though genitive das Gewitters is also possible with an article). Names of people take a genitive -s prefixed before the noun with no article (Davids Auto), except names ending in -s/-x, which take an apostrophe instead (Hans' Auto). Geographical names can be prefixed the same way when they have no article (Deutschlands Süden) or suffixed in the ordinary genitive pattern (der Süden Deutschlands) — but countries that do take an article (die Schweiz) can only use the suffixed pattern (die Hauptstadt der Schweiz). Some geographical names instead form a fixed adjective-like prefix rather than a true genitive (Schweizer Uhren, Berliner Luft).

rules.rule: The -e- before genitive -s is skipped for foreign/loanwords.
rules.note: des Chefs, des Jobs (not des Chefes, des Jobes)

rules.rule: A noun with no article and no adjective has no genitive form — use von + dative instead.
rules.note: der Einsatz von Robotern (not der Einsatz Robotern)

rules.rule: Geographic names: prefixed genitive (no article) OR suffixed genitive; countries with an article only use the suffixed form. Some geographic names form a fixed adjective-prefix instead of a true genitive.
rules.note: Deutschlands Süden / der Süden Deutschlands; die Hauptstadt der Schweiz (not Schweizs Hauptstadt); Berliner Luft

examples.de: Das ist das Büro von Herrn Wagner.
examples.en: That's Mr. Wagner's office.

examples.de: Ich mag den Geschmack von Bier.
examples.en: I like the taste of beer.

examples.de: Die Hauptstadt der Schweiz ist Bern.
examples.en: The capital of Switzerland is Bern.

commonMistakes.wrong: der Einsatz Robotern
commonMistakes.why: A noun with no article/adjective can't form a genitive at all — von + dative fills that gap.

commonMistakes.wrong: Schweizs Hauptstadt
commonMistakes.why: Countries that take an article (die Schweiz) can't be prefixed in the genitive; only the suffixed pattern with der/des works for them.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Adding the -graf ending group, der Herr's unique pattern, and das Herz's partial declension
explanation: Building on the core n-Deklination groups from B1 (male people/animals ending in -e; -and/-ant/-ent/-at/-ist endings; a memorized irregular list), this unit adds nouns ending in -graf (der Geograf, der Astronaut also joins the irregular list) and clarifies two special cases. der Herr takes -n in the singular (den Herrn, dem Herrn, des Herrn) but -en in the plural (die Herren, den Herren) — a rare mismatch between singular and plural endings within the same noun. das Herz is the one neuter exception to the whole n-Deklination pattern, and it only partially follows the rule: the accusative stays unchanged (das Herz), while dative and genitive do take endings (dem Herzen, des Herzens) — though in everyday and medical usage, Herz is increasingly treated as a fully regular noun instead. Across the board, the n-Deklination is used less and less; the -(e)n ending is frequently dropped in both speech and writing.

rules.rule: Additional endings group: -graf (der Geograf); additional irregular list members include der Astronaut.
rules.note: der Geograf, des Geografen

rules.rule: der Herr: singular +n (den/dem/des Herrn), plural +en (die/den Herren).
rules.note: A rare singular/plural mismatch in endings.

rules.rule: das Herz: accusative unchanged, dative/genitive take endings (dem Herzen, des Herzens) — the one neuter exception, and only partial.
rules.note: Colloquially and medically, Herz is often fully regularized instead.

examples.de: Ich spreche mit dem Geografen.
examples.en: I'm speaking with the geographer.

examples.de: Die Herren warten schon.
examples.en: The gentlemen are already waiting.

examples.de: Der Arzt untersucht das Herz. Er hört dem Herzen zu.
examples.en: The doctor examines the heart. He listens to the heart.

commonMistakes.wrong: die Herrn (plural)
commonMistakes.why: der Herr switches to -en in the plural, even though the singular oblique cases use just -n.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Normal, n-Deklination, and adjective-as-noun declension side by side, plus the indefinite plural genitive gap
explanation: This unit places the three noun-declension systems next to each other for direct comparison: the normal pattern (der Mann, des Mannes), the n-Deklination (der Herr, des Herrn), and adjectives used as nouns (der Alte, ein Alter — following adjective endings, not noun endings, as covered in Units 65-66/Book 1). One structural gap applies to both the normal pattern and the n-Deklination: there is no indefinite plural genitive form at all (no equivalent of 'einer' for an indefinite plural) — this must always be replaced with von + dative. Adjectives-as-nouns are the exception: they do have a genitive plural indefinite form (der Alten / Alter). A further reminder for adjectives-as-neutral-nouns: after alles/das, the ending is -e; after etwas/nichts/viel/wenig/ein bisschen, it's -es; and in the dative, this type of noun always ends in -em regardless of which quantity word precedes it.

rules.rule: Normal and n-Deklination nouns have no indefinite plural genitive — use von + dative instead.
rules.note: der Freunde (definite, fine) but von Freunden (indefinite, not 'einer Freunde')

rules.rule: Adjectives-as-nouns DO have an indefinite plural genitive.
rules.note: der Alten (definite) / Alter (indefinite plural genitive)

rules.rule: Adjective-as-neutral-noun endings: alles/das + -e; etwas/nichts/viel/wenig/ein bisschen + -es; dative always -em.
rules.note: alles Gute; etwas Gutes; mit etwas Gutem

examples.de: Das Schicksal vieler Kinder ist ungewiss.
examples.en: The fate of many children is uncertain. (using von+dative-style indefinite plural)

examples.de: Das ist die Meinung der Alten.
examples.en: That's the opinion of the elderly.

examples.de: Mit allem Guten wünsche ich dir Glück.
examples.en: With all good wishes, I wish you luck.

commonMistakes.wrong: eines Kindern Erlebnis (attempting an indefinite plural genitive for a normal noun)
commonMistakes.why: Normal (and n-Deklination) nouns have no indefinite plural genitive form at all; von + dative fills that specific gap.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Standalone pronouns replacing a noun already mentioned: einer, keiner, welcher, meiner, and the declension of 'man'
explanation: When a noun has already been mentioned and you want to refer to 'one (of them)' without repeating it, German uses einer/eine/eins (indefinite), keiner/keine/kein(e)s (negative), welcher/welche/welches (matching a specific one already named), or meiner/deiner/seiner... (possessive) as standalone pronouns — all declined through the cases like the corresponding article, though the dative plural of welcher has no strong ending pattern of its own in this construction (it takes -en directly, like an adjective would). For an uncountable noun with no plural, welch- (with no ending) substitutes rather than welcher/welche/welches. The indefinite pronoun einer can be intensified with irgend- for extra vagueness (irgendeiner, irgendwelche). 'man' itself declines: nominative man, accusative einen, dative einem — a detail often overlooked since 'man' is usually only seen in the nominative.

rules.rule: Standalone pronouns replacing an already-mentioned noun: einer/eine/eins, keiner/keine/kein(e)s, welcher/welche/welches, meiner/deiner/seiner..., declined through the cases like their matching article.
rules.note: Ich brauche keine Socken, aber bringst du mir welche mit?

rules.rule: For uncountable nouns, welch- (no ending) replaces welcher/welche/welches.
rules.note: Ich trinke Wein. Möchtest du auch welchen?

rules.rule: 'man' declines: nominative man, accusative einen, dative einem.
rules.note: Wenn man krank ist, schreibt einen der Arzt krank und gibt einem ein Rezept.

examples.de: Brauchst du ein Taschentuch? Ich habe noch eins.
examples.en: Do you need a tissue? I still have one.

examples.de: Meine Schuhe sind zu eng. Mit welchen kann ich besser gehen?
examples.en: My shoes are too tight. Which ones can I walk better in?

examples.de: Wenn man krank ist, gibt einem der Arzt ein Rezept.
examples.en: When you're sick, the doctor gives you a prescription.

commonMistakes.wrong: Möchtest du auch welchen Wein? (adding a noun after this standalone pronoun use)
commonMistakes.why: welch- here stands alone, replacing the previously mentioned uncountable noun (Wein) rather than being used as an article before a repeated noun.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: man, alle, jeder, jemand, niemand for people — grammatical number and how they're generalized
explanation: Five words cover indefinite reference to people, each with its own grammatical behavior. man is grammatically singular and generalizes across all people, often used to depersonalize an opinion or experience (Wenn man reist, erweitert man seinen Horizont). alle is grammatically plural, referring to everyone in general (Alle können mitmachen; dative allen, genitive aller). jeder/jede is grammatically singular, referring to any single individual taken generically (Jeder/Jede kann mitmachen); alle and jeder can also function as an article directly before a noun — alle only before a plural noun, jeder only before a singular one. jemand (someone, an unspecified person) and niemand (no one, its negation) are both grammatically singular, and can optionally be declined, though this is increasingly dropped in casual speech (mit jemandem or mit jemand are both heard).

rules.rule: man = generalizing, singular. alle = everyone, plural. jeder/jede = any one individual, singular.
rules.note: Wenn man reist, ... / Alle können mitmachen. / Jeder kann mitmachen.

rules.rule: alle and jeder can also function as an article: alle only before plural nouns, jeder only before singular nouns.
rules.note: alle Menschen; jeder Mann; jedes Auto

rules.rule: jemand/niemand = someone/no one, singular; declension is optional and often dropped in casual speech.
rules.note: Hast du mit jemand(em) gesprochen?

examples.de: Wenn man berühmt ist, kommen alle und jeder will ein Autogramm.
examples.en: When you're famous, everyone comes and each person wants an autograph.

examples.de: Kennt jemand den Mann da?
examples.en: Does anyone know that man?

examples.de: Niemand will ein Autogramm von ihm.
examples.en: No one wants his autograph.

commonMistakes.wrong: Alle ist froh. (treating alle as grammatically singular)
commonMistakes.why: alle is grammatically plural and takes a plural verb, unlike man or jeder, which are singular.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: alles/nichts/etwas for things (grammatically singular); alle/beide/einige/manche work for both people and things with different grammatical number
explanation: alles, nichts, and etwas refer to things or abstract concepts and are always grammatically singular, even though 'alles' conceptually covers many things at once (Alles ist gut). These three can also stand directly before a nominalized adjective (etwas Schönes, nichts Gutes, alles Gute). A separate group — alle, beide, einige, manche — can refer to either things or people, but the grammatical number differs by which one they refer to: for things, they behave grammatically singular (alles, beides, einiges, manches — note the different form!) with dative allem/beidem/einigem/manchem and genitive replaced by von; for people, they behave grammatically plural (alle, beide, einige, manche) with dative allen/beiden/einigen/manchen and genitive aller/beider/einiger/mancher. These pronouns can also stand for concrete things when the context makes clear which things are meant, even without switching form.

rules.rule: alles/nichts/etwas: things/abstracts, always grammatically singular; can precede a nominalized adjective.
rules.note: Alles ist gut. / etwas Schönes

rules.rule: alle/beide/einige/manche for people: grammatically plural. For things: different forms (alles/beides/einiges/manches), grammatically singular.
rules.note: Alle sind froh. (people, plural) vs. Alles ist gut. (things, singular)

rules.rule: For things, genitive is replaced by von + dative in this group; for people, a true genitive exists (aller, beider, einiger, mancher).
rules.note: von allem, von beidem (things) vs. aller, beider (people)

examples.de: Tee oder Kaffee? Beide trinken beides.
examples.en: Tea or coffee? They both drink both.

examples.de: Einige sind schon angekommen.
examples.en: Some (people) have already arrived.

examples.de: Hier stehen viele Autos, alle sind zufällig rot.
examples.en: There are many cars here, all of them happen to be red.

commonMistakes.wrong: Alle ist gut. (mixing up the things-form with the people-form)
commonMistakes.why: Referring to things/abstracts requires the singular form alles, not the plural people-form alle.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: The full case-by-case adjective table, the genitive-masculine/neuter exception, and small spelling quirks
explanation: This unit lays out the complete adjective-ending system across all four cases and all genders in one table, confirming and extending the 'signal' principle from earlier levels: the case/gender signal sits either on the article or the adjective, never absent entirely. In the accusative masculine, in the plural with any article, and throughout the entire dative and genitive, the adjective takes an additional -n. The one true exception is the genitive masculine and neuter without an article: there, the adjective takes only -n (not the expected strong -es), because the noun itself already carries the genitive -s, and marking the signal twice would be redundant. A few smaller rules round this out: after mein/dein/etc., adjective endings match the pattern used after kein; multiple adjectives before the same noun all take the same ending; a predicate adjective (after the noun, following sein) never takes any ending; viel and wenig before uncountable nouns take no ending; mehr is never declined at all; and adjectives ending in -el drop their e when a further ending is added (komfortabel → ein komfortables Zimmer).

rules.rule: Additional -n on the adjective: masculine accusative, plural with any article, and the entire dative and genitive (except one case below).
rules.note: einem schnellen Zug; den langen Staus; des schnellen Zuges

rules.rule: Exception: genitive masculine/neuter with NO article — adjective takes only -n, not -es, since the noun's own -s already signals genitive.
rules.note: schnellen Zuges (not schnelles Zuges)

rules.rule: viel/wenig before uncountables: no ending. mehr: never declined. -el adjectives drop the e before an ending.
rules.note: viel Zeit; mehr Bücher; ein komfortables Hotelzimmer (from komfortabel)

examples.de: Mit dem schnellen Auto steht man oft in einem langen Stau.
examples.en: With the fast car, you often end up in a long traffic jam.

examples.de: Sie hat viele Bücher, er hat mehr Bücher.
examples.en: She has many books, he has more books.

examples.de: Ein komfortables Hotelzimmer wäre schön.
examples.en: A comfortable hotel room would be nice.

commonMistakes.wrong: schnelles Zuges (adding -es in the genitive without an article)
commonMistakes.why: The genitive masculine/neuter without an article is the one exception where the adjective takes only -n, since the noun already marks the genitive with its own -s.

commonMistakes.wrong: komfortabeles Zimmer
commonMistakes.why: Adjectives ending in -el drop their e before adding a further ending.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: wie vs. als for comparisons, the 'one of the best' pattern, aller- intensifying a superlative, and superlative adverbs without am
explanation: For comparisons, (genau)so/gleich + the plain adjective + wie expresses equality ('as...as'), while the comparative form + als expresses inequality ('...er than') — also extended by anders als ('different from') and umgekehrt als ('the opposite of'). A special construction — einer/eine der + superlative + genitive plural — expresses 'one of the best/most...' (Er ist einer der besten Autoren Deutschlands); this genitive is always plural and always paired with a superlative adjective. The prefix aller- can intensify a superlative even further (am allerschönsten, das schönste aller Gebäude). Separately, a handful of adjectives have superlative-derived adverbs used without am, whose meaning shifts slightly from the ordinary superlative: frühestens, spätestens, höchstens, mindestens, erstens, zweitens — 'Er muss schnellstens kommen' means it's urgent, not literally 'fastest of all'.

rules.rule: (genau)so/gleich + adjective + wie = equal. Comparative + als (also: anders als, umgekehrt als) = unequal.
rules.note: Montag war es gleich warm wie Dienstag. / Sonntag war es heißer als Samstag.

rules.rule: einer/eine der + superlative + genitive plural = 'one of the best/most...'
rules.note: Sie war eine der schönsten Frauen der Welt.

rules.rule: aller- intensifies a superlative further. Some superlative-derived adverbs are used without am and shift meaning.
rules.note: am allerschönsten; Er muss schnellstens kommen. (= as fast as possible, urgently)

examples.de: Er ist einer der besten Autoren Deutschlands.
examples.en: He's one of the best authors in Germany.

examples.de: Das schönste aller Gebäude steht in Rom.
examples.en: The most beautiful of all buildings is in Rome.

examples.de: Bitte antworten Sie spätestens morgen.
examples.en: Please reply by tomorrow at the latest.

commonMistakes.wrong: einer der beste Autor Deutschlands
commonMistakes.why: This construction requires the superlative adjective with a genitive plural noun, not a singular noun with an unmarked adjective.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

topic: Partizip I und II als Adjektiv (Vertiefung)
summary: Partizip II as an adjective adds passive/completed meaning; for sein-Perfekt verbs it's active instead, and reflexive pronouns behave differently for each
explanation: Partizip I as an adjective (Unit 80, Book 1) describes an action happening at the same time and actively performed by the noun — 'ein malendes Mädchen' is a girl who is painting. Partizip II as an adjective adds either a passive or a completed/prior-time meaning: 'ein gemaltes Mädchen' is a girl who has been painted (passive) — but for verbs that form their Perfekt with sein, Partizip II as an adjective keeps an active meaning instead, simply marking that the action is completed: 'ein angekommener Zug' is a train that has arrived, not a train something was done to. Partizip II as an adjective can only be built from transitive verbs (verbs that take an accusative object) when used passively. Reflexive pronouns behave differently for the two: they appear before Partizip I (eine sich automatisch öffnende Tür) but disappear entirely with Partizip II. The construction sein + Partizip II, widely used to describe a resulting state (Die Tür ist geöffnet), is often given its own name in grammar references: the 'Zustandspassiv' (stative passive).

rules.rule: Partizip I as adjective = active, simultaneous. Partizip II as adjective = passive/completed — but active/completed for sein-Perfekt verbs.
rules.note: ein malendes Mädchen (active, now) vs. ein gemaltes Mädchen (passive, already painted) vs. ein angekommener Zug (active, sein-verb, already happened)

rules.rule: Reflexive pronouns appear before Partizip I but disappear with Partizip II.
rules.note: eine sich öffnende Tür / eine geöffnete Tür

rules.rule: sein + Partizip II describing a resulting state is sometimes called the Zustandspassiv.
rules.note: Die Tür ist geöffnet.

examples.de: Ein viel zu spät angekommener Zug hat den Anschluss verpasst.
examples.en: A train that arrived far too late missed the connection.

examples.de: Eine sich automatisch öffnende Tür ist praktisch.
examples.en: An automatically opening door is convenient.

examples.de: Ein gekochtes Ei schmeckt mir gut.
examples.en: I like a boiled egg.

commonMistakes.wrong: ein gekommenes Zug (treating a sein-Perfekt verb's Partizip II as passive)
commonMistakes.why: For verbs that use sein in the Perfekt, Partizip II as an adjective carries an active, completed meaning (the train has arrived), not a passive one — there's no 'doer' acting on the train.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Konjunktiv 1 formation; the wir/sie and often ich forms get replaced by Konjunktiv 2 because they look identical to the indicative
explanation: When reporting what someone else said, German can simply use the indicative with dass, or use Konjunktiv 1 to signal neutrality or distance from the claim — this is common in formal writing like news reports. Konjunktiv 1 is built from the bare verb stem plus its own set of endings. The catch: the wir and sie(plural) forms are always identical to the ordinary present tense, and the ich-form usually is too, so using them wouldn't clearly signal that you're quoting rather than stating a fact yourself — for that reason, these forms get replaced by the würde-construction (or hätte/wäre/could-form) from Konjunktiv 2 instead. The du/ihr forms of Konjunktiv 1 are old-fashioned in real usage and are also typically replaced by Konjunktiv 2. Only the 3rd person singular (er/sie/es) is reliably different from the indicative, so it's the one form always usable in genuine Konjunktiv 1. sein has its own special short forms throughout (sei, sei(e)st, sei, seien, seiet, seien). For future or passive reported statements, werden itself goes into Konjunktiv 1 (er werde...), or is likewise replaced by würde. Reported questions keep the original question word, or use ob for a yes/no question, with the verb in Konjunktiv.

rules.rule: Konjunktiv 1 = verb stem + Konjunktiv endings. wir/sie forms (and often ich) are identical to the indicative and get replaced with Konjunktiv 2 (würde-form) to signal reported speech clearly.
rules.note: er kaufe (genuine Konjunktiv 1) but wir würden kaufen (replacing wir kaufen, which looks indicative)

rules.rule: du/ihr forms of Konjunktiv 1 are outdated and also typically replaced by Konjunktiv 2. Only 3rd person singular is reliably distinct and always usable.
rules.note: Only er/sie/es forms are dependably recognizable as Konjunktiv 1.

rules.rule: sein has its own full set of short forms: sei, sei(e)st, sei, seien, seiet, seien. For future/passive reported speech, werden goes into Konjunktiv 1 or is replaced by würde.
rules.note: Er sagt, er sei fertig. / Er sagt, er werde bald kommen.

examples.de: Er behauptet, die Leute seien faul.
examples.en: He claims the people are lazy.

examples.de: Sie sagt, sie würden morgen ankommen.
examples.en: She says they'll arrive tomorrow. (wir/sie-form replaced by würde)

examples.de: Er fragte, ob er einfache Leute kenne.
examples.en: He asked whether he knew simple people.

commonMistakes.wrong: Sie sagen, sie kaufen ein neues Auto. (as an attempt at Konjunktiv 1 for wir/sie, using a form identical to the indicative)
commonMistakes.right: Sie sagen, sie würden ein neues Auto kaufen.
commonMistakes.why: The genuine Konjunktiv 1 wir/sie form looks exactly like the indicative present, so it fails to signal reported speech — the würde-form is used instead precisely to make the quoting clear.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Past reported speech uses haben/sein in Konjunktiv 1 (or replaced by Konjunktiv 2) plus the participle — only one past form exists
explanation: Reporting something in the past uses haben or sein in Konjunktiv 1 plus the past participle, following exactly the same sein/haben choice as the ordinary Perfekt. Whenever the Konjunktiv 1 form (habe/sei) would be identical to the indicative — which happens for ich, wir, and sie(plural) — it gets replaced by the Konjunktiv 2 equivalent (hätte/wäre) instead, for the same clarity reason as in the present tense. With a modal verb, the past reported form uses habe (Konjunktiv 1, or hätte if replaced) plus the verb's infinitive plus the modal's infinitive — a double infinitive, just like the ordinary Perfekt of modals. The passive past reported form uses sei (or wäre) plus the participle plus worden. Just as in ordinary Konjunktiv 2, there is only one past-tense form in Konjunktiv 1 too — it corresponds to whatever indicative tense (Präteritum, Perfekt, or Plusquamperfekt) the meaning calls for. Whether a piece of reported speech appears in the present or past Konjunktiv depends entirely on the meaning of what's being reported, not on whether the introducing verb (sagt/sagte/hat gesagt) itself is present or past.

rules.rule: Past reported speech: habe/sei (Konjunktiv 1, or hätte/wäre if identical to indicative) + past participle — same sein/haben choice as ordinary Perfekt.
rules.note: Er sei gekommen. / Ich hätte geworfen. (ich-form replaced)

rules.rule: With a modal: habe/hätte + verb infinitive + modal infinitive (double infinitive).
rules.note: Er habe kaufen wollen. Sie hätten sich einigen können.

rules.rule: Passive past reported speech: sei/wäre + participle + worden.
rules.note: Die Dose sei geworfen worden.

rules.rule: Only one past form exists in reported speech, just as in Konjunktiv 2; the choice between present and past Konjunktiv depends on the reported meaning, independent of the introducing verb's own tense.
rules.note: Er sagt/sagte/hat gesagt, er sei gerade erst gekommen. (all three introducing forms work with the same reported past)

examples.de: Der Mann sagt, er sei gerade erst gekommen.
examples.en: The man says he only just arrived.

examples.de: Der Verkäufer behauptet, der Mann habe die Dose geworfen.
examples.en: The salesman claims the man threw the can.

examples.de: Sie sagte, sie habe gehen müssen.
examples.en: She said she'd had to go.

commonMistakes.wrong: Er sagte, er ist gekommen. (using plain indicative instead of any Konjunktiv form when reporting)
commonMistakes.why: Reported speech in a formal or distancing register uses Konjunktiv (1, or 2 as substitute), not the plain indicative, even though the indicative with dass is also grammatically possible in less formal contexts.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Extending während/nachdem/bevor/wenn/als with bis, ehe, solange, sobald/sowie, and sooft
explanation: This unit widens the temporal-conjunction toolkit already familiar from earlier levels (während, nachdem, bevor, seit(dem), wenn, als) with five more precise options. bis marks the end of a phase or action ('Bis das Essen fertig ist, ...'). ehe is simply a synonym for bevor. solange marks two parallel activities or states that continue until some endpoint ('Solange ich koche, bleibt die Katze neben mir sitzen'). sobald and sowie both mean 'as soon as', marking the very start of an action. sooft means 'every time', marking a repeated action. Like the other temporal conjunctions, all of these can also open the sentence, moving to position 1 with the main clause's verb following immediately after the comma.

rules.rule: bis = end of a phase/action. ehe = synonym for bevor.
rules.note: Bis das Essen fertig ist, ... / Ehe ich eine Katze hatte, ...

rules.rule: solange = parallel activities/states until an endpoint. sobald/sowie = as soon as (start of an action). sooft = every time (repeated action).
rules.note: Solange ich koche, ... / Sobald ich esse, ... / Sooft ich sie rufe, ...

rules.rule: All temporal conjunctions can move the subordinate clause to position 1, with the main clause verb following immediately.
rules.note: Sobald ich esse, will die Katze auch ihr Futter.

examples.de: Bis der Zug ankommt, lese ich noch etwas.
examples.en: Until the train arrives, I'll read a bit more.

examples.de: Solange es regnet, bleiben wir drinnen.
examples.en: As long as it's raining, we'll stay inside.

examples.de: Sooft ich ihn anrufe, ist er beschäftigt.
examples.en: Every time I call him, he's busy.

commonMistakes.wrong: Sobald ich esse, will die Katze auch ihr Futter haben will. (double verb placement)
commonMistakes.right: Sobald ich esse, will die Katze auch ihr Futter haben.
commonMistakes.why: The main clause after a fronted temporal Nebensatz still follows ordinary verb-second order, with the verb appearing once, right after the comma.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: weil vs. da for reasons (da usually opens the sentence and never answers a direct 'why'); obwohl for concession
explanation: weil and da both introduce a reason, but they behave differently. weil-clauses most often follow the main clause. da-clauses most often open the sentence, in position 1, and — importantly — a da-clause is never used to directly answer a spoken 'Warum...?' question; it's reserved for giving background reasoning within a larger statement, often something already somewhat obvious or contextual. obwohl introduces a concessive clause (a reason you might expect to lead to the opposite outcome) — 'Obwohl ich spät aufgestanden bin, habe ich meine S-Bahn noch bekommen.' Two rarer written synonyms of obwohl exist: obschon, obzwar, and obgleich.

rules.rule: weil-clauses usually follow the main clause. da-clauses usually open the sentence and are never used to directly answer 'Warum...?'.
rules.note: Ich komme spät, weil mein Bus eine Panne hatte. / Da der Nahverkehr schlecht finanziert wird, wundert mich das nicht.

rules.rule: obwohl = concessive (a reason that would normally lead to the opposite outcome). Rarer written synonyms: obschon, obzwar, obgleich.
rules.note: Obwohl ich spät aufgestanden bin, habe ich meine S-Bahn noch bekommen.

examples.de: Ich habe Glück gehabt, obwohl ich spät aufgestanden bin.
examples.en: I got lucky, even though I got up late.

examples.de: Da der Bus so oft ausfällt, nehme ich lieber das Fahrrad.
examples.en: Since the bus is cancelled so often, I'd rather take my bike.

commonMistakes.wrong: Warum kommst du spät? – Da mein Bus eine Panne hatte. (answering a direct question with a da-clause)
commonMistakes.right: Weil mein Bus eine Panne hatte.
commonMistakes.why: A da-clause is never used to directly answer a spoken 'why' question — weil is the natural choice there; da is reserved for background reasoning stated within a larger sentence.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: sodass for a straightforward consequence; so/dermaßen/derart...dass for an emphasized one, tied to intensity
explanation: A consecutive clause states the consequence or result of the situation described in the main clause. sodass introduces this plainly, with no extra emphasis (Ich war spät, sodass ich den Bus verpasst habe). so, dermaßen, or derart placed before an adjective in the main clause — paired with dass introducing the consequence in the subordinate clause — adds emphasis, stressing exactly how extreme the quality was (Ich war so spät, dass ich den Bus verpasst habe; Ich hatte eine derartige Verspätung, dass...). If there's no adjective to attach to, so/dermaßen/derart goes with the verb instead, and the intensified quality has to be inferred from context (Ich bin so gerannt, dass ich außer Atem war — understood as 'so fast'). These consecutive connectors can never move to position 1 in the sentence.

rules.rule: sodass = plain consequence, no emphasis.
rules.note: Ich war spät, sodass ich den Bus verpasst habe.

rules.rule: so/dermaßen/derart + adjective, ..., dass = emphasized consequence, stressing the adjective.
rules.note: Ich war so spät, dass ich den Bus verpasst habe.

rules.rule: Without an adjective, so/dermaßen/derart attaches to the verb instead, with the intensified quality inferred from context. These connectors cannot occupy position 1.
rules.note: Ich bin so gerannt, dass ich außer Atem war.

examples.de: Der Akku war leer, sodass ich die Nachricht nicht lesen konnte.
examples.en: The battery was dead, so I couldn't read the message.

examples.de: Ich war so müde, dass ich sofort einschlief.
examples.en: I was so tired that I fell asleep immediately.

commonMistakes.wrong: Sodass ich den Bus verpasst habe, war ich spät. (moving sodass to position 1)
commonMistakes.right: Ich war spät, sodass ich den Bus verpasst habe.
commonMistakes.why: Consecutive clauses can't be fronted to position 1 — they always follow the main clause they describe the consequence of.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: wenn/falls for conditions (combinable with nur/sogar/außer); während/wohingegen for contrast
explanation: wenn and falls both introduce a conditional clause ('under the condition that...'); wenn can also be read temporally depending on context, while falls only ever has a conditional meaning. Either can combine with nur ('only if'), sogar ('even if', highlighting something exceptional), or außer ('except if') for more precise conditions. On the contrast side, während can be read either temporally or adversatively depending on context (Während ich immer das neueste Handy habe, benutzt du eine Antiquität — clearly a contrast here, not a simultaneous-action sense). wohingegen turns the previous statement into an explicit contrast with what follows, and can always be replaced by a new main clause introduced with dagegen.

rules.rule: wenn (also possibly temporal) and falls (only conditional) introduce a condition; combine with nur/sogar/außer for precision.
rules.note: Falls ich Zeit habe, komme ich. / Nur wenn ich Zeit habe, komme ich.

rules.rule: während can be temporal or adversative depending on context. wohingegen always marks contrast and is replaceable by dagegen.
rules.note: Während ich Sport treibe, liest du. (temporal) vs. Während ich sparsam bin, gibst du viel aus. (adversative)

examples.de: Falls ich es schaffe, komme ich heute noch zu dir.
examples.en: If I manage it, I'll come to you today after all.

examples.de: Du gibst dauernd Geld für Handys aus, wohingegen ich meins spare.
examples.en: You constantly spend money on phones, whereas I save mine.

commonMistakes.wrong: Treating während as always temporal
commonMistakes.right: Check the context — während can just as easily signal a contrast, especially when the two halves of the sentence describe opposing behaviors.
commonMistakes.why: während is genuinely ambiguous between a temporal and an adversative reading; only the content of the sentence disambiguates it.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: indem for 'how' by simple method; dadurch dass for 'how/by what means', which can also be split for emphasis
explanation: Modal clauses of method answer the question 'wie?' — by what method or means something is done. indem describes a straightforward method (Sie können den Motorraum öffnen, indem Sie hier drehen). dadurch dass also answers 'wie?'/'wodurch?', but has an extra structural feature: 'dadurch' can be pulled out and placed elsewhere in the main clause for emphasis, stressing whichever part of the sentence it now sits next to (Ich kam dadurch noch pünktlich, dass mir der Autodienst geholfen hat — emphasizing 'noch pünktlich'). dadurch dass can also carry a causal meaning (a reason, similar to weil) rather than a purely methodical one — but when it's used causally, it can no longer be reworded with indem, since indem is strictly about method.

rules.rule: indem = method, answers 'wie?'.
rules.note: Sie öffnen den Motorraum, indem Sie an dem Griff drehen.

rules.rule: dadurch dass = method, answers 'wie?'/'wodurch?'; dadurch can be separated and placed elsewhere in the main clause for emphasis.
rules.note: Der Motorraum öffnet sich dadurch, dass Sie am Griff drehen.

rules.rule: dadurch dass can also express a cause (like weil) rather than a method — in that use, it cannot be reworded with indem.
rules.note: Sie hat viele Vorteile, dadurch dass sie gut Deutsch spricht. (causal, not indem-replaceable)

examples.de: Sie können das Gerät reinigen, indem Sie die Abdeckung öffnen.
examples.en: You can clean the device by opening the cover.

examples.de: Man kann eine Sprache lernen, dadurch dass man viel liest.
examples.en: You can learn a language by reading a lot.

commonMistakes.wrong: Sie hat viele Vorteile, indem sie gut Deutsch spricht. (using indem for a causal meaning)
commonMistakes.right: Sie hat viele Vorteile, dadurch dass sie gut Deutsch spricht.
commonMistakes.why: indem is strictly about method; when dadurch dass is used causally rather than methodically, it can't be swapped for indem.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: The zu-infinitive can point to the same time as the main clause or look back before it, in both active and passive form
explanation: A zu-infinitive clause has no meaning of its own beyond a grammatical function, but it does mark relative timing. When built as zu + plain infinitive (or, in the passive, zu + participle + werden), it describes something simultaneous with the main clause's own time: 'Wir haben Angst, zu spät zu kommen' (the risk of coming late is happening now, at the same time as having the fear). When built as zu + participle + sein/haben in the infinitive (a 'perfect infinitive'), it always looks back to a point before the main clause's own time, regardless of whether the main clause itself is present or past: 'Wir haben Angst, zu spät gekommen zu sein' and 'Wir hatten Angst, zu spät gekommen zu sein' both mean the lateness happened before the fear, just anchored at different points. The same logic extends to the passive: 'geführt zu werden' (simultaneous passive) vs. 'geführt worden zu sein' (retrospective passive).

rules.rule: zu + infinitive (or zu + participle + werden, passive) = simultaneous with the main clause's time.
rules.note: Wir haben Angst, einen Fehler zu machen. / vom Navi falsch geführt zu werden.

rules.rule: zu + participle + sein/haben (infinitive) = retrospective, before the main clause's time, regardless of whether the main clause is present or past.
rules.note: Wir haben/hatten Angst, einen Fehler gemacht zu haben.

examples.de: Es ist schön, eine tolle Oper zu hören.
examples.en: It's lovely to hear a great opera. (simultaneous)

examples.de: Wir hoffen, nicht zu spät gekommen zu sein.
examples.en: We hope we haven't arrived too late. (retrospective)

commonMistakes.wrong: Wir hoffen, nicht zu spät zu kommen. (when the lateness already happened, before the hoping)
commonMistakes.right: Wir hoffen, nicht zu spät gekommen zu sein.
commonMistakes.why: If the arriving already happened before the hoping, the retrospective (perfect) infinitive is needed, not the simultaneous plain infinitive.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

topic: Nebensatz mit dass und Infinitiv mit zu
summary: Same subject → either a zu-infinitive or a dass-clause works; different subjects → only dass works
explanation: When the main clause's subject is also implied as the subject of the following action, both a zu-infinitive clause and a dass-clause (repeating the subject explicitly) are grammatically available, and speakers can choose either ('Ich habe das Gefühl, dicker zu werden' or 'Ich habe das Gefühl, dass ich dicker werde'). But if the two clauses actually have different subjects, only the dass-clause works, since a zu-infinitive clause has no room for its own separate subject. Both the zu-infinitive clause and the dass-clause can also open the sentence, taking position 1. A useful related idiom: 'gerade/schon dabei sein' + a zu-infinitive clause describes being in the middle of doing something right now, similar to a progressive tense.

rules.rule: Same subject in both clauses: zu-infinitive OR dass-clause, either works.
rules.note: Ich habe das Gefühl, dicker zu werden. / Ich habe das Gefühl, dass ich dicker werde.

rules.rule: Different subjects: only the dass-clause works.
rules.note: Ich habe das Gefühl, dass mein Mann dicker wird.

rules.rule: 'gerade/schon dabei sein' + zu-infinitive = currently in the middle of doing something.
rules.note: Ich bin gerade dabei, etwas abzunehmen.

examples.de: Ich freue mich schon darauf, die Oper zu sehen.
examples.en: I'm already looking forward to seeing the opera.

examples.de: Ich freue mich, dass mein Mann jetzt abnimmt.
examples.en: I'm happy that my husband is losing weight now.

examples.de: Ich bin gerade dabei, die Küche aufzuräumen.
examples.en: I'm in the middle of tidying the kitchen right now.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich freue mich, mein Mann abzunehmen. (using a zu-infinitive when the subjects differ)
commonMistakes.right: Ich freue mich, dass mein Mann abnimmt.
commonMistakes.why: Since the subject of the second clause (mein Mann) differs from the main clause subject (ich), only a dass-clause can express this — a zu-infinitive clause has no room for a separate subject.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

topic: Finale und modale Infinitiv- und Nebensätze
summary: um...zu (goal), anstatt...zu (alternative/trade-off), and ohne...zu (without a consequence)
explanation: Beyond um...zu, which expresses a goal and has möchten/wollen already built into its meaning (Unit 74, Book 1), two more infinitive clauses without a subject of their own express related but distinct ideas. anstatt...zu (or the full clause anstatt dass, when subjects differ) expresses an alternative or trade-off — doing one thing instead of another (Ich esse zu Hause Obst, anstatt ins Café zu gehen). ohne...zu (or ohne dass) expresses an action happening without an expected consequence following it (Ich mache Sport und esse fettarm, ohne abzunehmen). In every one of these constructions, the subject of the main clause is assumed to be the subject of the infinitive clause too, and zu is placed directly before the final infinitive — inside a separable verb, between the prefix and the stem.

rules.rule: anstatt...zu = alternative/trade-off ('instead of').
rules.note: Ich esse zu Hause Obst, anstatt ins Café zu gehen.

rules.rule: ohne...zu = without an expected consequence.
rules.note: Ich mache Sport, ohne abzunehmen.

rules.rule: The infinitive clause has no subject of its own; zu goes directly before the final infinitive, inside a separable verb's prefix.
rules.note: ..., ohne aufzugeben.

examples.de: Er kocht zu Hause, anstatt jeden Tag ins Restaurant zu gehen.
examples.en: He cooks at home instead of going to a restaurant every day.

examples.de: Sie hat die Prüfung bestanden, ohne viel zu lernen.
examples.en: She passed the exam without studying much.

commonMistakes.wrong: anstatt ins Café gehen zu (misplacing zu)
commonMistakes.why: zu goes directly before the final infinitive, not tacked on separately at the end.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

topic: Relativpronomen im Nominativ, Akkusativ und Dativ (Vertiefung)
summary: The reference noun sets gender/number; the verb or preposition sets case; welcher/welche/welches as a stylistic alternative
explanation: This unit restates and reinforces the core relative-clause principle already established at B1: the Bezugswort (the noun the relative clause describes) determines the relative pronoun's gender and number, while the verb inside the relative clause — or a preposition, if one governs the pronoun — determines its case. A relative clause is a subordinate clause, so its verb goes to the end, and it usually sits directly after its Bezugswort, which frequently places it in the middle of the main clause, requiring a comma both before and after it. One stylistic option worth knowing: welcher, welche, and welches can substitute for der/die/das as a relative pronoun in written German, specifically to avoid an awkward repetition when the relative pronoun would otherwise look identical to a following article — though this comes across as heavier and is generally not recommended.

rules.rule: Bezugswort sets gender/number of the relative pronoun; the verb or preposition inside the clause sets its case.
rules.note: Herrn und Frau Meyer, denen wir die Idee verdanken, ... (plural, dative from verdanken)

rules.rule: welcher/welche/welches can substitute for der/die/das as a relative pronoun in writing, mainly to avoid an awkward repetition — but this is stylistically heavier and best avoided.
rules.note: Die Kollegin, welche die Passwörter vergibt, ...

examples.de: Mein besonderer Dank gilt Clemens, von dem wir heute einige Lieder hören werden.
examples.en: My special thanks go to Clemens, from whom we'll hear some songs today.

examples.de: Ohne Herrn Schmalstock, der bei der Technik geholfen hat, hätten wir es nicht geschafft.
examples.en: Without Mr. Schmalstock, who helped with the tech, we wouldn't have managed it.

commonMistakes.wrong: Herrn und Frau Meyer, den wir die Idee verdanken (using singular den for a plural reference)
commonMistakes.right: Herrn und Frau Meyer, denen wir die Idee verdanken
commonMistakes.why: The Bezugswort here is plural (Herrn und Frau Meyer), so the relative pronoun must be the dative plural denen, not a singular form.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: dessen (masc/neut) and deren (fem/plural); the noun that follows has no article, and its own case depends on its own role
explanation: The genitive relative pronoun is dessen for masculine and neuter, and deren for feminine and plural. When it's followed directly by a noun (showing possession, like 'die Frau, deren Hund...'), that noun takes no article at all — the Bezugswort still determines the gender/number of dessen/deren itself, but the case of the noun following it (and of any adjective attached to it) is governed independently, by whatever role that noun plays in the rest of the relative clause — its own verb or a preposition acting on it, not on dessen/deren. This means dessen/deren itself never changes form to match that following noun's case; only the noun (and its adjective, if any) does.

rules.rule: Genitive relative pronoun: dessen (masc/neut), deren (fem/plural) — matching the Bezugswort's gender/number.
rules.note: Die Frau, deren Hund gerade meine Katze jagt, ist meine Nachbarin.

rules.rule: The noun following dessen/deren has no article; its own case is set by its role in the clause (its verb or a preposition), not by dessen/deren.
rules.note: Die Frau, für deren Kinder (Akkusativ) ich ein Geschenk gekauft habe, ist meine Nachbarin.

rules.rule: An adjective on that following noun matches the noun's own case, not dessen/deren's form.
rules.note: Die Frau, für deren nette Kinder ich ein Geschenk gekauft habe, ...

examples.de: Der Sportler, dessen Trainer viel Erfahrung hat, ist deutscher Meister geworden.
examples.en: The athlete whose coach has a lot of experience became German champion.

examples.de: Die Politikerin, deren Partei große Hoffnungen auf sie setzt, hat gute Chancen.
examples.en: The politician whose party is putting great hopes on her has good chances.

commonMistakes.wrong: Die Frau, deren Hunds gerade meine Katze jagt. (adding a genitive ending to the following noun)
commonMistakes.right: Die Frau, deren Hund gerade meine Katze jagt.
commonMistakes.why: dessen/deren already carries the genitive meaning; the following noun stays in whatever case its own role in the clause requires — here nominative, since Hund is the subject of jagt.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: wo/wohin/woher for places, als for a past time point, was for indefinite pronouns/superlatives/whole clauses
explanation: Beyond der/die/das, several other words serve as relative pronouns for specific situations. wo, wohin, and woher refer to general locations or place names — though for a concrete, specific place, an+dem (or a matching preposition) is usually preferred over wo (Das ist die Schule, in der ich gelernt habe rather than wo). als serves as a relative pronoun for a point in time when the sentence describes something in the past (Das war die Zeit, als man noch geträumt hat). was serves as a relative pronoun after an indefinite pronoun (etwas, alles, nichts) or a nominalized superlative, and also when the relative clause refers back to the content of an entire preceding sentence rather than to one specific noun — in that whole-sentence use, it's especially common in spoken German. When was would need a preposition, wo(r) + preposition is used instead, exactly like the question-word pattern.

rules.rule: wo/wohin/woher = general locations/place names (concrete places prefer an dem / a matching preposition instead).
rules.note: Das ist der Ort, wo das Essen wächst. / but: die Schule, in der ich gelernt habe

rules.rule: als = a point in time, only when the sentence is set in the past.
rules.note: Das war die Zeit, als man noch geträumt hat.

rules.rule: was = after etwas/alles/nichts/a nominalized superlative, or referring to an entire preceding sentence; wo(r)+preposition when was would need one.
rules.note: Er hat mir viel erzählt, was mich gefreut hat. / ..., worüber ich mich gefreut habe.

examples.de: Das ist der Platz, wohin wir nur in der Fantasie reisen können.
examples.en: That's the place we can only travel to in our imagination.

examples.de: Das war die Zeit, als man noch geträumt hat.
examples.en: That was the time when people still dreamed.

examples.de: Er hat mir viel erzählt, wovon er begeistert war.
examples.en: He told me a lot about what he was excited about.

commonMistakes.wrong: die Schule, wo ich gelernt habe (for a specific, concrete place)
commonMistakes.right: die Schule, in der ich gelernt habe
commonMistakes.why: wo works for general locations, but a concrete, specific place is usually better expressed with a preposition + dem/der.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Adding teils...teils, zwar...aber, einerseits...andererseits to the double-connector family
explanation: Beyond sowohl...als auch, nicht nur...sondern auch, weder...noch, and entweder...oder (already familiar from B1), three more double connectors round out this family. teils...teils expresses a partial mix of both things ('some of A, some of B' — Viele Menschen benutzen ihr Smartphone teils zum Telefonieren, teils als Internetzugang). zwar...aber sets up a concession before a contrasting point, and can run positive-then-negative or negative-then-positive (Im Internet zu surfen ist zwar interessant, aber es kostet auch viel Zeit). einerseits...andererseits frames two distinct sides or aspects of an issue (Einerseits ist das Internet ein gutes Informationsmedium, andererseits werden dort auch falsche Informationen verbreitet). je...desto/umso (already covered at B1) is grouped here too as part of the same family of paired connectors.

rules.rule: teils...teils = a partial mix of both.
rules.note: Er nutzt sein Handy teils zum Telefonieren, teils zum Surfen.

rules.rule: zwar...aber = concession then contrast (either order of positive/negative).
rules.note: Das Auto ist zwar teuer, aber es ist auch sehr sicher.

rules.rule: einerseits...andererseits = two distinct aspects of one issue.
rules.note: Einerseits spart man Zeit, andererseits verliert man den persönlichen Kontakt.

examples.de: Sie arbeitet teils von zu Hause, teils im Büro.
examples.en: She works partly from home, partly in the office.

examples.de: Der Job ist zwar anstrengend, aber auch sehr interessant.
examples.en: The job is demanding, but also very interesting.

examples.de: Einerseits will ich reisen, andererseits fehlt mir das Geld.
examples.en: On one hand I want to travel, on the other hand I lack the money.

commonMistakes.wrong: Der Job ist zwar anstrengend, andererseits auch interessant. (mixing halves of two different double connectors)
commonMistakes.right: Der Job ist zwar anstrengend, aber auch interessant.
commonMistakes.why: zwar always pairs with aber, not with andererseits, which belongs to its own separate pair (einerseits...andererseits).

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: A fuller negative-word set — nirgends/nirgendwo, nirgendwohin, noch kein/noch nie — plus un-/in-/-los word formation
explanation: Beyond nicht, kein, and the core opposite-pairs already familiar (Unit 15, A1), several more negative words fill in specific gaps. nirgends and nirgendwo both mean 'nowhere' for a static location; nirgendwohin means 'to nowhere' for a destination. noch kein is the negative of schon ein/schon eine ('not yet a...', declined like kein); noch nie is the negative of schon immer ('never yet had/done'); noch nie/noch nicht both negate schon (oft) in the sense of prior experience ('haven't yet ever been...'). kein...mehr negates schon + noch (eine) ('no more left'), and is declined. Word-formation also builds negation directly onto adjectives: un- is the general-purpose negative prefix; in- is reserved for foreign/loan words (tolerant → intolerant); the suffix -los always carries a negative, 'without X' connotation and is grammatically neutral in gender since it attaches to any noun stem (fantasielos = unimaginative, literally 'without fantasy').

rules.rule: nirgends/nirgendwo = nowhere (location). nirgendwohin = to nowhere (destination).
rules.note: Man findet sie nirgendwo. / Ohne Fahrkarte kommen Sie nirgendwohin.

rules.rule: noch kein (declined) = not yet a. noch nie = never yet. kein...mehr (declined) = no more left.
rules.note: Ich habe noch keine Karte gekauft. / Ich habe keine Karte mehr.

rules.rule: un- = general negative prefix. in- = only for loanwords. -los = 'without X', always negative.
rules.note: ungültig; intolerant; fantasielos

examples.de: Ohne Fahrkarte kommen Sie nirgendwohin.
examples.en: Without a ticket you won't get anywhere.

examples.de: Ich war noch nie im Ausland.
examples.en: I've never been abroad.

examples.de: Er ist fantasielos.
examples.en: He's unimaginative.

commonMistakes.wrong: unfantasievoll (using un- when a dedicated -los form exists)
commonMistakes.why: Some concepts have a specific -los negative form rather than the general un- prefix; fantasielos is the established word, not unfantasievoll.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: irgend- combines with question words, the indefinite article, and some indefinite pronouns to mean 'some unspecified/arbitrary'
explanation: The prefix irgend- adds a sense of 'some unspecified, arbitrary one' to a range of words, and is mostly used in spoken, informal German — depending on tone, it can come across as dismissive. Standing alone (without a following noun), it combines with question words for people (irgendjemand, irgendwer, irgendeiner — all with the same meaning), things (irgend(et)was, irgendeins, irgendwelche), places (irgendwo, irgendwohin, irgendwoher), time (irgendwann), and manner (irgendwie, often used loosely before an adjective). As an article directly before a noun, irgend- combines with the indefinite article in the singular (irgendein Mann, fully declinable through all four cases) and with welche in the plural (irgendwelche Leute, also fully declinable).

rules.rule: Standalone (no noun): irgendjemand/irgendwer/irgendeiner (people); irgend(et)was/irgendeins/irgendwelche (things); irgendwo/irgendwohin/irgendwoher (place); irgendwann (time); irgendwie (manner).
rules.note: Irgendjemand hat meine Schlüssel irgendwohin gelegt.

rules.rule: As an article before a noun: irgend + indefinite article in the singular (fully declined); irgend + welche in the plural (fully declined).
rules.note: irgendein Mann, irgendeinem Mann; irgendwelche Leute, irgendwelchen Leuten

examples.de: Irgendwer hat meine Schlüssel irgendwohin gelegt.
examples.en: Someone put my keys somewhere.

examples.de: Das kommt mir irgendwie komisch vor.
examples.en: That seems somehow odd to me.

examples.de: Hat irgendjemand irgendetwas gesehen?
examples.en: Did anyone see anything?

commonMistakes.wrong: irgendwelcher Mann (using plural welche-form for a singular noun)
commonMistakes.why: The singular uses irgend + the indefinite article (irgendein); irgendwelche is reserved for the plural.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

topic: Position und Direktion (rauf, runter, stehen, stellen, legen)
summary: hin (away from speaker) vs. her (toward speaker), now often merged into rauf/runter/rein/raus in casual speech
explanation: The distinction between hin (movement away from the speaker) and her (movement toward the speaker) technically applies to a whole family of location words — oben/unten/drüben/drinnen/draußen and their direction forms — but modern colloquial German has largely stopped distinguishing them precisely, merging both directions into shortened forms: rauf-, runter-, rüber-, rein-, raus- can now mean movement in either direction depending on context, rather than strictly hin or her. Alongside this, this unit reconfirms the position/direction verb pairs already covered at B1 (stellen/stehen, setzen/sitzen, legen/liegen, hängen/hängen): the direction verbs are regular and take an accusative object; the position verbs are irregular and take no object.

rules.rule: hin = away from the speaker; her = toward the speaker — but colloquial German often merges these into rauf-/runter-/rüber-/rein-/raus- regardless of direction.
rules.note: Komm rauf! (regardless of whether you're technically moving hin or her relative to the speaker)

rules.rule: Direction verbs (regular, take accusative object) vs. position verbs (irregular, no object): stellen/stehen, setzen/sitzen, legen/liegen, hängen/hängen.
rules.note: Er stellt die Vase auf den Tisch. / Die Vase steht auf dem Tisch.

examples.de: Geh schon mal rauf, ich komme gleich nach.
examples.en: Go on up, I'll follow in a minute.

examples.de: Komm doch runter!
examples.en: Come on down!

commonMistakes.wrong: Insisting on the strict hin/her distinction in casual conversation
commonMistakes.right: In everyday spoken German, rauf/runter/rein/raus are used regardless of direction relative to the speaker; the strict hin/her distinction is more a written or formal-register feature now.
commonMistakes.why: Modern usage has largely blurred this distinction, so overly rigid application of hin/her can sound stilted.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: es as a genuine pronoun, as a purely grammatical placeholder, and as a slot-filler that disappears when the sentence is rearranged
explanation: 'es' plays three distinct roles. First, it's a genuine pronoun: standing for a neuter subject or object already mentioned, for an adjective, or for an entire preceding statement. Second, it's a purely grammatical, meaning-empty subject or object required by German syntax, without which the sentence wouldn't be complete: for weather (es regnet), for describing one's physical/emotional state (es geht mir gut), for sounds and noises (es klingelt), for fixed thematic expressions (es geht um, es handelt sich um, es kommt darauf an), for a group of idiomatic expressions where es is an unspecific object (ich habe es eilig, ich meine es gut), and in the construction sein + two nominatives (Sie ist es). Third, 'es' functions as a placeholder that disappears entirely once the sentence is rearranged: it can stand in for a following subordinate clause moved to the end (Es ist wichtig, dass du kommst = Dass du kommst, ist wichtig), or it fills position 1 simply because that position can't be left empty — in a subjectless passive sentence, or to emphasize another sentence part by pushing it out of position 1.

rules.rule: Genuine pronoun: subject/object already mentioned, an adjective, or a whole preceding statement.
rules.note: Das Insekt ist lästig. Es ist lästig.

rules.rule: Purely grammatical/empty: weather, physical/emotional state, sounds, thematic expressions (es geht um...), certain idioms, and sein + two nominatives.
rules.note: es regnet; es geht mir gut; es handelt sich um; Sie ist es.

rules.rule: Disappearing placeholder: stands for a following clause moved to the end, or fills position 1 that would otherwise be empty (subjectless passive, or emphasis elsewhere).
rules.note: Es ist wichtig, dass du kommst. = Dass du kommst, ist wichtig. / Es wird getanzt. = Heute wird getanzt.

examples.de: Es geht um eine wichtige Entscheidung.
examples.en: It's about an important decision.

examples.de: Es ist schön, dass du kommst.
examples.en: It's nice that you're coming.

examples.de: Es sind viele Gäste gekommen.
examples.en: Many guests came.
