commonMistakes.wrong: Viele Gäste es sind gekommen. (keeping 'es' after another element takes position 1)
commonMistakes.why: The placeholder 'es' only exists to fill position 1 when nothing else does; once another element (like Viele Gäste) takes that position, 'es' disappears entirely.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Noun (carries the meaning) + weak-content verb: eine Entscheidung treffen, Kritik üben — mostly formal, with specific negation rules
explanation: A Funktionsverbgefüge pairs a noun that carries the real meaning with a verb that contributes very little content of its own, functioning together as one unit — the noun (with its preposition, if any) sits in the Verbgefähre position from Unit 5, at the end of the clause or just before the second verb part. These are especially common in formal writing — news articles, scientific and bureaucratic texts — but a handful are common in speech too: Abschied nehmen, Freundschaft schließen, einen Rat geben, Kritik üben. Structurally they come in two shapes: preposition + noun + verb (in Kauf nehmen, zur Kenntnis nehmen) and accusative + verb (Kritik üben, einen Antrag stellen); dative and genitive versions exist but are rare. Negation follows special rules: with a preposition, negate with nicht placed right before the whole prepositional phrase, never with kein; without a preposition, ordinary kein/nicht rules apply, though when the noun has no article in the singular, both nicht and kein are technically possible and nicht is the recommended choice.

rules.rule: Funktionsverbgefüge = noun (carries meaning) + weak verb; the noun (with any preposition) is a Verbgefährte, at the end or before the second verb part.
rules.note: Wir müssen jetzt eine Entscheidung treffen.

rules.rule: Forms: preposition + noun + verb, or accusative + verb (dative/genitive rare).
rules.note: in Kauf nehmen; Kritik üben; einen Antrag stellen

rules.rule: Negation with a preposition: nicht before the whole phrase, never kein. Without a preposition: normal kein/nicht rules, but nicht is recommended when the noun has no article.
rules.note: etwas nicht in Auftrag geben (not: etwas in keinen Auftrag geben); nicht Kritik üben (recommended) or keine Kritik üben

examples.de: Wir haben letztes Jahr Abschied genommen.
examples.en: We said goodbye last year.

examples.de: Die Firma hat einen Antrag gestellt.
examples.en: The company submitted an application.

examples.de: Er übt nicht gern Kritik.
examples.en: He doesn't like criticizing.

commonMistakes.wrong: etwas in keinen Auftrag geben
commonMistakes.why: When a Funktionsverbgefüge has a preposition, negation must be nicht placed before the whole phrase — kein isn't used with these prepositional forms.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: da- covers place, direction, time, pronoun, and conjunction roles — extending far beyond the da(r)+preposition pattern
explanation: da- is one of the most flexible words in German, and this unit draws its many roles together. As a place adverb, da means 'there', referring to a location already established (Da ist Assenheim). Combined with a preposition, it forms the da(r)+preposition pattern already familiar (daneben, darauf). As a direction adverb, da combines with hin/her/rüber/runter (dahin, unlike the dative-style prepositional combos). As a time adverb, da means 'at that point' — referring back to a moment already set up earlier in the same sentence or context, distinct from damals, which points to a whole distant, established period of the past rather than one specific moment; da also combines with prepositions for time (danach, davor). dabei specifically marks two simultaneous actions, and has a common idiomatic use meaning 'that's no big deal' (Was ist schon dabei?). As a pronoun, da(r)+preposition can refer to a thing, or to an entire preceding statement, or introduce a following subordinate clause. Finally, da and damit function as subordinating conjunctions: da for a cause (reviewed in Unit 63) and damit for a purpose (reviewed in Unit 74, Book 1).

rules.rule: Place: da = there. Direction: da + hin/her/rüber/runter. Time: da = at that specific point (vs. damals = a distant established period); da + preposition (danach, davor) for time too.
rules.note: Da ist Assenheim. / Ich fahre nach Rom. Fährst du auch dahin? / Da stand plötzlich eine Kuh auf dem Gleis.

rules.rule: dabei = two simultaneous actions, or idiomatically 'that's no big deal'.
rules.note: Ich bin gerade dabei, den Kaffee zu machen. / Was ist schon dabei?

rules.rule: As a pronoun: refers to a thing, an entire preceding statement, or introduces a following clause. As a conjunction: da = cause, damit = purpose.
rules.note: Da ich ein Jobangebot hatte, bin ich umgezogen. / Ich muss mich beeilen, damit der Bericht fertig wird.

examples.de: Ich war letzte Woche mit dem Zug unterwegs. Da stand plötzlich eine Kuh auf dem Gleis.
examples.en: I was traveling by train last week. At that point a cow suddenly stood on the tracks.

examples.de: Er hört dabei Musik.
examples.en: He listens to music while doing it.

examples.de: Was ist schon dabei, wenn ich mal spät komme?
examples.en: What's the big deal if I'm a bit late sometimes?

commonMistakes.wrong: Damals stand plötzlich eine Kuh auf dem Gleis. (using damals for one specific moment just described)
commonMistakes.right: Da stand plötzlich eine Kuh auf dem Gleis.
commonMistakes.why: damals refers to a distant, generally-established period of the past; da refers to one specific moment already set up in the immediate context — they aren't interchangeable.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: denn, doch, auch, bloß, eben, and aber each add a specific conversational tone, understood only from context
explanation: Modal particles adjust the tone of a sentence without changing its factual content, and they're almost impossible to pin to one fixed meaning — the same particle can shift with context and intonation, and they belong to informal spoken German, avoided in formal speech or writing. aber in an exclamation signals surprise or strong emotion (Du bist aber groß geworden!). auch in a yes/no question signals worry or concern (Hast du auch den Schlüssel mitgenommen?); in a W-question it makes the question sound rhetorical or reproachful (Warum hat er das auch gemacht?). bloß in a W-question signals bewilderment (Was hat er bloß?); in a command, it signals a warning or threat (Komm bloß nicht zu spät!). denn in a question is often a reaction to a situation, and depending on tone can express doubt, surprise, reproach, or friendliness (Was ist denn hier passiert?). doch covers the widest range: in a statement it implies the listener should already know something, often with mild reproach; in a command it sounds friendlier; in an exclamation it intensifies surprise; in a wish it intensifies the longing. eben in a statement signals resignation, a simple acceptance that something is just the way it is (Er war eben schon vor uns da).

rules.rule: aber (exclamations) = surprise/emotion. auch (yes/no questions) = worry; auch (W-questions) = rhetorical/reproachful tone.
rules.note: Hast du auch die Fahrkarte dabei?

rules.rule: bloß (W-questions) = bewilderment; bloß (commands) = warning/threat. denn (questions) = reaction to a situation, tone-dependent.
rules.note: Was hat er bloß? / Geh bloß nicht dorthin! / Kommt Dennis denn heute?

rules.rule: doch = reproach (statements), friendlier tone (commands), intensified surprise (exclamations), intensified longing (wishes). eben = resignation/acceptance.
rules.note: Er war eben schon vor uns da.

examples.de: Was ist denn hier passiert?
examples.en: What on earth happened here?

examples.de: Probier doch mal, es schmeckt lecker.
examples.en: Go on, try it, it tastes great.

examples.de: Er ist eben vor uns da gewesen.
examples.en: He just happened to be there before us.

commonMistakes.wrong: Stressing modal particles heavily in speech, expecting the meaning to come through emphasis alone
commonMistakes.right: Modal particles carry tone but stay unstressed; their meaning comes from context and the sentence type (question, command, exclamation, wish), not from vocal emphasis.
commonMistakes.why: Overemphasizing a particle can make it sound like a content word being highlighted, which distorts the intended nuance rather than conveying it.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Comma placement between clauses (subordinate, coordinate) and between sentence parts (lists, appositions)
explanation: German comma rules mostly separate clauses from each other. A subordinate clause embedded inside a main clause takes a comma both before and after it, and this includes relative clauses and zu-infinitive clauses (though the comma before a zu-infinitive clause isn't strictly obligatory — it's still recommended to always include it). No comma is needed when two subordinate clauses are joined by und or oder. Between two main clauses, a comma is optional if there's no connector at all (a period also works there), but a comma is required whenever the sentences are joined by aber, sondern, jedoch, doch, or denn, even in shortened/elliptical sentences, and a comma may optionally appear when two main clauses are joined by und or oder. Separately, commas also separate parts within a single clause: items in a list (except right before und, oder, and sowie), and an apposition (an inserted phrase renaming or describing something, set off with commas on both sides). No comma follows position 1 — with the single exception of a subordinate clause occupying that position, which does take a comma after it, as already established.

rules.rule: A subordinate clause (including relative clauses) embedded in a main clause takes a comma before and after it. No comma when two subordinate clauses are joined by und/oder.
rules.note: Ich gehe gerne wandern, weil mir die Bewegung guttut. / Das Café, das ich dir zeigen möchte, liegt im Wald.

rules.rule: Between two main clauses: comma optional with no connector; comma required with aber/sondern/jedoch/doch/denn, even if shortened; comma optional with und/oder.
rules.note: Ich würde auch gerne klettern, aber ich bin nicht schwindelfrei.

rules.rule: Within a clause: commas separate list items (except right before und/oder/sowie) and set off an apposition on both sides.
rules.note: Wir haben Suppe, Salat und Torte gegessen. / Mein Freund, ein passionierter Bergsteiger, fand die Wanderung langweilig.

examples.de: Ich hoffe, im Urlaub eine Wandertour zu machen.
examples.en: I hope to go on a hiking tour during my vacation.

examples.de: Wir haben einen Kaffee, eine Schokolade oder einen Tee bestellt.
examples.en: We ordered a coffee, a chocolate, or a tea.

examples.de: Mein Freund, ein passionierter Bergsteiger, fand die Tour langweilig.
examples.en: My friend, a passionate mountaineer, found the tour boring.

commonMistakes.wrong: Wir sind nicht mit dem Auto gefahren aber zu Fuß gelaufen. (omitting the required comma before aber)
commonMistakes.right: Wir sind nicht mit dem Auto gefahren, aber zu Fuß gelaufen.
commonMistakes.why: A comma before aber joining two main clauses is required, even when the second clause is shortened/elliptical.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved for cross-reference only (BK2-n)

summary: Whole-sentence auch sits where nicht sits; as a focus particle, auch (and similar words) goes right before the stressed element it highlights
explanation: When auch refers to the entire sentence, it occupies the same position as nicht (Unit 6) — or sits directly before nicht if both are present. When auch works as a focus particle instead, highlighting one specific sentence part, it moves directly before that part, which then receives spoken stress: 'Auch ich schenke dir dieses Jahr Blumen' highlights the subject (not just someone else), while 'Ich schenke dir dieses Jahr auch Blumen' highlights the object (not just something else). Several other words behave the same way as focus particles, each with a slightly different implication: ebenfalls/ebenso/gleichfalls signal 'this one too, not just the others already mentioned'; nur/bloß/lediglich/allein/ausschließlich/einzig signal 'this one and only this one'; sogar/selbst/nicht einmal signal something unexpected or surprising; gerade/genau/eben/ausgerechnet/insbesondere signal that this particular one is especially notable. None of these focus particles can stand alone in position 1.

rules.rule: Whole-sentence auch: same position as nicht, or directly before nicht if both appear.
rules.note: Ich kann mich heute auch nicht um meinen Kollegen kümmern.

rules.rule: Focus-particle auch (and ebenfalls/nur/sogar/gerade and similar words): directly before the stressed element it highlights.
rules.note: Auch ich schenke dir Blumen. / Ich schenke dir auch Blumen.

rules.rule: These focus particles can never stand alone in position 1.
rules.note: Auch cannot open a sentence on its own without the element it highlights immediately following.

examples.de: Ich schenke dir dieses Jahr auch Blumen.
examples.en: I'm giving you flowers this year too. (highlighting 'Blumen')

examples.de: Sogar meine Schwester hat geholfen.
examples.en: Even my sister helped.

examples.de: Heute konnte ich lediglich eine Aufgabe fertig machen.
examples.en: Today I could only get one task finished.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich auch schenke dir Blumen. (placing auch after the subject when it should highlight the subject itself)
commonMistakes.why: The focus particle goes directly before the element it highlights — to highlight the subject, auch must precede it, not follow it.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: New information (indefinite article) goes toward the end; known information (definite article) goes toward the left; position 1 shapes the text's structure
explanation: German sentences generally place the most important, newest information toward the right/end of the sentence — this is typically the information introduced with an indefinite article, while already-known information (typically definite-article) sits further left, closer to tekamolo's normal slot. This applies even with two objects: whichever one is 'new' shifts rightward, regardless of its case. Position 1 itself shapes how a text feels: putting a time expression there repeatedly gives the text a chronological structure; putting a place expression there gives it a spatial structure; putting almost any other element there creates strong emphasis, but this is unusual enough that it should be used sparingly and only when you're confident about it. When a subordinate clause occupies position 1, the main clause that follows often includes a small pointing-back pronoun or adverb (like dann, damit, dabei) referring to it. Several things can never occupy position 1 at all: nicht/überhaupt nicht/gar nicht, reflexive pronouns, accusative es, a standalone focus or modal particle, and almost every separable prefix.

rules.rule: New information (often indefinite article) shifts toward the end of the sentence; known information (often definite article) sits further left.
rules.note: Der Kellner serviert dem Gast einen Kaffee. (new: einen Kaffee, right) vs. Der Kellner serviert den Kaffee einem Gast. (new: einem Gast, right)

rules.rule: Position 1 shapes text structure: temporal phrases → chronological text; lokal phrases → spatial text; other elements → strong, rare emphasis.
rules.note: Am Dienstag bin ich in die Stadt gegangen. (chronological framing)

rules.rule: Cannot occupy position 1: nicht/überhaupt nicht/gar nicht, reflexive pronouns, accusative es, standalone focus/modal particles, almost all separable prefixes.
rules.note: None of these can stand as the sole content of position 1.

examples.de: Der Kellner serviert dem Gast einen Kaffee.
examples.en: The waiter serves the guest a coffee. (the coffee is the new information)

examples.de: Gründlich habe ich den ganzen Abend aufgeräumt.
examples.en: Thoroughly, I cleaned up the whole evening. (strong emphasis on gründlich)

commonMistakes.wrong: Nicht kann ich das machen. (trying to front nicht into position 1)
commonMistakes.why: nicht (and its intensified forms überhaupt nicht/gar nicht) can never occupy position 1 on its own.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

topic: Konjunktiv 2 der Vergangenheit: Passiv und Modalverb-Kombination
summary: Passive Konjunktiv 2 past uses wäre + participle + worden; with a modal, hätte + participle + werden + modal infinitive
explanation: Extending Konjunktiv 2's single past-tense form (B2) into the passive: the passive Konjunktiv 2 past is built with wäre + past participle + worden — the same worden used in the ordinary passive perfect. Combined with a modal verb, the construction chains together as hätte + past participle + werden + the modal's own infinitive, a four-part structure that's rarely used in practice because of its length. A related word-order rule applies whenever a subordinate clause contains three verb forms (a modal plus two infinitives, as here): the conjugated verb (hätte) moves to sit before both infinitives, rather than after them at the very end as the basic subordinate-clause rule would suggest.

rules.rule: Passive Konjunktiv 2 past: wäre + past participle + worden.
rules.note: Das Paket wäre gebracht worden.

rules.rule: Passive Konjunktiv 2 past with a modal: hätte + past participle + werden + modal infinitive.
rules.note: Das Paket hätte gebracht werden müssen.

rules.rule: In a subordinate clause with three verb forms, the conjugated verb moves before both infinitives.
rules.note: ..., weil das Paket hätte gebracht werden müssen.

examples.de: Das Paket wäre pünktlich gebracht worden.
examples.en: The package would have been delivered on time.

examples.de: Das Paket hätte gebracht werden müssen.
examples.en: The package should have had to be delivered.

commonMistakes.wrong: Das Paket hätte gebracht werden müssen worden. (adding worden unnecessarily to the modal+passive chain)
commonMistakes.right: Das Paket hätte gebracht werden müssen.
commonMistakes.why: The modal-combined passive past uses werden as a plain infinitive at the end, not the reduced worden form, which belongs specifically to the non-modal passive perfect/Konjunktiv construction.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

topic: Irreale Folgen und beinahe eingetretene Konsequenzen
summary: zu...als dass + Konjunktiv 2 states a negative consequence that didn't/couldn't happen; beinahe/fast + Konjunktiv 2 past describes something that almost happened
explanation: zu + adjective in the main clause, paired with als dass + Konjunktiv 2 in the subordinate clause, expresses a consequence so extreme that the expected positive outcome couldn't actually happen: 'Er ist viel zu arrogant, als dass er zuhören würde' implies he is so arrogant that he doesn't listen — the opposite of what a normal outcome would be. This construction is grammatically related to the irreal comparisons in Unit 13's main content, but conveys a negative, unrealized consequence rather than a hypothetical similarity. Separately, beinahe or fast combined with the Konjunktiv 2 past describes something that came very close to happening but ultimately didn't: 'Ich wäre fast auf ihn hereingefallen' means the speaker almost got fooled, but didn't.

rules.rule: zu + adjective (main clause) + als dass + Konjunktiv 2 (subordinate clause) = a consequence too extreme to happen as expected.
rules.note: Er ist viel zu arrogant, als dass er zuhören würde.

rules.rule: beinahe/fast + Konjunktiv 2 past = something that almost happened but didn't.
rules.note: Ich wäre fast auf ihn hereingefallen.

examples.de: Sie ist zu müde, als dass sie noch arbeiten könnte.
examples.en: She's too tired to still be able to work.

examples.de: Er hätte beinahe den Zug verpasst.
examples.en: He almost missed the train.

commonMistakes.wrong: Er ist zu arrogant, dass er nicht zuhört. (using a plain dass-clause with the indicative)
commonMistakes.right: Er ist zu arrogant, als dass er zuhören würde.
commonMistakes.why: This specific construction requires als dass with Konjunktiv 2, not a plain dass-clause with the indicative, to convey the unrealized/negative consequence.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: The passive extends into every remaining tense: Plusquamperfekt, Futur 1/2, and both Konjunktiv 1 forms
explanation: Completing the passive's tense range: Plusquamperfekt uses war + participle + worden. Futur 1 uses wird + participle + werden (as an infinitive). Futur 2, rarely used, adds a further layer: wird + participle + worden + sein. Konjunktiv 1 present uses werde + participle; Konjunktiv 1 past uses sei + participle + worden. These forms exist mostly for completeness and for recognizing them in formal or literary text — day-to-day use strongly favors the simpler Präsens, Präteritum, and Perfekt forms already covered at B2.

rules.rule: Plusquamperfekt: war + participle + worden. Futur 1: wird + participle + werden. Futur 2 (rare): wird + participle + worden + sein.
rules.note: Die Gruppe war bereits informiert worden. / wird bald informiert werden. / wird wohl bis morgen informiert worden sein.

rules.rule: Konjunktiv 1 present: werde + participle. Konjunktiv 1 past: sei + participle + worden.
rules.note: Er sagt, die Gruppe werde informiert. / sei informiert worden.

examples.de: Die Gruppe war schon vor der Abreise informiert worden.
examples.en: The group had already been informed before departure.

examples.de: Die Gruppe wird bestimmt bald informiert werden.
examples.en: The group will surely be informed soon.

commonMistakes.wrong: Die Gruppe war informiert geworden.
commonMistakes.why: worden, not geworden, is used across every passive past tense form, including the Plusquamperfekt.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

topic: Passiv mit Modalverben: seltene Zeiten und wollen→sollen
summary: Rarely-used passive-with-modal tenses, plus the rule that an active wollen becomes sollen in the corresponding passive
explanation: Passive combined with a modal extends, in principle, to every tense — Plusquamperfekt, Futur 1, Futur 2, Konjunktiv 2 past, Konjunktiv 1 past — but these forms are rarely used in practice because they chain together too many verb parts to sound natural; German prefers the Präteritum-with-modal passive instead (Unit 15, B2) even when describing something further in the past. One meaning-based rule worth remembering: when the active sentence's modal is wollen, the corresponding passive sentence uses sollen instead of wollen, since wollen expresses the wish of an active subject, which the passive removes: 'Man will hier eine neue U-Bahn-Strecke bauen' becomes 'Hier soll eine neue U-Bahn-Strecke gebaut werden.'

rules.rule: Passive-with-modal exists in principle for every tense, but the more complex forms (Plusquamperfekt, Futur, Konjunktiv past) are rare in practice; Präteritum is preferred.
rules.note: Die Gruppe musste informiert werden. (preferred over more complex forms)

rules.rule: An active wollen becomes sollen in the corresponding passive sentence.
rules.note: Man will die Strecke bauen. → Die Strecke soll gebaut werden.

examples.de: Hier soll eine neue U-Bahn-Strecke gebaut werden.
examples.en: A new subway line is meant to be built here.

commonMistakes.wrong: Hier will eine neue U-Bahn-Strecke gebaut werden.
commonMistakes.right: Hier soll eine neue U-Bahn-Strecke gebaut werden.
commonMistakes.why: wollen expresses an active subject's own wish, which doesn't survive into the passive — sollen takes its place to express the same underlying intention impersonally.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: sich+verb, the modal Partizip (Gerundiv), colloquial gehören/bekommen+participle, and fixed noun-verb combinations all express passive-like meaning
explanation: Beyond the alternatives already covered at B2 (lassen+sich, sein+zu, -bar/-abel/-lich), several more forms carry a passive-like sense. sich + verb (with no other subject named, and usually with a manner adverb) expresses a general possibility, close to a kann-passive: 'Das Buch liest sich gut' means the book can be read easily; the doer is never mentioned, and if there's no other subject, 'es' fills that role. The modal Partizip (also called the Gerundiv) is zu + Partizip I placed before a noun, and only works for verbs that can independently form a werden-passive; its meaning covers muss/soll/kann or darf nicht, decided by context — 'die zu verkaufenden Bücher' means books that must/should be sold. gehören + Partizip II is a colloquial equivalent of muss/sollte werden: 'Das Buch gehört ins Fenster gestellt.' bekommen or kriegen + Partizip II is also colloquial, always names who receives the action, and only works with verbs that normally take a dative object — that dative object becomes the subject: 'Er bekommt das Buch geschenkt' (from 'Man schenkt ihm das Buch'). Finally, certain fixed noun-verb combinations — with finden, genießen, kommen, stehen, bekommen, erhalten, erfahren, gehen, gelangen — carry a passive-like sense on their own: 'Das Lehrbuch findet an vielen Schulen Verwendung' means the textbook is used at many schools.

rules.rule: sich + verb (usually with a manner adverb, never naming the doer) = general possibility, close to kann...werden. If no other subject, use es.
rules.note: Das Buch liest sich gut. Hier schläft es sich gut.

rules.rule: Modal Partizip (zu + Partizip I before a noun, only for werden-passive-capable verbs) = muss/soll/kann/darf nicht, decided by context.
rules.note: die zu verkaufenden Bücher

rules.rule: gehören + Partizip II (colloquial) = muss/sollte werden. bekommen/kriegen + Partizip II (colloquial, only dative-object verbs, dative becomes subject, names the recipient) = a personalized passive.
rules.note: Das Buch gehört ins Fenster gestellt. / Er bekommt das Buch geschenkt.

rules.rule: Fixed noun-verb combinations with finden/genießen/kommen/stehen/bekommen/erhalten/erfahren/gehen/gelangen carry passive-like meaning.
rules.note: Das Lehrbuch findet Verwendung. (= wird verwendet)

examples.de: Dieser Roman liest sich sehr gut.
examples.en: This novel reads very well.

examples.de: Die auszustellenden Bilder liegen hier.
examples.en: The pictures to be exhibited are here.

examples.de: Er bekommt zum Geburtstag ein Buch geschenkt.
examples.en: He's given a book as a birthday present.

commonMistakes.wrong: Er wird das Buch geschenkt bekommen. (over-formalizing the colloquial bekommen-passive)
commonMistakes.why: bekommen/kriegen + participle is inherently a present-tense colloquial construction — layering Futur onto it defeats its casual, everyday register.

commonMistakes.wrong: Das Auto gehört gewaschen zu werden. (adding zu werden onto gehören+participle)
commonMistakes.why: gehören + participle already carries the full 'should be done' meaning on its own; no additional zu werden is needed.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: The impersonal passive: verb always 3rd person singular, 'es' fills position 1 only when nothing else does, and it disappears in subordinate clauses
explanation: German can build a passive sentence with no subject at all, corresponding in meaning to an active sentence with the impersonal 'man'. This 'unpersönliches Passiv' always keeps its verb in the 3rd person singular, regardless of what else is in the sentence. 'es' appears only to fill position 1 when nothing else takes that slot — 'Es wird viel gelacht' — and it disappears entirely in a subordinate clause, since position 1 there is already taken by the connector: 'Ich glaube, dass viel gelacht wird.' This construction appears in three main situations: with certain dative-object verbs, where the dative object simply stays dative rather than becoming a subject ('Ihm wird geholfen'); with verbs that never had an accusative object to begin with ('Auf der Party wurde viel getanzt'); and with reflexive verbs, where the reflexive pronoun 'sich' is kept as-is — this last type is colloquial, often carries a demanding/imperative tone, and frequently appears with the particle aber or mal ('Jetzt wird sich aber mal gewaschen!'). The impersonal passive itself is rare in formal or written registers.

rules.rule: Verb always 3rd person singular. 'es' fills position 1 only if nothing else does; it disappears in subordinate clauses.
rules.note: Es wird viel gelacht. / Ich glaube, dass viel gelacht wird.

rules.rule: Occurs with dative-object verbs (dative object stays dative), verbs with no accusative object, and reflexive verbs (sich is retained, often colloquial/imperative-toned with aber/mal).
rules.note: Ihm wird geholfen. / Auf der Party wurde viel getanzt. / Jetzt wird sich aber mal gewaschen!

rules.rule: The impersonal passive is rarely used in formal/written German.
rules.note: It's primarily a spoken-register construction.

examples.de: Heute wird viel gelacht.
examples.en: There's a lot of laughing today.

examples.de: Am Wochenende wurde nicht gearbeitet.
examples.en: There was no working over the weekend.

examples.de: Leider wurde mir nicht zugehört.
examples.en: Unfortunately I wasn't listened to.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich glaube, dass es viel gelacht wird. (keeping es inside a subordinate clause)
commonMistakes.right: Ich glaube, dass viel gelacht wird.
commonMistakes.why: es only exists to occupy position 1 when nothing else fills it; inside a subordinate clause, the connector already takes that slot, so es disappears.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

topic: Wann ist Passiv möglich, wann nicht?
summary: A full checklist: transitive verbs allow full passive; some intransitive verbs allow only impersonal passive; several verb categories block passive entirely
explanation: Passive with a full set of personal forms is only possible for verbs with an accusative object (transitive verbs) — 'Die Ärztin operiert den Patienten' becomes 'Der Patient wird operiert.' Other verbs can sometimes still form an impersonal passive (Unit 18) if they're intransitive but still have an active subject that's genuinely the cause or agent of the action — 'Die Zuschauer klatschen' becomes 'Es wird geklatscht'; 'Sie hilft dem Kollegen' becomes 'Dem Kollegen wird geholfen.' No passive at all is possible for several distinct categories: verbs with no true active subject (besitzen, haben, es gibt, erhalten, bekommen, kriegen); verbs whose accusative object is the 'experiencer' of a physical or emotional state rather than something acted upon (frieren, jucken, freuen, ärgern); verbs expressing a change of state (wachsen, sterben) or a state itself (dauern, wohnen, sein); verbs whose accusative object is really a measurement of size, price, or time (enthalten, umfassen); verbs of knowing (kennen, wissen, erfahren, kennenlernen); verbs whose accusative object is the subject's own body part; fixed idiomatic expressions (Funktionsverbgefüge) where the verb has a transferred, non-literal meaning; modal verbs; impersonal verbs describing weather or natural occurrence (regnen); and reflexive verbs.

rules.rule: Full personal passive: only transitive verbs (those with an accusative object).
rules.note: Die Ärztin operiert den Patienten. → Der Patient wird operiert.

rules.rule: Impersonal passive only: intransitive verbs that still have a genuine active subject/agent.
rules.note: Die Zuschauer klatschen. → Es wird geklatscht.

rules.rule: No passive at all: verbs with no true active subject, experiencer-verbs, state/state-change verbs, measurement verbs, knowledge verbs, body-part-object verbs, idiomatic Funktionsverbgefüge, modal verbs, weather verbs, reflexive verbs.
rules.note: besitzen, frieren, wachsen, dauern, enthalten, kennen, regnen, sich freuen — none of these form a passive.

examples.de: Der Patient wird von der Ärztin operiert.
examples.en: The patient is operated on by the doctor.

examples.de: Für die Kinder wird gesorgt.
examples.en: The children are being taken care of.

commonMistakes.wrong: Es wird geregnet.
commonMistakes.right: There is no passive form of regnen — it stays Es regnet.
commonMistakes.why: regnen is an impersonal verb of natural occurrence with no genuine active agent at all, so it cannot form a passive of any kind, personal or impersonal.

commonMistakes.wrong: 1 Liter wird von der Flasche enthalten.
commonMistakes.why: enthalten's accusative object is a measurement, not something being acted upon, so it can't be passivized.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: laut/zufolge/nach/gemäß signal a reported, neutral source (paired with the indicative, not Konjunktiv); hinsichtlich/bezüglich/entsprechend mark reference or agreement
explanation: A small group of prepositions signal that a claim comes from a reported source, functioning much like Konjunktiv 1 does — expressing neutrality or distance from the claim — but they're grammatically paired with the plain indicative, not the Konjunktiv. laut + dative (occasionally genitive, often used without an article or with the indefinite article) is the most common: 'Laut Statistik sind 80% der Deutschen übergewichtig.' zufolge + dative always follows its noun. nach and gemäß (both dative) can appear before or after their noun, with gemäß especially common in legal/administrative contexts. A separate group marks reference to a topic: hinsichtlich + genitive (or the equivalents in Hinsicht auf / mit Blick auf + accusative) means 'regarding, from the perspective of'; bezüglich + genitive (or in Bezug auf + accusative) means 'in relation to'; entsprechend + dative (either position around its noun) means 'in accordance with, matching'.

rules.rule: Reported-source prepositions: laut (+dative, often no article), zufolge (+dative, always after the noun), nach/gemäß (+dative, either position) — paired with the indicative, not Konjunktiv.
rules.note: Laut Statistik sind 80% übergewichtig. / Der Statistik zufolge...

rules.rule: Reference prepositions: hinsichtlich/bezüglich (+genitive; or in Hinsicht auf / in Bezug auf +accusative); entsprechend (+dative, either position).
rules.note: Er ist hinsichtlich seines Verhaltens zu kritisieren. / Wir haben alles Ihrem Wunsch entsprechend arrangiert.

examples.de: Laut einer neuen Studie schlafen die Deutschen zu wenig.
examples.en: According to a new study, Germans sleep too little.

examples.de: Ich möchte etwas bezüglich der Rechnung anmerken.
examples.en: I'd like to note something regarding the invoice.

commonMistakes.wrong: Laut Statistik seien 80% übergewichtig. (using Konjunktiv after a reported-source preposition)
commonMistakes.why: Even though these prepositions serve the same distancing function as Konjunktiv 1, they're grammatically paired with the plain indicative, not the Konjunktiv.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: Formal-register prepositions with transparent meanings: zuliebe, zugunsten, mittels/mithilfe/anhand, zwecks, entgegen, ungeachtet, seitens, anstelle
explanation: A set of formal prepositions have meanings transparent enough to guess from their components, hence 'sprechende' (speaking/self-explanatory) prepositions. zuliebe + dative (always after the noun) means 'for the sake of', expressing a reason rooted in caring about someone. zugunsten + genitive (rarely after the noun, with dative) means 'in favor of, to someone's benefit'; its opposite is zuungunsten. mittels, mithilfe, and anhand (all + genitive) all mean 'by means of / using', covering an instrument or method. zwecks + genitive (usually without an article) means 'for the purpose of'. entgegen + dative (rarely after the noun) means 'contrary to, against what was expected'. ungeachtet + genitive (rarely after the noun) means 'regardless of, without paying attention to'. seitens or vonseiten + genitive means 'on the part of, from the side of'. anstelle (identical to anstatt) + genitive means 'in place of'. Two more fixed prepositional phrases: im Falle + genitive ('in the event that', conditional) and im Gegensatz zu + dative ('in contrast to', adversative).

rules.rule: zuliebe (+dative, after noun) = for the sake of. zugunsten (+genitive) = in favor of; zuungunsten = its opposite.
rules.note: Er lernt seinen Eltern zuliebe fleißig. / Er verzichtet zugunsten seiner Schwester auf das Geld.

rules.rule: mittels/mithilfe/anhand (+genitive) = by means of. zwecks (+genitive, usually no article) = for the purpose of.
rules.note: mittels eines Drahtes; zwecks Gewichtsreduktion

rules.rule: entgegen (+dative) = contrary to. ungeachtet (+genitive) = regardless of. seitens/vonseiten (+genitive) = on the part of. anstelle=anstatt (+genitive) = in place of.
rules.note: Entgegen deiner Vermutung habe ich alles erledigt.

examples.de: Mithilfe des Wörterbuchs konnte ich den Text verstehen.
examples.en: With the help of the dictionary, I could understand the text.

examples.de: Ungeachtet seiner langjährigen Mitarbeit wurde ihm gekündigt.
examples.en: Regardless of his many years of work, he was let go.

examples.de: Anstelle eines Autos kaufen wir uns ein Fahrrad.
examples.en: Instead of a car, we're buying a bike.

commonMistakes.wrong: zugunsten mir (informal dative substitution without checking whether the genitive noun has an article/adjective)
commonMistakes.right: zugunsten meiner Schwester (genitive) or, if no article/adjective, mir zugunsten (dative, postposition)
commonMistakes.why: zugunsten defaults to genitive; the dative alternative is specifically for when the noun that follows has no article or adjective.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

topic: Bedeutungen von in, an, auf, über, unter, vor
summary: Extended, non-literal meanings of the core Wechselpräpositionen beyond their basic spatial sense
explanation: Beyond their core spatial meanings, these six prepositions carry a wide range of extended senses worth learning as a set. in marks a resulting state (sich verwandeln in) or an emotional/color state in fixed phrases (in Sorge, im Ärger, der Pulli in Rot). an marks contact in an abstract sense (sich gewöhnen an) and, before a number, means 'approximately' (an die 20 Jahre). auf marks orientation toward the future (hoffen auf) or focus (achten auf) with accusative, and a basis with dative (basieren auf); it also appears in manner expressions (auf diese Weise, auf Deutsch) and can mark a target percentage (auf 55% steigen). über marks an emotional or purely factual topic (lachen über, sprechen über), can be a postposition meaning 'the whole ... through' (die Feiertage über), and before a number means 'more than' (über 100 Leute). unter means 'among' in a group sense (unter den Zuschauern) or introduces a condition (unter Umständen, unter der Bedingung). vor marks a cause behind an unconscious/involuntary reaction (vor Angst zittern, reviewed from Unit 25) and, temporally, can simply mean 'earlier' (vor drei Jahren = 'three years ago', also covered at B1).

rules.rule: in = resulting state, or emotional/color states in fixed phrases. an = abstract contact, or 'approximately' before a number.
rules.note: sich verwandeln in; in Sorge sein; an die 20 Jahre

rules.rule: auf = future orientation/focus (Akkusativ) or basis (Dativ), manner, or approaching a percentage. über = topic, 'the whole ... through' (postposition), or 'more than' before a number.
rules.note: hoffen auf; basieren auf; auf 55% steigen; über 100 Leute

rules.rule: unter = among (a group), or introduces a condition. vor = cause of an unconscious reaction, or 'ago' temporally.
rules.note: unter den Zuschauern; unter der Bedingung; vor Angst zittern

examples.de: Es kommen an die 20 Leute zur Party.
examples.en: About 20 people are coming to the party.

examples.de: Über 100 Personen haben teilgenommen.
examples.en: More than 100 people took part.

examples.de: Unter bestimmten Bedingungen ist das möglich.
examples.en: Under certain conditions, that's possible.

commonMistakes.wrong: um die 20 Jahre (using um instead of an for an approximate number)
commonMistakes.why: The 'approximately' sense before a number specifically uses an, not um, which has its own separate 'approximately' use for clock times and dates instead.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

topic: Bedeutungen von um, bei, von, nach, aus, mit, zu
summary: Extended, non-literal meanings of these seven common prepositions beyond location and basic use
explanation: These seven prepositions similarly carry rich extended meanings. um marks a difference or rate of change (um 1 Prozent steigen) alongside its intensity-object use (sich bemühen um). bei marks a condition (bei Bestehen der Prüfung, bei klarem Verstand, bei Weitem). von marks a genitive-replacement possessive, especially common in speech (die Frau von meinem Bruder = meines Bruders Frau). nach marks reported opinion in the fixed phrase 'meiner Meinung nach'. aus marks the material something is made of (aus Leder) or, extending Unit 25's emotional-cause pattern, the emotional reason behind a deliberate action (aus Liebe töten). mit marks an instrument, a companion, a means of transport, or — in a fixed idiom — a condition (mit Glück, 'with luck'). zu marks a goal or purpose (zum Lesen braucht man...) and appears before ordinal-style expressions of grouping (zu zweit, zu dritt, zum ersten Mal).

rules.rule: um = rate of difference. bei = condition. von = genitive-replacement possessive (esp. in speech).
rules.note: um 1 Prozent steigen; bei Bestehen der Prüfung; die Frau von meinem Bruder

rules.rule: nach = reported opinion (fixed phrase). aus = material, or emotional reason behind a deliberate action.
rules.note: meiner Meinung nach; aus Leder; aus Liebe

rules.rule: mit = instrument/companion/transport, or a fixed condition idiom. zu = goal/purpose, or grouping before numbers.
rules.note: mit Glück; zu zweit; zum ersten Mal

examples.de: Die Preise sind um 1 Prozent gestiegen.
examples.en: Prices have risen by 1 percent.

examples.de: Bei klarem Verstand hätte er das nicht gemacht.
examples.en: In his right mind, he wouldn't have done that.

examples.de: Wir sind zu dritt angereist.
examples.en: We arrived as a group of three.

commonMistakes.wrong: Meiner Meinung zufolge ist das falsch. (substituting zufolge into a fixed idiom)
commonMistakes.right: Meiner Meinung nach ist das falsch.
commonMistakes.why: This is a fixed idiomatic phrase using nach specifically — zufolge, though a synonym elsewhere, doesn't substitute into this particular expression.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: A small closed set of verbs — nennen, kosten, lehren, schimpfen, angehen, anhören, abfragen — take two accusative objects, one always a person
explanation: A small, specific group of verbs takes two accusative objects at once rather than the more usual accusative+dative pattern: nennen, kosten, lehren, schimpfen, angehen, anhören, and abfragen. In every one of these, one accusative object is always a person and the other is always a thing — 'Er nannte ihn einen Träumer' (ihn = person, einen Träumer = thing/description). This is a genuinely small, closed list, not a productive pattern, so these verbs simply need to be memorized individually rather than derived from a rule.

rules.rule: nennen, kosten, lehren, schimpfen, angehen, anhören, abfragen take two accusative objects; one is always a person, the other always a thing.
rules.note: Er nannte ihn einen Träumer. / Das kostet ihn viel Kraft.

rules.rule: This is a small, closed, memorized list — not a productive or predictable pattern.
rules.note: No other common verbs follow this structure outside this specific group.

examples.de: Sie lehrte ihn das Schwimmen.
examples.en: She taught him swimming.

examples.de: Er schimpfte sie eine Lügnerin.
examples.en: He called her a liar.

commonMistakes.wrong: Er nannte ihm einen Träumer. (using dative for the person)
commonMistakes.why: This specific verb group takes two accusatives, not accusative+dative — the person is also accusative here, unlike most dative-involving verb patterns.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: A formal, legal-register group of genitive-only and nominative+accusative+genitive verbs
explanation: A group of formal, mostly legal-register verbs takes a genitive object either alone alongside the subject, or alongside both an accusative and the subject. The nominative+genitive group (sich annehmen, sich bedienen, bedürfen, sich bemächtigen, sich enthalten, sich erbarmen, sich erfreuen, gedenken, sich rühmen, sich schämen) can have either a person or a thing in both the nominative and genitive slots — 'Die Sache bedarf der Klärung' (thing+thing) and 'Jeder Mensch bedarf eines Freundes' (person+person) are both valid. The nominative+accusative+genitive group (anklagen, beschuldigen, bezichtigen, entbinden, entheben, überführen, verdächtigen, berauben) follows a stricter pattern: the accusative is always a person, and the genitive is always a thing, and these verbs are frequently used in the passive: 'Der Mann wurde des Mordes angeklagt.' Both groups belong to elevated, formal written German. Some adjectives behave similarly with a genitive complement (Er ist sich seiner Sache sicher). In everyday modern German, several of these verbs are increasingly replaced with a preposition instead of the genitive (sich schämen für rather than sich schämen + genitive).

rules.rule: Nominative + Genitiv only (formal): sich annehmen, sich bedienen, bedürfen, sich bemächtigen, sich enthalten, sich erbarmen, sich erfreuen, gedenken, sich rühmen, sich schämen.
rules.note: Die Sache bedarf der Klärung.

rules.rule: Nominative + Akkusativ + Genitiv (accusative always a person, genitive always a thing; often passive): anklagen, beschuldigen, bezichtigen, entbinden, entheben, überführen, verdächtigen, berauben.
rules.note: Man verdächtigte ihn des Mordes. / Der Mann wurde des Mordes angeklagt.

rules.rule: In modern spoken German, some of these verbs are replaced by a preposition instead of the genitive.
rules.note: Er schämt sich für seine Tat. (rather than seiner Tat)

examples.de: Jeder Mensch bedarf eines Freundes.
examples.en: Every person needs a friend.

examples.de: Der Angeklagte ist des Delikts überführt.
examples.en: The accused has been proven guilty of the offense.

commonMistakes.wrong: Man verdächtigte ihn den Mord.
commonMistakes.why: verdächtigen takes accusative for the person and genitive for the thing — den Mord is the wrong case entirely for this verb's second object.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: When a subordinate clause contains a modal, a second verb, and the conjugated auxiliary, the conjugated verb moves before both infinitives
explanation: Ordinarily, a subordinate clause pushes its conjugated verb all the way to the end. But when the clause contains three verb elements at once — typically a double infinitive (modal + verb) plus the conjugated helper verb that governs them — the strict 'verb at the very end' rule bends: the conjugated verb moves to sit before both infinitives instead of after them. 'Ich bin nicht gekommen, weil ich arbeiten habe müssen' is not used; instead, the correct order is 'weil ich habe arbeiten müssen', with habe placed before the double infinitive arbeiten müssen.

rules.rule: In a subordinate clause with three verb elements (double infinitive + conjugated auxiliary), the conjugated verb moves before both infinitives, not after them.
rules.note: ..., weil ich habe arbeiten müssen. (not: weil ich arbeiten müssen habe.)

examples.de: Ich bin nicht gekommen, weil ich habe arbeiten müssen.
examples.en: I didn't come because I had to work.

examples.de: Sie war müde, weil sie hat einkaufen gehen müssen.
examples.en: She was tired because she'd had to go shopping.

commonMistakes.wrong: ..., weil ich arbeiten müssen habe.
commonMistakes.why: With three verb elements in a subordinate clause, the conjugated auxiliary moves ahead of the double infinitive rather than following the usual strict verb-final rule.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: werden + perfect infinitive (participle + sein/haben) expresses an assumption about the past, or a completed future event
explanation: Futur 2 is built with werden plus a 'perfect infinitive' — the past participle plus sein or haben, itself in infinitive form, at the very end of the clause. It expresses two related ideas: an assumption looking back at the past (matching the same function werden already has for the present via Futur 1, but shifted one step earlier in time), or a future event framed as already completed relative to some other point ('Wenn die Präsidentin ihre Rede beendet haben wird, wird die Diskussion beginnen' — the speech-ending is framed as finished before the discussion starts). In practice, this second meaning is very often expressed more simply with the ordinary Perfekt plus a time expression instead of the full Futur 2 construction.

rules.rule: Futur 2 = werden + past participle + sein/haben (as an infinitive, at the end).
rules.note: Du wirst wohl gestern spät ins Bett gekommen sein.

rules.rule: Meaning: an assumption about the past, or a future event framed as already completed at some reference point.
rules.note: Wenn sie die Rede beendet haben wird, wird die Diskussion beginnen.

rules.rule: In practice, Perfekt + a time expression often replaces the full Futur 2 construction for the 'completed future' meaning.
rules.note: Wenn sie die Rede heute Abend beendet hat, beginnt die Diskussion.

examples.de: Er wird wohl seinen Zug verpasst haben.
examples.en: He probably missed his train.

examples.de: Bis morgen werden wir die Arbeit beendet haben.
examples.en: By tomorrow we'll have finished the work.

commonMistakes.wrong: Er wird wohl seinen Zug verpassen haben. (using the plain infinitive instead of the perfect infinitive)
commonMistakes.right: Er wird wohl seinen Zug verpasst haben.
commonMistakes.why: Futur 2 specifically needs the perfect infinitive (participle + sein/haben), not the plain infinitive, to express a look back at a completed event.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

topic: Überblick über die Zeiten im Deutschen
summary: A consolidating map of all six tenses (Plusquamperfekt to Futur 2) across active, passive, and both Konjunktivs
explanation: This unit is a comprehensive review table placing every German tense side by side: Plusquamperfekt (vorvergangenheit, used for what had already happened before another past event), Präteritum (used for longer narratives, literature, news, and always for modal/helper verbs), and Perfekt (the default for speech, emails, and brief messages) form the past-tense trio; Präsens, Futur 1, and Futur 2 extend into the present and future. Each of these six has a corresponding passive form (all using werden/wurde/ist...worden and their extensions), a Konjunktiv 2 form (collapsing into the single past form already established), and a Konjunktiv 1 form (used for reported speech). Seeing all of these together clarifies that German's tense system, though it looks complex piece by piece, is built from a small number of consistently-reused components: a helper verb (sein/haben/werden), a participle, and an infinitive, recombined in different orders and combinations.

rules.rule: The core past-tense trio: Plusquamperfekt (vorvergangenheit), Präteritum (narrative/literary, and always for modals/helper verbs), Perfekt (default for speech/writing).
rules.note: See B1 Units 49-50 and B2 Unit 38 for detailed usage rules.

rules.rule: Every tense has a passive counterpart (via werden/wurde/worden) and both Konjunktiv forms — all built from the same recurring components (helper verb, participle, infinitive) recombined differently.
rules.note: This is a structural map, not new grammar — see the corresponding individual units for each combination.

examples.de: Ich hatte gelacht. Ich lachte. Ich habe gelacht.
examples.en: I had laughed. I laughed. I have laughed. (Plusquamperfekt, Präteritum, Perfekt)

examples.de: Ich bin operiert worden. Ich war operiert worden.
examples.en: I was operated on. I had been operated on. (Perfekt and Plusquamperfekt, passive)

commonMistakes.wrong: Treating each tense as an unrelated form to memorize separately
commonMistakes.right: Recognize that all forms recombine the same small set of pieces — sein/haben/werden, a participle, and an infinitive — in predictable patterns.
commonMistakes.why: Seeing the shared structure across tenses makes the whole system far easier to produce correctly than memorizing each combination in isolation.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

topic: Vermutungen über die Vergangenheit mit Modalverben
summary: müssen/dürfen/können express the same certainty scale about the past, using modal + perfect infinitive
explanation: Just as werden extends into Futur 2 to express an assumption about the past (Unit 39), the modal verbs müssen, dürfen, and können extend the present-tense certainty scale from Unit 42 into the past using the same structure: the modal (in present tense or Konjunktiv 2) plus a perfect infinitive (participle + sein/haben, itself as an infinitive) at the end. The certainty percentages carry over unchanged: muss = ~99%, müsste = ~85%, dürfte = ~75%, kann/könnte/mag = ~30-50%. 'Sie muss wohl zu Fuß gegangen sein' expresses near-certainty about a past event, mirroring 'Sie muss gleich da sein' for the present. This also extends to the passive: 'Der Aufzug dürfte noch nicht reparoert worden sein' — though passive assumptions about the present specifically require an added time expression to sound natural, while passive assumptions about the past do not.

rules.rule: Modal (present or Konjunktiv 2) + perfect infinitive (participle + sein/haben as infinitive) = assumption about the past, same certainty scale as the present-tense version.
rules.note: Sie muss wohl zu Fuß gegangen sein. (= sie ist bestimmt zu Fuß gegangen)

rules.rule: Extends to the passive: modal + participle + worden + sein.
rules.note: Der Aufzug dürfte noch nicht reparoert worden sein.

rules.rule: Passive assumptions about the present need an added time expression; passive assumptions about the past do not.
rules.note: Er dürfte gerade operiert werden. (needs 'gerade') vs. Er dürfte operiert worden sein. (no time word needed)

examples.de: Sie muss wohl zu Fuß die Treppe hochgekommen sein.
examples.en: She must have walked up the stairs.

examples.de: Sie könnte Lust gehabt haben, Sport zu treiben.
examples.en: She might have felt like exercising.

commonMistakes.wrong: Sie muss wohl zu Fuß gegangen. (dropping sein from the perfect infinitive)
commonMistakes.right: Sie muss wohl zu Fuß gegangen sein.
commonMistakes.why: The perfect infinitive requires sein or haben as an infinitive at the very end, alongside the participle — it can't be dropped.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: be-, ent-, er-, ver-, zer- each carry a distinct meaning pattern, though exceptions exist
explanation: The always-inseparable prefixes (be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, miss-, ver-, zer-) mostly have no independent word meaning, but several of the most productive ones do follow recognizable patterns. be- often makes a verb transitive (giving it an accusative object) without adding much independent meaning of its own — 'Ich steige auf den Berg' (intransitive, with a preposition) becomes 'Ich besteige den Berg' (transitive, direct object), with the core meaning barely changed. ent- often means 'taking something away' (entdecken can mean uncovering/removing a cover, though its everyday sense is 'to discover'). er- often means 'reaching an end point or goal' (erreichen), or combines with an adjective to mean 'making something that way' (erschweren = to make more difficult, from schwer + machen). ver- often signals 'doing something wrongly' — frequently with reflexive verbs (sich verschreiben = to make a writing mistake) — or 'reaching an end state' (verdursten = to die of thirst), or combines with an adjective to mean 'making something that way' (verschönern = to make more beautiful). zer- generally means breaking into pieces or destruction (zerreißen = to tear apart).

rules.rule: be- often makes a verb transitive with little independent meaning change.
rules.note: auf den Berg steigen → den Berg besteigen

rules.rule: ent- often means removal. er- often means reaching an endpoint/goal, or 'making + adjective'.
rules.note: entdecken (uncover); erreichen (reach); erschweren (make harder)

rules.rule: ver- often means doing something wrongly (frequently reflexive), reaching an end state, or 'making + adjective'. zer- generally means breaking apart/destruction.
rules.note: sich verschreiben (make a writing error); verdursten (die of thirst); verschönern (make prettier); zerreißen (tear apart)

examples.de: Er hat sich in der Prüfung verschrieben.
examples.en: He made a slip of the pen in the exam.

examples.de: Wir haben unsere Wohnung verschönert.
examples.en: We've made our apartment prettier.

examples.de: Er hat vor Wut den Brief zerrissen.
examples.en: He tore up the letter in anger.

commonMistakes.wrong: Treating all these prefix meanings as absolute rules with no exceptions
commonMistakes.right: Use these as memory aids for the majority pattern, but expect individual verbs to sometimes diverge from the general meaning.
commonMistakes.why: These prefixes carry loose semantic tendencies, not strict rules — some verbs built with them don't fit the general pattern cleanly.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

topic: Trennbare und untrennbare Verben 2: um-, unter-, über-, wieder-, durch-
summary: Five prefixes can be either separable or inseparable — stress marks the difference, and meaning usually follows a concrete-vs-metaphorical pattern
explanation: Five prefixes — um-, unter-, über-, wieder-, and durch- — are sometimes separable and sometimes inseparable, and the surest test is stress: stress on the prefix itself means separable, stress on the syllable after the prefix means inseparable. For um- specifically, the meaning follows a clear split: separable when it describes a change of location, state, or direction ('die Mülltonne umfahren' = to knock the trash bin over while driving), inseparable when it describes a circular movement around something ('den Baum umfahren' = to drive around the tree without hitting it). For unter-, über-, wieder-, and durch-, a broader tendency holds: the concrete, literal meaning is usually separable ('die Suppe kocht über' = the soup boils over), while the metaphorical, figurative meaning is usually inseparable ('Er unterstellt mir eine Lüge' = he's insinuating I'm lying). One further detail for verbs with two prefixes stacked together: if the first prefix is inseparable, zu goes before the whole verb and no ge- appears in the participle ('die Pflicht, die Klasse zu beaufsichtigen', 'ich habe beaufsichtigt'); if the first prefix is separable and the second inseparable, zu is inserted between the two prefixes ('das Abonnement abzubestellen', 'ich habe abbestellt').

rules.rule: Stress on the prefix = separable; stress after the prefix = inseparable, for the five variable prefixes um-/unter-/über-/wieder-/durch-.
rules.note: UMfahren (separable, knock over) vs. umFAHren (inseparable, drive around)

rules.rule: um- specifically: separable = change of location/state/direction; inseparable = circular movement around something.
rules.note: die Mülltonne umfahren (separable) vs. den Baum umfahren (inseparable)

rules.rule: unter-/über-/wieder-/durch- generally: concrete/literal meaning often separable; metaphorical/figurative meaning often inseparable.
rules.note: die Suppe kocht über (separable, literal) vs. Er unterstellt mir eine Lüge (inseparable, figurative)

rules.rule: Stacked prefixes: first prefix inseparable → zu before the whole verb, no ge-. First separable, second inseparable → zu inserted between them.
rules.note: zu beaufsichtigen, beaufsichtigt / abzubestellen, abbestellt

examples.de: Ich fahre fast jeden Tag die Mülltonne um.
examples.en: I knock the trash bin over almost every day.

examples.de: Ich umfahre den Baum vorsichtig.
examples.en: I carefully drive around the tree.

examples.de: Bitte unterschreiben Sie hier.
examples.en: Please sign here.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich fahre den Baum um. (meaning to drive carefully around it)
commonMistakes.why: Separable umfahren means knocking something over; the circular, avoiding-it sense requires the inseparable form, umfahren, stressed on the second syllable.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

topic: Genitiv: derer und Genitivrelativpronomen ohne Nomen
summary: derer as an alternative to deren when standing alone, and genitive relative pronouns governed by genitive verbs or prepositions with no following noun
explanation: When a genitive relative pronoun doesn't stand directly before a noun (unlike the possessive use in Unit 71's main content), an alternative form, derer, can replace deren in the feminine and plural — this happens specifically when the pronoun's genitive role comes from a genitive-governing verb (like bedürfen, Unit 32) or a genitive-governing preposition (like infolge) rather than from showing possession of a following noun. 'Die Vorbereitungen, derer/deren dieses Projekt bedarf, brauchen noch Zeit' and 'Sie waren genervt von den Streitigkeiten, infolge derer/deren die Arbeit stockte' both work, with derer being the more traditional choice in this specific 'no following noun' context.

rules.rule: derer can replace deren (feminine/plural) specifically when the genitive relative pronoun has no following noun, governed instead by a genitive verb or preposition.
rules.note: die Vorbereitungen, derer/deren dieses Projekt bedarf, ...

rules.rule: This differs from the possessive genitive use (dessen/deren + noun with no article), where derer is not used.
rules.note: Compare: die Frau, deren Hund... (possessive, deren only, no derer alternative here)

examples.de: Die Streitigkeiten, infolge derer die Arbeit stockte, waren unnötig.
examples.en: The disputes, as a result of which the work stalled, were unnecessary.

commonMistakes.wrong: die Frau, derer Hund bellt (using derer with a following noun)
commonMistakes.why: derer is only an alternative when the genitive relative pronoun has no following noun; the possessive use before a noun always uses deren/dessen.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

topic: Folgepronomen für Indefinitpronomen (man, jeder, jemand, niemand, alle)
summary: Each indefinite pronoun for people has its own matching follow-up pronoun and possessive when the sentence continues to refer to the same person(s)
explanation: When a sentence continues past man, jeder/jede, jemand, niemand, or alle and needs to refer back to the same person(s) again, a specific matching pronoun and possessive article is used for each, rather than defaulting to one generic choice. man is followed by man itself, or sein as the possessive. jeder/jede is followed by er/sie, with sein/ihr as the possessive. jemand is followed by er, with sein as the possessive. niemand is followed by er, with sein as the possessive. alle is followed by sie, with ihr as the possessive — since alle is grammatically plural (Unit 53's main B2 content), its follow-up pronoun is plural too, unlike the other four, which are all grammatically singular.

rules.rule: man → man / sein. jeder/jede → er/sie / sein/ihr. jemand → er / sein. niemand → er / sein. alle → sie / ihr (plural, since alle itself is grammatically plural).
rules.note: Man sollte sein Auto stehen lassen, wenn man betrunken ist. / Alle sind froh, wenn sie sicher ankommen und ihren Führerschein nicht verlieren.

examples.de: Jeder sollte sein Auto stehen lassen, wenn er betrunken ist.
examples.en: Everyone should leave their car parked if they're drunk.

examples.de: Wenn die Polizei jemanden kontrolliert, der betrunken Auto fährt, verliert er seinen Führerschein.
examples.en: If the police check someone who's driving drunk, he loses his license.

commonMistakes.wrong: Alle sind froh, wenn man sicher ankommt. (mixing man into an alle-continuation)
commonMistakes.right: Alle sind froh, wenn sie sicher ankommen.
commonMistakes.why: Once alle has been introduced, the continuing reference should use sie (plural), matching alle's own grammatical number, not the generic singular man.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: A wider set of 'Artikelwörter' (dieser, jener, mancher, solcher, was für ein, irgendein, and plural-only words) all trigger the same adjective-ending patterns as der/ein
explanation: Beyond der/die/das and ein, a broader category of words function as articles and trigger the same adjective declension patterns. Definite-type Artikelwörter, usable in singular and plural, include dieser, jeder (plural: alle), jener, welcher, mancher, and solcher — after any of these, adjectives decline exactly as they would after the definite article. A further group is usable only in the plural: beide, die beiden, alle, sämtliche. Indefinite-type Artikelwörter, usable in singular and plural, include was für ein and irgendein — after these, adjectives decline as they would after ein. A further group is usable only in the plural: wenige, einige, mehrere, etliche, viele, and lauter — after these (except lauter, which never takes any ending itself and doesn't change the adjective's ending pattern either) adjectives decline like they would after kein. Numbers themselves never affect adjective endings. When two Artikelwörter stack together before the same noun, the second one (positioned right next to the adjective) determines the adjective's ending — but if einige, viele, or mehrere combine with another Artikelwort, they behave like ordinary adjectives themselves rather than true articles.

rules.rule: Definite-type (singular+plural): dieser, jeder (plural alle), jener, welcher, mancher, solcher — decline the following adjective like after der.
rules.note: Dieses kleine Kind isst Schokolade.

rules.rule: Plural-only definite-type: beide, die beiden, alle, sämtliche. Plural-only indefinite-type: wenige, einige, mehrere, etliche, viele (decline the adjective like after kein), lauter (no ending at all, doesn't affect the adjective's pattern).
rules.note: Viele kleine Kinder mögen Schokolade. / Lauter kleine Kinder.

rules.rule: Numbers don't affect adjective endings. When two Artikelwörter combine, the second (nearest the adjective) decides the ending; einige/viele/mehrere combined with another Artikelwort act like adjectives themselves.
rules.note: (drei) schwarze Katzen; viele unserer Freunde = viele von unseren Freunden

examples.de: Manches kleine Kind mag keine Schokolade.
examples.en: Some small child doesn't like chocolate.

examples.de: Irgendein kleines Kind hat das gemacht.
examples.en: Some child or other did that.

examples.de: Mehrere kleine Kinder haben mitgemacht.
examples.en: Several small children took part.

commonMistakes.wrong: lauter kleines Kind (declining lauter as if it were a normal article)
commonMistakes.why: lauter is an exception: it never takes an ending itself and always appears with a plural noun, and adjectives after it take the standard plural form rather than following any special pattern.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

topic: Wiedergabe von Aufforderungen, Gerüchten und Selbstaussagen
summary: Reported commands use a modal in Konjunktiv, chosen by politeness/urgency; sollen reports a rumor; wollen reports someone's claim about themselves, with implied doubt
explanation: Reporting an imperative in indirect speech always uses a modal verb in the Konjunktiv, and which modal is chosen depends on how polite or urgent the original command was: mögen reports a polite request ('Er bat sie, sie möge bitte kommen'); sollen reports a general instruction or request ('Sie sagte ihm, er solle sie in Ruhe lassen' — sollen can also stay in the plain indicative here); müssen, nicht dürfen, or nicht sollen report a firm order or prohibition ('Er schrie den Hund an, er dürfe nicht bellen und müsse endlich leise sein'). Separately, sollen + infinitive reports a rumor or secondhand claim, distancing the speaker from its truth ('Ich habe gelesen: Sänger X gibt keine Konzerte mehr' becomes 'Sänger X soll keine Konzerte mehr geben'). And wollen + infinitive reports someone's claim about themselves, again signaling the speaker's distance or skepticism toward that self-report ('Herr X sagt: Ich bin der Größte' becomes 'Herr X will der Größte sein').

rules.rule: Reported imperative: modal in Konjunktiv, chosen by politeness/urgency — mögen (polite request), sollen (instruction, or plain indicative), müssen/nicht dürfen/nicht sollen (order/prohibition).
rules.note: Er bat sie, sie möge kommen. / Sie sagte, er solle sie in Ruhe lassen.

rules.rule: sollen + infinitive reports a rumor (secondhand claim, distancing the speaker).
rules.note: Sänger X soll keine Konzerte mehr geben.

rules.rule: wollen + infinitive reports someone's claim about themselves, signaling the speaker's doubt.
rules.note: Herr X will der Größte sein.

examples.de: Die Lehrerin sagte, die Schüler sollten den Text lesen.
examples.en: The teacher said the students should read the text.

examples.de: Die Schauspielerin soll 10 kg abgenommen haben.
examples.en: The actress is said to have lost 10 kg.

examples.de: Herr Y will als Erster im Ziel gewesen sein.
examples.en: Mr. Y claims he was first to the finish line.

commonMistakes.wrong: Sänger X will keine Konzerte mehr geben. (using wollen for a rumor about someone else)
commonMistakes.right: Sänger X soll keine Konzerte mehr geben.
commonMistakes.why: sollen reports a rumor or secondhand claim about someone; wollen is reserved specifically for a person's claim about themselves.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: zumal adds a second, extra reason as an afterthought, and can't open the sentence
explanation: zumal introduces a reason that comes as an addition or afterthought to a reason already given — it's used to add extra supporting weight to a point already made, rather than to introduce the main reason itself. Like the 'weiterführende Nebensätze' family (clauses that build on a preceding statement rather than standing independently), a zumal-clause can only follow the statement it supports; it can never open the sentence. It often appears on its own, without an accompanying main clause immediately after it, especially when the whole sentence has already made its main point and the zumal-clause simply reinforces it.

rules.rule: zumal introduces a secondary, reinforcing reason (an afterthought), always following the statement it supports — never at the start of the sentence.
rules.note: ..., zumal auch die Ausbildung der Fahrer immer schlechter geworden ist.

examples.de: Das überrascht mich nicht, zumal der öffentliche Verkehr so schlecht finanziert wird.
examples.en: That doesn't surprise me, especially since public transport is so poorly funded.

commonMistakes.wrong: Zumal die Ausbildung schlechter geworden ist, überrascht mich das nicht. (fronting zumal)
commonMistakes.right: Das überrascht mich nicht, zumal die Ausbildung schlechter geworden ist.
commonMistakes.why: zumal belongs to the 'weiterführende' family of connectors, which build on a statement already made and can never open the sentence.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: weshalb/weswegen turn the whole preceding sentence into a reason for what follows; zu...als dass (+ Konjunktiv 2) states a negative consequence
explanation: weshalb and weswegen both work like the 'weiterführende Nebensätze' family: they take the entire preceding statement and turn it into the reason behind the clause that follows, and — like zumal — they can always be replaced by starting a fresh main clause with deshalb/deswegen/darum instead. A separate construction, zu + adjective in the main clause paired with als dass + Konjunktiv 2 in the subordinate clause, expresses a negative consequence — something that doesn't or can't happen because of how extreme the adjective's quality is: 'Ich war zu spät, als dass ich den Bus noch bekommen hätte' means the lateness was severe enough that catching the bus wasn't possible.

rules.rule: weshalb/weswegen turn a whole preceding statement into a reason for what follows; replaceable by deshalb/deswegen/darum as a fresh main clause.
rules.note: Ich war sehr spät, weshalb ich auch den Bus verpasst habe.

rules.rule: zu + adjective, ..., als dass + Konjunktiv 2 = a negative consequence (something that didn't/couldn't happen).
rules.note: Ich war zu spät, als dass ich den Bus noch bekommen hätte.

examples.de: Ich hatte kein Ladekabel dabei, weshalb ich mein Handy nicht laden konnte.
examples.en: I didn't have a charging cable, which is why I couldn't charge my phone.

examples.de: Er war zu müde, als dass er noch hätte fahren können.
examples.en: He was too tired to be able to drive anymore.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich war zu spät, als dass ich den Bus bekommen habe. (using indicative instead of Konjunktiv 2)
commonMistakes.right: Ich war zu spät, als dass ich den Bus bekommen hätte.
commonMistakes.why: The zu...als dass construction specifically requires Konjunktiv 2 to express that the outcome didn't happen.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

topic: Sofern, gesetzt den Fall, vorausgesetzt dass, und der uneingeleitete Konditionalsatz
summary: Formal conditional connectors, plus the verb-first conditional clause with no conjunction at all
explanation: Three more formal, mostly written-register connectors express a condition alongside wenn/falls: sofern, gesetzt den Fall dass, and vorausgesetzt dass — all roughly meaning 'provided that, on the condition that'. Separately, German can express a condition with no conjunction at all, simply by moving the verb to the very front of the clause — the same word order used for yes/no questions, but functioning here as a conditional clause instead: 'Komme ich heute nicht mehr, rufe ich dich an' means the same as 'Wenn ich heute nicht mehr komme, rufe ich dich an.' This uneingeleitete Konditionalsatz often uses sollte to soften the condition, and it's rarely used in casual spoken German, belonging more to written or formal registers.

rules.rule: sofern, gesetzt den Fall (dass), vorausgesetzt dass = formal synonyms for wenn/falls.
rules.note: Sofern ich Zeit habe, komme ich.

rules.rule: Uneingeleiteter Konditionalsatz: verb moves to the very front, no conjunction at all — same word order as a yes/no question, but meaning 'if...'. Often uses sollte; rare in casual speech.
rules.note: Sollte ich Zeit haben, komme ich noch heute.

examples.de: Vorausgesetzt, dass das Wetter mitspielt, machen wir einen Ausflug.
examples.en: Provided the weather cooperates, we'll go on an outing.

examples.de: Komme ich heute nicht mehr, rufe ich dich morgen an.
examples.en: If I don't come today, I'll call you tomorrow.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich komme heute nicht mehr, rufe ich dich an. (keeping the subject-first order while intending a conditional meaning)
commonMistakes.right: Komme ich heute nicht mehr, rufe ich dich an.
commonMistakes.why: The uneingeleiteter Konditionalsatz specifically requires the verb to lead, with no subject or conjunction before it — subject-first order here would just read as two separate statements.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: wodurch turns the preceding sentence into the means/method behind what follows, replaceable with dadurch
explanation: wodurch belongs to the 'weiterführende Nebensätze' family: it takes the entire content of the preceding sentence and turns it into the method or means by which the following action happens, and it can always be reworded as a fresh main clause starting with dadurch. Like dadurch dass (B2), wodurch can sometimes carry a causal rather than purely methodical sense depending on context.

rules.rule: wodurch = takes the preceding statement as the means/method for what follows; replaceable by dadurch as a fresh main clause.
rules.note: Ich drehte an dem Griff, wodurch sich der Motorraum öffnete. = ...Dadurch öffnete sich der Motorraum.

examples.de: Er hat viel gelernt, wodurch er die Prüfung bestanden hat.
examples.en: He studied a lot, which is how he passed the exam.

commonMistakes.wrong: Wodurch er viel gelernt hat, hat er die Prüfung bestanden. (fronting wodurch)
commonMistakes.right: Er hat viel gelernt, wodurch er die Prüfung bestanden hat.
commonMistakes.why: Like other 'weiterführende' connectors, wodurch builds on a statement already made and cannot open the sentence.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: Modals, lassen, hören, sehen use a double infinitive in the Perfekt; bleiben, gehen, lernen use a normal ge-participle instead
explanation: The verbs that take a bare infinitive without zu (modals, lassen, hören, sehen, gehen, bleiben, lernen — B1 Unit 69) split into two groups when it comes to forming the Perfekt. Modal verbs, lassen, hören, and sehen use a double infinitive: the main verb's infinitive followed by the modal/lassen/hören/sehen's own infinitive, both staying uninflected. bleiben, gehen, and lernen, by contrast, take an entirely ordinary ge-...-t/ge-...-en participle in the Perfekt, with no double infinitive at all: 'Ich bin drei Stunden sitzen geblieben', 'Wir sind essen gegangen', 'Ich habe nie singen gelernt.'

rules.rule: Double infinitive in the Perfekt: modal verbs, lassen, hören, sehen.
rules.note: Ich habe das Auto stehen lassen. Ich habe den Star singen hören.
