rules.rule: Ordinary ge-participle in the Perfekt (no double infinitive): bleiben, gehen, lernen.
rules.note: Ich bin sitzen geblieben. Wir sind essen gegangen. Ich habe singen gelernt.

examples.de: Ich bin drei Stunden in der Oper sitzen geblieben.
examples.en: I stayed sitting in the opera for three hours.

examples.de: Wir sind nach der Oper essen gegangen.
examples.en: We went out to eat after the opera.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ich bin sitzen bleiben. (using the double-infinitive pattern for bleiben)
commonMistakes.why: bleiben (along with gehen and lernen) forms an ordinary ge-participle in the Perfekt, unlike modals/lassen/hören/sehen, which use the double infinitive.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

topic: Infinitivsatz wenn Subjekt = Objekt des Nebensatzes
summary: A zu-infinitive clause is also possible when the main clause's object is the implied subject of the infinitive action
explanation: The usual rule for zu-infinitive clauses is that the main clause's subject is also the implied subject of the infinitive (Unit 68's core B2 content). But a zu-infinitive clause is also possible in one further case: when the main clause's object — not its subject — is the one implied to perform the infinitive's action. 'Er bat sie, ihn anzurufen' means 'he asked her to call him' — the object 'sie' is who does the calling, matching the object of the main verb bat (bitten + accusative person). This works because the infinitive clause's implied subject lines up with an object already present in the main clause, rather than needing its own separate subject.

rules.rule: A zu-infinitive clause is also possible when the main clause's object is the implied subject of the infinitive action.
rules.note: Er bat sie, ihn anzurufen. (sie = the implied subject of anzurufen)

examples.de: Sie überredete ihn, mitzukommen.
examples.en: She persuaded him to come along.

examples.de: Der Lehrer forderte die Schüler auf, ruhig zu sein.
examples.en: The teacher asked the students to be quiet.

commonMistakes.wrong: Er bat sie, dass er sie anruft. (defaulting to a dass-clause when a zu-infinitive would work cleanly)
commonMistakes.why: Since the main clause's object (sie) matches the implied subject of the infinitive action, a zu-infinitive clause works naturally here without needing a full dass-clause.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: Reinforcing that the genitive relative pronoun's own form never changes to match the case of the noun/adjective that follows it
explanation: This unit reinforces a subtle point about the genitive relative pronoun (dessen/deren) worth stating clearly on its own: dessen and deren never change form based on the case of the noun that follows them — that noun's case is entirely independent, governed by its own role (via a verb or preposition) inside the relative clause. This sometimes creates sentences where dessen/deren sits right next to a noun in a completely different case from what a learner might expect, since there's no case-agreement between the two.

rules.rule: dessen/deren never change form to agree with the case of the following noun/adjective — that noun's case comes purely from its own grammatical role in the clause.
rules.note: Die Frau, für deren Kinder ich einkaufe, ... (deren stays deren regardless of Kinder being accusative here)

examples.de: Der Sportler, dessen Erfolge alle bewundern, trainiert hart.
examples.en: The athlete whose successes everyone admires trains hard.

commonMistakes.wrong: Die Frau, für derer Kinder ich einkaufe. (attempting to inflect the genitive pronoun to match an accusative noun)
commonMistakes.right: Die Frau, für deren Kinder ich einkaufe.
commonMistakes.why: dessen/deren stay fixed regardless of the case the following noun needs — there's no agreement between them.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: wer...der / wem...dessen / wessen...dessen make a general statement about a type of person; was...das does the same for things
explanation: A distinctive construction makes a general, universal statement about any person fitting a description, using two linked clauses. The first clause is a relative clause beginning with wer, wen, wem, or wessen (its case depending on its own role inside that clause); the second clause is the main clause, beginning with a matching demonstrative pronoun — der, den, dem, dessen (again, its own case depending on its role in the main clause). 'Wer im Schlaraffenland lebt, dem geht es gut' means 'anyone who lives in the land of plenty is doing well' — a generalization covering every person of that type, not one specific individual. If the case in the main clause happens to match the case in the relative clause, the demonstrative pronoun can often simply be dropped. The same pattern extends to things using was...(das).

rules.rule: wer/wen/wem/wessen (relative clause, generalizing about people) + der/den/dem/dessen (main clause, matching demonstrative) — each pronoun's case set independently by its own clause.
rules.note: Wer im Schlaraffenland lebt, dem geht es gut.

rules.rule: If the case matches in both clauses, the demonstrative pronoun can often be dropped.
rules.note: Wer im Schlaraffenland lebt, (der) muss nicht arbeiten.

rules.rule: The same pattern extends to things with was...(das).
rules.note: Was dir gut schmeckt, (das) solltest du genießen.

examples.de: Wer viel arbeitet, dem bleibt wenig Freizeit.
examples.en: Whoever works a lot has little free time left.

examples.de: Was dir gut schmeckt, solltest du genießen.
examples.en: Whatever tastes good to you, you should enjoy.

commonMistakes.wrong: Wer viel arbeitet, er hat wenig Freizeit. (using a personal pronoun instead of a demonstrative)
commonMistakes.right: Wer viel arbeitet, dem bleibt wenig Freizeit.
commonMistakes.why: This generalizing construction requires a demonstrative pronoun (der/dem/den/dessen) in the main clause, not an ordinary personal pronoun.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: nicht nur...sondern auch needs its own subject+verb after sondern if the second clause has a different structure; je...desto can include an article-noun phrase
explanation: Two structural refinements apply to the double connectors already covered. With nicht nur...sondern auch, if the part after sondern needs its own subject and conjugated verb (rather than just continuing the same verb from before nicht nur), that subject and verb are placed directly between sondern and auch: 'Sie ist nicht nur sehr schön, sondern sie arbeitet auch viel.' With je...desto/umso, when a noun with an article is involved, that article goes before je or desto/umso, and the comparative adjective still attaches directly to the noun: 'Ein je schnelleres Auto man fährt, ein desto vorsichtigerer Fahrer muss man sein.'

rules.rule: nicht nur...sondern auch: if the second part needs its own subject+verb, they go between sondern and auch.
rules.note: Sie ist nicht nur schön, sondern sie arbeitet auch viel.

rules.rule: je...desto/umso with an article-noun phrase: the article precedes je/desto/umso, with the comparative adjective still attached to the noun.
rules.note: Ein je schnelleres Auto man fährt, ein desto vorsichtigerer Fahrer muss man sein.

examples.de: Das Internet ist nicht nur ein gutes Informationsmedium, sondern es ist auch eine Kommunikationsplattform.
examples.en: The internet isn't just a good information medium, it's also a communication platform.

commonMistakes.wrong: Sie ist nicht nur schön, sondern auch sie arbeitet viel. (placing the subject after auch)
commonMistakes.right: Sie ist nicht nur schön, sondern sie arbeitet auch viel.
commonMistakes.why: When the second clause needs its own subject, it goes right after sondern and before auch, not after auch.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

topic: Funktionsverbgefüge 2: Bedeutungen und Beziehung zum einfachen Verb
summary: Funktionsverbgefüge express three 'voices' (active, passive-process, passive-state) and relate to simple verbs in several distinct ways
explanation: In a Funktionsverbgefüge, the verb has almost entirely lost its original meaning, existing mainly to support the noun that carries the real content. These verbs sort into three groups by the perspective they express. Active-voice verbs describe someone actively causing a state: versetzen, bringen, stellen, setzen, ziehen, schenken, treten (in Aufregung versetzen = to upset someone). Passive-process verbs describe undergoing a change into a state: geraten, kommen, finden, gelangen (in Aufregung geraten = to become upset — geraten specifically adds a sense of 'against one's will'). Passive-state verbs describe simply being in a state: sein, sich befinden, genießen, stehen, bekommen, erhalten, erfahren (in Aufregung sein = to be upset). Comparing Funktionsverbgefüge to their related simple verbs reveals several different relationships: sometimes an exact simple-verb equivalent exists (eine Entscheidung treffen = entscheiden); sometimes a verb from the same word family exists but with a different meaning (eine Absage erteilen is not the same as absagen); sometimes the meaning is nearly identical but the two are used in different registers (Hilfe leisten, formal, vs. helfen, everyday — 'Bitte leiste mir bei dieser Aufgabe Hilfe' would sound wrong; only the simple verb helfen fits casual contexts); sometimes the grammar changes while the meaning stays close (eine Frage stellen, with an accusative object, vs. fragen, with a dative object: Ich stelle dir eine Frage vs. Ich frage dich); and sometimes no simple-verb equivalent exists at all (in Kraft treten, ein Geschäft abschließen, etwas zur Verfügung stellen). Funktionsverbgefüge also vary in flexibility: some are fully fixed and lexicalized, taking no article or adjective and negatable only with nicht (etwas in Kauf nehmen); others are more flexible and often combine with an adjective (eine gute/schlechte Entscheidung treffen).

rules.rule: Active voice: versetzen, bringen, stellen, setzen, ziehen, schenken, treten. Passive-process: geraten (implies against one's will), kommen, finden, gelangen. Passive-state: sein, sich befinden, genießen, stehen, bekommen, erhalten, erfahren.
rules.note: in Aufregung versetzen / geraten / sein

rules.rule: Relationship to simple verbs varies: exact equivalent, related-but-different word family, same meaning but different register, same meaning but different grammar, or no simple equivalent at all.
rules.note: eine Entscheidung treffen = entscheiden; Hilfe leisten (formal) vs. helfen (everyday); in Kraft treten (no equivalent)

rules.rule: Some Funktionsverbgefüge are fully fixed (no article/adjective, negatable only with nicht); others flexibly combine with an adjective.
rules.note: etwas in Kauf nehmen (fixed) vs. eine gute Entscheidung treffen (flexible)

examples.de: Der morgige Termin versetzt sie in Aufregung.
examples.en: Tomorrow's appointment is upsetting her.

examples.de: Sie gerät leicht in Aufregung.
examples.en: She gets upset easily.

examples.de: Das Geschäft ist heute abgeschlossen worden.
examples.en: The deal was closed today.

commonMistakes.wrong: Bitte leiste mir bei dieser Aufgabe Hilfe. (using the formal Funktionsverbgefüge in a casual request)
commonMistakes.right: Bitte hilf mir bei dieser Aufgabe.
commonMistakes.why: Hilfe leisten is formal register; in an everyday, casual request, the simple verb helfen is the natural choice instead.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: Converting a sentence into a dense noun phrase: a full mapping of sentence roles to noun-phrase equivalents
explanation: German can compress an entire sentence into a noun phrase, a technique called Nominalisierung, typical of formal writing like news articles, scientific texts, and bureaucratic documents, because it lets more information fit into a single sentence. Each sentence element has a corresponding noun-phrase form: the subject of an intransitive or reflexive verb (or any verb with no accusative object) becomes a genitive ('Der Arzt erscheint' → 'das Erscheinen des Arztes'); an accusative object also becomes a genitive ('Er verstand den Text' → 'das Verstehen des Textes'); when both a subject and an accusative object are present, the object becomes the genitive and the subject becomes a durch-phrase ('Der Arzt operiert den Patienten' → 'die Operation des Patienten durch den Arzt'); a prepositional object stays a prepositional object; a personal pronoun becomes a possessive article; an adverb becomes an adjective with an ending; negation or limitation words become either an adjective or a noun (nicht helfen → die fehlende Hilfe, or das Fehlen der Hilfe); von in a passive sentence becomes durch + accusative in the noun phrase; a subordinate-clause connector becomes a preposition; and a modal verb's meaning becomes a noun expressing that same idea (müssen → die Pflicht, können → die Möglichkeit). Because nominalized phrases compress so much information, they're sometimes genuinely ambiguous and can only be resolved by context — 'das Bild des Königs' could mean either a picture the king owns or a picture depicting the king.

rules.rule: Intransitive/reflexive subject (or any subject with no accusative object) → genitive. Accusative object → genitive. Both together → object becomes genitive, subject becomes durch-phrase.
rules.note: Der Arzt erscheint. → das Erscheinen des Arztes. / Der Arzt operiert den Patienten. → die Operation des Patienten durch den Arzt.

rules.rule: Prepositional object stays the same. Personal pronoun → possessive article. Adverb → adjective (with ending). Negation/limitation → adjective or noun.
rules.note: sich bemühen um → die Bemühungen um; unermüdlich helfen → seine unermüdliche Hilfe; nicht helfen → die fehlende Hilfe / das Fehlen der Hilfe

rules.rule: von in a passive sentence → durch + accusative. Subordinate connector → preposition. Modal verb → a noun expressing its meaning.
rules.note: vom Arzt operiert → die Operation durch den Arzt; weil... → wegen...; müssen → die Pflicht

examples.de: Die Freude des Patienten war groß.
examples.en: The patient's joy was great. (from: Der Patient freut sich.)

examples.de: Die Bemühungen um den Patienten waren erfolgreich.
examples.en: The efforts on behalf of the patient were successful. (from: Er bemühte sich um den Patienten.)

examples.de: Wegen des Erscheinens des Arztes konnte die Operation beginnen.
examples.en: Because of the doctor's arrival, the operation could begin.

commonMistakes.wrong: die Operation den Patienten durch den Arzt (leaving the object un-genitivized)
commonMistakes.right: die Operation des Patienten durch den Arzt
commonMistakes.why: When both a subject and accusative object nominalize together, the object becomes genitive and the subject becomes a durch-phrase — the object can't stay in its original accusative form.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: A noun can be specified by attributes before it (adjectives, participles) and after it (genitive, relative clauses, prepositional phrases, appositions...)
explanation: A noun (the Bezugswort) can be described more precisely by attributes placed both before it (Linksattribute) and after it (Rechtsattribute), and recognizing which noun a long chain of attributes belongs to is the key skill for reading dense, formal German. Linksattribute are typically adjectives, participles (Partizip I or the modal Partizip/Gerundiv), which can themselves be extended with preceding modifiers — numbers, reflexive pronouns, prepositional phrases, or adverbs — all placed before the adjective or participle itself: 'die zwei modernen, sich in einer Stunde automatisch von selbst reinigenden Öfen'. Rechtsattribute include a genitive ('des neuen Herdes'), a relative clause ('der gestern angeschlossen wurde'), a prepositional phrase ('mit dem tollen Grill'), an adverb ('dort'), an apposition ('ein modernes Gerät'), a zu-infinitive clause ('einen Ofen zu kaufen'), a dass-clause ('dass wir den Ofen kaufen'), or a comparison with als/wie ('als der Ofen'). A single noun can carry both types of attribute simultaneously, on either side.

rules.rule: Linksattribute (before the noun): adjectives, Partizip I, modal Partizip — themselves extendable with numbers, reflexive pronouns, prepositional phrases, adverbs, all placed before the adjective/participle.
rules.note: die zwei modernen, sich automatisch reinigenden Öfen

rules.rule: Rechtsattribute (after the noun): genitive, relative clause, prepositional phrase, adverb, apposition, zu-infinitive clause, dass-clause, or als/wie comparison.
rules.note: der Ofen des neuen Herdes, der gestern angeschlossen wurde

examples.de: Der moderne, sich von selbst reinigende Ofen des neuen Herdes funktioniert leider nicht.
examples.en: The modern, self-cleaning oven of the new stove unfortunately doesn't work.

examples.de: Die Entscheidung, einen Ofen zu kaufen, war richtig.
examples.en: The decision to buy an oven was right.

commonMistakes.wrong: Misreading a long Linksattribut chain and losing track of which noun it belongs to
commonMistakes.right: Scan to the end of the noun phrase first to identify the Bezugswort, then work back through the attributes describing it.
commonMistakes.why: Extended Linksattribute can stack several modifiers before the adjective, making the noun phrase long — identifying the final noun first makes the structure much easier to parse.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: Every temporal relationship can be expressed three ways: a preposition+noun, a subordinate-clause connector, or a main-clause adverb
explanation: This unit organizes every temporal relationship already learned into one three-column system, which is genuinely useful for varying your style and understanding formal texts. For two parallel activities: während (preposition + genitive), während (subordinate connector), or währenddessen/gleichzeitig (adverb). For a sequence, action 1 then action 2: nach (preposition + dative), nachdem (subordinate connector), or danach/nachher (adverb). For a sequence, action 2 stated before action 1: vor (preposition + dative), bevor (subordinate connector), or vorher/davor/zuvor (adverb). For the end of a phase: bis (preposition, only before an article-less noun; bis zu + dative when an article is present), bis (subordinate connector), or bis dann (adverb). For a beginning in the past that continues now: seit (preposition + dative), seit(dem) (subordinate connector), or seitdem (adverb). For a routine or repeated action: bei (preposition + dative), wenn (subordinate connector), or dabei/jedesmal (adverb). For a single past event: bei (preposition + dative), als (subordinate connector), or da (adverb). Each of these three forms carries the same core meaning but differs stylistically — nominal (prepositional) structures are typical of formal written texts, while connector and adverb structures are more typical of everyday speech and general writing.

rules.rule: Parallel activities: während (+genitive) / während (Nebensatz) / währenddessen, gleichzeitig (adverb).
rules.note: Während des Tanzens filmt mich mein Vater. / Während ich tanze, ... / Ich tanze, währenddessen filmt mich mein Vater.

rules.rule: Sequence 1→2: nach(+dativ)/nachdem/danach,nachher. Sequence 2 stated before 1: vor(+dativ)/bevor/vorher,davor,zuvor.
rules.note: Nach dem Tanzen bin ich müde. / Nachdem ich getanzt habe, ... / Ich tanze. Danach bin ich müde.

rules.rule: End of a phase: bis (no article)/bis zu (+dativ, with article) / bis / bis dann. Ongoing since the past: seit(+dativ)/seit(dem)/seitdem.
rules.note: Bis zum Auftritt bin ich nervös. / Seit dem Tanzen fühle ich mich wohl.

examples.de: Während des Essens hört er Musik.
examples.en: While eating, he listens to music. (prepositional)

examples.de: Während er isst, hört er Musik.
examples.en: While he eats, he listens to music. (subordinate clause)

examples.de: Er isst. Währenddessen hört er Musik.
examples.en: He eats. Meanwhile he listens to music. (adverb)

commonMistakes.wrong: Treating the three forms (preposition, connector, adverb) as fully interchangeable in any register
commonMistakes.right: Nominal/prepositional structures suit formal written texts; connector and adverb structures suit everyday speech and general writing — choose based on register, not just meaning.
commonMistakes.why: Although all three convey the same underlying relationship, they carry different stylistic weight, and using a heavily nominal structure in casual speech can sound stiff.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

topic: Präposition – Adverb – Konnektor 2 (kausal, konzessiv, konsekutiv, adversativ)
summary: The same three-way system for reason, concession, consequence, and contrast — including many synonym adverbs for 'therefore'
explanation: The same preposition/connector/adverb system covers four more relationships. For a reason (kausal): wegen or aufgrund (preposition + genitive), weil or da (subordinate connector), nämlich (adverb, never in position 1) or denn (a Hauptsatzkonnektor in position 0). For a concession (konzessiv, a counter-argument): trotz or ungeachtet (preposition + genitive), obwohl (subordinate connector), dennoch/trotzdem/allerdings (adverb) or aber (position 0); the zwar (position 1 or 3)...aber (position 0) pattern is another common way to express this. For a consequence (konsekutiv): infolge (preposition + genitive), weshalb/weswegen/sodass (subordinate connector), or a long list of adverb synonyms all meaning roughly 'therefore' — deshalb, deswegen, darum, daher, also, infolgedessen, folglich, aus diesem Grund, somit, demnach. For a contrast (adversativ): im Gegensatz zu (preposition + dative), während or wo(hin)gegen (subordinate connector), dagegen/demgegenüber/im Gegensatz dazu (adverb) or doch/aber (position 0).

rules.rule: Kausal: wegen/aufgrund (+genitiv) / weil, da / nämlich (adverb, never position 1), denn (position 0).
rules.note: Wegen ihres Talents hat sie Erfolg. / Sie hat Erfolg, weil sie talentiert ist. / Sie ist nämlich talentiert.

rules.rule: Konzessiv: trotz/ungeachtet (+genitiv) / obwohl / dennoch, trotzdem, allerdings (adverb), aber (position 0); also zwar...aber.
rules.note: Trotz des Regens gehen wir spazieren. / Obwohl es regnet, ... / Es regnet. Trotzdem gehen wir.

rules.rule: Konsekutiv: infolge (+genitiv) / weshalb, weswegen, sodass / many synonym adverbs meaning 'therefore' (deshalb, deswegen, darum, daher, also, infolgedessen, folglich, aus diesem Grund, somit, demnach). Adversativ: im Gegensatz zu (+dativ) / während, wo(hin)gegen / dagegen, demgegenüber, im Gegensatz dazu (adverb), doch/aber (position 0).
rules.note: Infolge des Streiks kamen viele zu spät. / Er ist reich; sie dagegen ist arm.

examples.de: Sie hat großen Erfolg, denn sie ist talentiert.
examples.en: She's very successful, because she's talented.

examples.de: Plastik zersetzt sich nicht, weshalb es in den Ozeanen große Mengen an Plastikmüll gibt.
examples.en: Plastic doesn't decompose, which is why there's so much plastic waste in the oceans.

examples.de: Sie ist reich, wohingegen er kaum Geld hat.
examples.en: She's rich, whereas he barely has any money.

commonMistakes.wrong: Nämlich sie ist talentiert. (fronting nämlich into position 1)
commonMistakes.why: nämlich can never occupy position 1 — it always sits later in the sentence, typically right after the verb or subject.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: The same three-way system for method, instrument, alternative, missing consequence, comparison, condition, and purpose
explanation: The remaining relationships complete this system. For method (Art und Weise): mit, mittels, or mithilfe (preposition + dative/genitive), indem (subordinate connector), or damit/dadurch/so/auf diese Weise (adverb). For instrument/means: durch (preposition + accusative), dadurch dass or wodurch (subordinate connector), or dadurch (adverb). For an alternative: (an)statt (preposition + genitive), (an)statt dass or (an)statt...zu (subordinate connector), or stattdessen (adverb). For a missing consequence: ohne (preposition + accusative), ohne dass or ohne...zu (subordinate connector). For a comparison: nach, gemäß, or entsprechend (preposition + dative), wie (subordinate connector), or (genau)so (adverb). For a condition (konditional): bei (preposition + dative) or im Falle (preposition + genitive), wenn/falls/sofern or an uneingeleiteter Konditionalsatz (subordinate connector), sonst/andernfalls (adverb) or vorausgesetzt, es sei denn (position 0). For a purpose (final): zu (preposition + dative), zwecks (preposition + genitive, only with verb-derived nouns), or für (preposition + accusative, only with verb-derived nouns); damit or um...zu (subordinate connector); dazu/dafür (adverb).

rules.rule: Method: mit/mittels/mithilfe (+dativ/genitiv) / indem / damit, dadurch, so, auf diese Weise. Instrument: durch (+akkusativ) / dadurch dass, wodurch / dadurch.
rules.note: Mit Geduld kann man das schaffen. / Indem man Geduld hat, ... / Man hat Geduld, dadurch schafft man das.

rules.rule: Alternative: (an)statt (+genitiv) / (an)statt dass, (an)statt...zu / stattdessen. Missing consequence: ohne (+akkusativ) / ohne dass, ohne...zu.
rules.note: Anstatt eines Autos kaufen wir Fahrräder. / Anstatt dass wir ein Auto kaufen, ...

rules.rule: Comparison: nach/gemäß/entsprechend (+dativ) / wie / (genau)so. Condition: bei (+dativ)/im Falle (+genitiv) / wenn, falls, sofern / sonst, andernfalls (adverb), vorausgesetzt, es sei denn (position 0). Purpose: zu (+dativ), zwecks/für (+genitiv/akkusativ, verb-derived nouns only) / damit, um...zu / dazu, dafür.
rules.note: Zwecks Gewichtsreduktion treibt er Sport. / Damit er abnimmt, treibt er Sport.

examples.de: Man kann eine Sprache lernen, indem man viel liest.
examples.en: You can learn a language by reading a lot.

examples.de: Bei guten Chancen werde ich weltberühmt.
examples.en: Given good odds, I'll become world-famous.

examples.de: Zwecks Gewichtsreduktion treibt er viel Sport.
examples.en: For the purpose of losing weight, he exercises a lot.

commonMistakes.wrong: zwecks des Sports (adding an article to a noun after zwecks)
commonMistakes.right: zwecks Sport / zwecks des Sporttreibens (if a genuine noun with article is needed, rephrase around a verb-derived noun)
commonMistakes.why: zwecks (like für in its final/purpose sense here) specifically pairs with a noun derived from a verb, and is typically used without an article.

bookReference: Grammatik aktiv B2-C1 (Cornelsen) - unit numbers preserved in ID where applicable (BK2C1-n)

summary: Recognizing (not necessarily producing) casual spoken-German features: contractions, dropped subjects, split question words, doubled da, and more
explanation: Casual spoken German diverges from the written standard in several recognizable ways, and the goal at this level is to understand these forms when you hear them, using them yourself only with caution since they vary by region and dialect. Prepositions often contract or slur together with the article that follows (vonner, beier, aufer, inner, inne, innen, aufs, übers, unters, vors, hinters, nebens) and full verb forms get shortened (stellstes for stellst du es; hab, hamse for habe, haben Sie/sie). Whole words get abbreviated or simplified (ma(l) for einmal; was for etwas; nix for nichts; nee for nein). The subject is often dropped entirely when it's already clear from context, so the sentence just starts with the conjugated verb ('Bin gerade erst angekommen' instead of 'Ich bin...'). Question words and adverbs get split apart just like separable verbs ('Wo fährst du hin?' instead of 'Wohin fährst du?'). The da(r)-pronoun sometimes gets doubled with a plain da for emphasis ('Da kommst du nicht drauf' instead of 'Darauf kommst du nicht'). For emphasis generally, a demonstrative pronoun in the same case can repeat the stressed sentence part ('Den Text, den habe ich nicht verstanden'), and with sein specifically, the general demonstrative das is always used this way regardless of the noun's actual gender ('Der Kuli, das ist mein Kuli'). A 'pointing' da can be added when the object being discussed can actually be pointed at, sometimes doubled with a following demonstrative pronoun too ('Die Übung da, die habe ich nicht verstanden'). weil and obwohl (normally subordinate-clause connectors) are sometimes used with ordinary main-clause word order in speech, often with a pause before the reason ('Ich komme nicht, weil: ich habe keine Lust'). A relative clause that comes after the main clause (rather than being embedded in the middle of it) is sometimes replaced entirely by a separate main clause with a demonstrative pronoun ('Ich kenne ein Management. Das hat Mist gebaut' instead of 'Ich kenne ein Management, das Mist gebaut hat'). And a separable verb's prefix is often not moved all the way to the end of the clause in speech, especially with certain prefixes ('Kommst du mit ins Kino?' instead of the fully separated written-standard form). All of these features vary by region and dialect; the recommendation is to learn to recognize and understand them, but use them only carefully and selectively yourself.

rules.rule: Phonetic contractions (vonner, beier, aufs, übers) and shortened verb forms (hab, hamse); shortened words (ma(l), was, nix, nee).
rules.note: Was issn das? (= Was ist denn das?)

rules.rule: Dropped subject when clear from context; question words/adverbs split like separable verbs; doubled da(r)-pronoun with plain da for emphasis.
rules.note: Bin gerade erst angekommen. / Wo fährst du hin? / Da kommst du nicht drauf.

rules.rule: Emphasis via a repeated demonstrative pronoun in the same case (das always with sein); weil/obwohl with main-clause word order (often with a pause); trailing relative clauses replaced by a separate main clause with a demonstrative; separable prefixes sometimes not moved to the very end.
rules.note: Den Text, den habe ich nicht verstanden. / Ich kenne ein Management. Das hat Mist gebaut.

examples.de: Fährst du mit dem Auto?
examples.en: Are you driving? (standard order kept here, but colloquial contractions common elsewhere)

examples.de: Der Kuli, das ist mein Kuli.
examples.en: The pen, that's my pen. (das used regardless of Kuli's gender)

examples.de: Kommst du mit ins Kino?
examples.en: Are you coming to the cinema? (mit not moved to the very end)

commonMistakes.wrong: Using these colloquial forms freely in formal writing or professional speech
commonMistakes.right: Reserve these forms for casual, informal spoken contexts; use the standard written forms in formal writing and professional registers.
commonMistakes.why: These features are recognizable markers of casual speech and can sound inappropriately informal or even careless in formal contexts.
